clause ( 2) of this clause provides that the salaries, allowances and
pensions payable to, and other terms and conditions of service of
the officers other employees of the Authority shall be such as may
be specified by the regulations.
Clause 18.—This clause provides for transfer of assets,
liabilities, etc., of the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board and saving of
its actions, etc. The said clause provides that the said Board shall
stand dissolved on establishment of the Nuclear Safety Regulatory
Authority and that all sums of money due to the Board immediately
before that date shall be deemed to be due to the Authority and that
all suits and other legal proceedings instituted or which could have
been instituted by or against the Board may be continued or may be
instituted by or against the Authority.
Sub-clause ( 2) of this clause provides that the Chairman and
Members of the Board shall be transferred as such to function as
Chairperson and Members under the Act and be deemed to be the
Chairperson and Members of the Authority under the Act until the
Chairperson and Members of the Authority are appointed in
accordance with the provisions of the Act.
Sub-clause ( 3) of this clause provides that every officer and
employee holding a post in Board shall hold the post in the Authority
by the same tenure and upon the same terms and conditions of
service including remuneration, leave, provident fund, retirement and
other terminal benefits as he would have held such post as if the
Act had not been passed and shall continue to do so as an officer
or employee of the Authority for a period of three years unless he
within three years opts not to be an employee of the Authority or
until his tenure, remuneration or other terms and conditions of
service are altered by the regulations.
Sub-clause ( 4) of this clause provides that every person who
opts not to be an employee of the Authority shall be governed by
the rules and orders as are applicable to the Central Government
officers and employees of equivalent rank. Sub-clause ( 5) of this
clause provides that the tenure, remuneration and other terms and
conditions of service including pension of any employee of the
Authority shall not be altered to his disadvantage without the
previous approval of the Central Government Sub-clause ( 6) of this
clause provides that after the dissolution of the Board such of the
functions and powers of Board as are vested in the Authority shall
be carried out by the Authority after such dissolution.
Clause 19.—This clause provides for jurisdiction of Authority.
The said clause provides that save as otherwise provided in sections
25 and 27, the jurisdiction of the Authority shall extend to all areas
to which this Act is applicable and activities relating to production,
development or use of atomic energy and radiation in all its
applications, or transport (within India or outside India), transfer by

53
sale or otherwise import, export or storage or disposal of nuclear
and radioactive material.
Clause 20.—This clause provides for functions of Authority. Sub-
section ( 1) of this clause provides that the Authority shall, subject
to the provisions of this Act and the rules and regulations made
thereunder, take measures, within its jurisdiction, to ensure that the
use of radiation and atomic energy is safe for the health of the
radiation workers, members of the public and the environment
Explanation to this sub-clause clarifies that the functions of the
Authority shall be confined only to ensure the radiation safety and
nuclear safety during activities relating to production, storage,
disposal, transport, transfer by sale or otherwise, import, export and
use of any nuclear material, radioactive material or any other
substance or equipment, and physical security of nuclear material,
radioactive material, and radiation and nuclear facilities and in no
case shall extend to the functions or any other matter which the
Central Government is required to discharge under the Atomic
Energy Act, 1962.
Sub-clause ( 2) of this clause provides that the Authority shall
also carry out other functions which inter alia includes ( a) devise
and implement policies and programmes for radiation safety and
nuclear safety to ensure that use of atomic energy or radiation in all
its applications is safe for the health of radiation workers and
members of public, and the environment; ( b) ensure high quality of
safety management at all places where nuclear and radiation related
activities are carried out; ( c) ensure transparency by systematic
public outreach on matters relating to nuclear safety without
disclosing sensitive information and compromising confidentiality of
commercially sensitive information of technology holders. Further, it
explains the expression “sensitive information” to mean information
pertaining to ( i) physical security of nuclear material and facilities,
or ( ii) reprocessing of spent fuel, enrichment of fissile material or
heavy water production technologies; ( iii) any information under
section 26 which has been accessed by the Authority or has come
to its knowledge or made available to it in the discharge of its
functions; ( d) strive to be a knowledge organisation with state of
the art scientific capabilities in the domain of its responsibilities,
arrange for and conduct research in areas relevant to its functions
and develop linkages with technical support organisations;
(e) interact with other bodies and international organisations engaged
in activities relevant to the functions of the Authority including
nuclear and radiation safety, physical security of nuclear material
and facilities, transportation of nuclear and radioactive materials and
nuclear and radiation safety and regulation. However, provided that
the Authority shall not interact with such bodies and international
organisations outside India without the prior approval of the Central
Government; ( f) advise the Central Government with respect to –
(i) safety of public and the environment; ( ii ) measurement
implement and co-ordinate a nationwide programme for
environmental surveillance to check any harmful build up of

54
radioactivity in the environment; (iii ) measures to ensure
establishment and maintenance of appropriate mechanisms and
plans for preparedness in response to nuclear and radiation
emergencies; ( g) notify the limits of radiation exposure to
radiation workers and the members of the public; ( h) specify by
regulations, the requisite qualification, the training required to the
persons for employment at premises or places where at any
activity relating to production, storage, disposal, transport and use
of any nuclear material, radioactive material or any other substance
or equipment used for production, or use of atomic energy is
carried out, and specify hours of work, minimum leave and
requirements of periodical medical examination of such employees;
(i) specify by regulations the requirement of approval to, or
licensing of, the persons referred to in clause ( h); (j) establish an
appropriate regulatory mechanism which shall provide for issue of
consents, monitoring of compliances, inspections and enforcement;
(k) develop and notify the standards and codes, and develop and
publish other supporting documents for safety in design, siting,
construction, commissioning, operation, quality assurance,
decommissioning, storage, transportation and other activities
related to plants, facilities, nuclear and radioactive wastes,
radiation sources and radioactive materials; ( l) issue, renew,
modify, suspend and revoke consents with specified conditions for
conduct of any activity which come under its jurisdiction for the
production, storage, disposal, transport (within and outside India),
transfer by sale or otherwise, import, export and use of any
nuclear material, radioactive material or any other substance, or
equipment used for production, or use of atomic energy; ( m) levy
fee, by regulation, for issue, modification and renewal of consents;
(n) take such measures as to enforce compliance of the provisions
of the Act by the holder of the consent; ( o) notify measures for
physical security within the area of main plant boundary, physical
protection of nuclear and radioactive materials under storage as
well as transport (within and outside India), and nuclear and
radiation facilities; ( p) engage with the consent of Head of
concerned bodies, the institutions, laboratories, agencies, technical
support organisations, industries, individual experts and
professionals of integrity and outstanding ability, who have
expertise in scientific, technical, sociological, legal and such other
disciplines related to nuclear, radiation and industrial safety to
assist the Authority in the discharge of its functions; ( q) discharge
its functions and powers in a manner consistent with the
international obligations of India; ( r) apprise, from time to time,
the National Disaster Management Authority established under
section 3 of the Disaster Management Act, 2005 regarding nuclear
safety and radiation safety measures and management of disaster
arising from nuclear incident notified under section 3 of the Civil
Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010 and coordinate with the
said Authority in the case of such disaster; ( s) notify nuclear
incident as required by section 3 of the Civil Liability for nuclear
Damage Act, 2010.

55
Sub-clause ( 3) of this clause provides that the Authority may,
for reasons to be recorded in writing, exempt, by notification,
subject to such conditions as may be specified by it in the
notification, any radioactive material, any class or classes of
radioactive material or any radiation generating plant from the
applicability of any of the provisions of the safety related regulations
or orders issued under this Act.
Clause 21.—This clause provides for Authority to Act in
interest of sovereignty and integrity of India. The said clause
provides that the Authority while discharging its powers and
functions, shall not act against the interest of the sovereignty and
integrity of India, the security of the State, friendly relations with
foreign States, public order, decency or morality.
Clause 22.—This clause provides for power of Authority to
give directions to owner of radioactive material, etc. The said clause
empowers the Authority to direct any owner of or holder of the
consent or any person dealing with radioactive material, radiation
source or facility to hand it over to the Central Government if in the
opinion of the Authority, continuation of such material or facility
under the control of its owner or the holder of the consent or any
such person is detrimental to the safety and physical security of
such material or facility or has a potential to be detrimental to the
safety of public or the environment. It also provides that the
Authority may advise the Central Government to take control of the
radioactive material or radiation source if owner thereof cannot be
identified.
Clause 23.—This clause provides for administration of
Factories Act, 1948. The said clause provides that notwithstanding
anything contained in the Factories Act, 1948, the Authority and
other regulatory bodies shall, subject to the rules made under the
Act, administer the Factories Act, 1948, and do all things for the
enforcement of its provisions, including the appointment of
inspecting staff, in any factory engaged in the development,
production and use of radiation and atomic energy, or any facility
engaged in research and development activities related to radiation or
atomic energy, and owned or administered by the Central
Government or any other authority or corporation established by it
or a Government company under the jurisdiction of the Authority or
the regulatory bodies, as the case may be. It further provides that
no authority under the Factories Act, 1948 shall have jurisdiction in
respect of the above functions.
Clause 24.—This clause provides for delegation of powers.
The said clause provides that the Authority may delegate to the
Chairperson or any Member or officer of the Authority or a State
Government or such officer or authority subordinate to the State
Government such of its powers and functions under the Act (except
the power to make regulations under section 51), as it may deem
necessary.

56
Clause 25.— This clause provides for establishment of
regulatory bodies. Sub-clause ( 1) of the said clause provides that
the Central Government may, for the purposes of national defence
and security, exempt any nuclear material, radioactive material,
facilities, premises and activities, the premises, assets and areas
associated with material and activities from the jurisdiction of the
Authority.
Sub-clause ( 2) of this clause provides that the Central
Government may, for the purposes of regulating the material,
facilities, activities referred to in clause ( a) or premises. assets and
areas referred to in clause ( b) of sub-section ( 1), by order, in
writing establish one or more regulatory bodies and demarcate
responsibility thereof to discharge one or more of the functions in
respect thereof which otherwise before such exemption were within
the jurisdiction of the Authority and such functions amongst other
things shall include to ( i) ensure that the use of radiation and atomic
energy is safe for the radiation workers, the members of the public
and the environment; ( ii) report to that Government release of
radiation or radioactive material exceeding specified limits from
facilities under its jurisdiction into any area falling within the
jurisdiction of the Authority.
Sub-clause ( 3) of this clause provides that the Central
Government may specify that the provisions of the Act shall subject
to such modifications or conditions or adaptation as it may specify,
apply to such regulatory bodies.
Clause 26.—This clause provides for prohibition of disclosure
of information. Sub-clause ( 1) of this clause provides that save as
otherwise provided in the Act, the regulatory bodies established
under sub-section ( 2) of section 25 of the Act shall not disclose to
any person the information relating to the activities falling unclear
their jurisdiction.
Sub-clause ( 2) of this clause provides that no Chairperson or
Member or officer or other employees or consultant or expert shall,
either during his employment with such regulatory bodies or after
cessation of such employment, disclose any confidential information
relating to activities falling under the jurisdiction of regulatory
bodies.
Clause 27.—This clause provides for power of Central
Government to carry out certain functions itself. The said clause
provides that notwithstanding anything contained in this Act or any
other law for the time being in force, the Central Government may
for the purpose of national defence and security by order exempt
any area, nuclear material, radioactive material, nuclear facility or
plant from jurisdiction of the Authority or other regulatory bodies
under the Act and carry out those functions itself in relation thereto
which but for such exemption would have been carried out by the
Authority or other regulatory bodies under the Act.

57
Clause 28.—This clause provides procedure for grant of
consent for carrying out activities related to nuclear material, etc.
Sub-clause ( 1) of this clause provides that every person shall, for
carrying out activity falling under the jurisdiction of the Authority
relating to production, storage, disposal, transport (within and
outside India), transfer by sale or otherwise, import, export and use
of any nuclear material, radioactive material or any other substance,
or equipment, etc., obtain the consent of the Authority and for that
purpose submit an application in the prescribed form and manner
along with such fee and accompanied by such documents and
information as may be specified by regulations. This clause also
provides the procedure for grant or refusal of consent.
Clause 29.—This clause provides for suspension and
cancellation of consent. This clause provides the grounds and
procedure fm revocation of consent granted under section 28 of the
Act. It also stipulates that where the Authority is satisfied that
pending the consideration of question of cancelling consent, it may
suspend the consent and require the grantee to show-cause as to
why the consent should not be cancelled.
Clause 30.—This clause provides for responsibilities of
grantee of consent. The said clause provides that every person who
has been granted consent shall be responsible for safety and
physical security of radiation and nuclear facility and radioactive and
nuclear material contained therein.
Clause 31.—This clause provides for power of Authority to
call for information, conduct investigation, etc. Sub-clause ( 1) of
the said clause provides that where the Authority considers it
expedient so to do. it may by order in writing, ( a) call upon any
owner or any person in charge of or managing director, director,
secretary or other officer of radiation or nuclear facility at any time
to furnish in writing such information or explanation relating to its
activities as the Authority may require to carry  out its functions
under this Act: or ( b) appoint one or more persons to make an
inquiry in relation to the affairs of any radiation or nuclear facility;
and ( c) direct any of its  officers or employees to inspect the books
or other documents of any radiation or nuclear facility,
Sub-clause ( 2) of the said clause provided that where any
inquiry in relation to the affairs of any person referred to in clause
(a) of sub-section ( 1) has been undertaken under that sub-section,
(a) every owner or managing director or director, manager,
secretary or other officer, if such person referred to in clause (a)
of sub-section (I) is a company; or ( b) every partner, manager,
secretary or other officer, if such person referred to in clause ( a)
of sub-section ( 1) is a firm; or ( c) every other person or body of
persons who has had dealings in the course of business with any
of the persons mentioned in clauses ( a) and ( b) of sub-section ( 1),
shall be bound to produce before the Authority making the inquiry,
all such books of account or other documents in his custody or

58
power relating to, or having a bearing on the subject-matter of such
inquiry and also to furnish to the Authority with any such statement
or information relating thereto, as the case may be, required of him
within such time as may be specified. Sub-clause ( 3) of the said
clause provides that every person referred to in clause (a) of sub-
section ( 1) shall maintain such records or other documents as may
be prescribed.
Clause 32.—This clause provides for power of Authority to
issue certain directions, The said clause provides that the Authority
may, for the purpose of discharge of its functions under this Act,
issue directions to the persons who have been granted consent
under the Act, as it may consider necessary.
Clause 33.—This clause provides for powers of inspection,
search and seizure. Sub-clause ( 1) of this clause provides that the
Authority or any other officer specially authorised by it in this
behalf may carry out such inspection or inquiry as may be
necessary, enter any building or place where the Authority has
reason to believe that any document or object relating to the subject
matter of the inquiry may be found, and may seize any such
document or object subject to the provisions of section 100 of the
Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 in so far as they may be applicable.
Sub-clause ( 2) of this clause provides that the Authority shall
have power of access to premises and places, vehicle, vessel or
aircraft where radiation is present or used or proposed to be used;
and documents; drawings, photographs, plans, models or any other
form which relates to or represents or illustrates any existing or
proposed plant, used or proposed to be used far the purpose of
producing, developing or using atomic energy or radiation.
Clause 34.—This clause provides far review of order of
Authority. The said clause provides that any person aggrieved by an
order made by the Authority under sections 28 and 29 may file an
application to the Authority far review of that order within a period
of thirty days from the date of such order. However, the Authority
may entertain such application after the expiry of the said period of
thirty days if it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not
filing it within that period. Further, notwithstanding the filing of an
application under this section, the aggrieved person shall abide by
the order in question, unless it has been stayed by a subsequent
order of the Authority in writing.
Sub-clause ( 2) of the said clause provides that every
application far review under sub-section ( 1) shall clearly state the
ground or grounds an which a review is sought.
Sub-clause ( 3) of the said clause provides that an application
for review filed before the Authority shall be heard and disposed of
as expeditiously as possible and endeavour shall be made to finally
dispose of the application within a period of ninety days from the
date of its filing.

59
Clause 35.—This clause provides far Appellate Authority. Sub-
clause ( 1) of this clause provides that the Council of Nuclear Safety
shall, as and when required, constitute by notification, an Appellate
Authority to hear appeals from any order or decision passed by the
Authority under section 28 or 29 or under sub-section ( 3) of section
34 as the case may be.
Sub-clause ( 2) of this clause provides that the Appellate
Authority shall consists of a Chairperson and not more than two
Members. Sub-clause ( 3) of this clause provides that the selection
of the Chairperson and Members of the Appellate Authority shall be
made by the Council in consultation with the Chief Justice  of India
or his nominee.
Sub-clause ( 4) of this clause provides that a person shall not
be qualified far appointment as the Chairperson or  a Member of the
Appellate Authority unless he in the case of Chairperson is or has
been a judge of the Supreme Court or the Chief Justice  of a High
Court and in case of a Member, is an eminent scientist and has held
the past of Secretary to the Government of India or any equivalent
post in the Department of the Central Government in the Ministries
or Departments or  an institution administered by that Government
dealing with science and technology.
Sub-clause ( 5) of this clause provides that the Central
Government or any person aggrieved by an order referred to in sub-
section ( l) may file an appeal before the Appellate Authority within
a period of thirty days from the date of such order. However, the
Authority may entertain such appeal after the expiry of the said
period of thirty days if it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause
for not filing the appeal within that period. Sub-clause ( 6) of this
clause provides far the manlier of filing appeal and the fees. Sub-
clause ( 7) thereof provides that every appeal shall be heard and
dispose of as expeditiously as possible within a period of ninety
days from the date its filing.
Clause 36.—This clause provides far budget. The said clause
provides that the Authority shall prepare budget in each financial
year far the next financial year showing the estimated receipts and
expenditure of the Authority and forward the same to the Central
Government.
Clause 37.—This clause provides for grants by Central
Government. The said clause provides that the Central Government
may after due appropriation made by Parliament by law in this
behalf, make to the Authority grants of such sums of money as are
required to be paid.
Clause 38.—This clause provides for annual statement of
accounts. Sub-clause ( 1) of the said clause provides that the
Authority shall maintain proper accounts and other relevant records
and prepare an annual statement of accounts in such form as may
be prescribed by the Central Government in consultation with the
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India.

60
Sub-clause ( 2) of the said clause provides that the accounts
of the Authority shall be audited by him at such intervals as may be
specified by him.
Sub-clause ( 3) of the said clause provides that the
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India or any person appointed
by him in connection with the audit of the accounts of the Authority
under this Act shall have the same rights, privileges and Authority
in connection with such audit, as the Comptroller and Auditor-
General of India generally has, in connection with the audit of the
Government accounts and, in particular, shall have the right to
demand the production of books, accounts, connected vouchers and
other documents and papers and to inspect any of the offices of the
Authority. Sub-clause ( 4) of the said clause provides that the
accounts of the Authority, as certified by Comptroller and Auditor-
General of India or any other person appointed by him in this
behalf, together with the audit report thereon, shall be forwarded
annually to the Central Government and the Central Government
shall cause the same to be laid before each House of Parliament.
Clause 39.—This clause provides for furnishing of returns,
etc., to the Central Government. Sub-clause ( 1) of the said clause
provides that the Authority shall furnish to the Central Government,
at such time and in such form and the manner as may be prescribed
or as the Central Government may direct, such returns and
statements and such particulars in regard to any matter under the
jurisdiction of the Authority, as the Central Government may, from
time to time, require. Sub-clause ( 2) of the said clause provides that
the Authority shall also prepare once every year, in such form and
at such time as may be prescribed, an annual report, giving a
summary of its activities during the previous year and copies of the
report shall be forwarded to the Central Government. Sub-clause ( 3)
of the said clause provides that a copy of the report shall be laid
by the Central Government before each House of Parliament.
Clause 40.—This clause provides for offences and penalties.
The said clause provides that whoever discloses any information
prohibited under section 26, contravenes any condition subject to
which a consent is granted under section 28, contravenes any order
made under section 31, obstructs any person authorised by the
Authority under section 33 in the exercise of the powers under that
section, contravenes any rule or regulation made under the Act or
any requirement, prohibition or restriction imposed under any such
rule or regulation or fails to comply with any direction, order or
decision of the Authority or other regulatory bodies under the Act,
shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend
to five years or with fine or with both.
Clause 41.—This clause provides for offences by companies.
Sub-clause ( 1) of the said clause provides that where an offence
under the Act has been committed by a company, every person who
at the time the offence was committed was in charge of, and was

61
responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the
company as well as the company shall be deemed to be guilty of
the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished
accordingly. However, nothing contained in the section shall render
any such person liable to any punishment if he proves that the
offence was committed without his knowledge or that he exercised
all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence.
Sub-clause ( 2) of the said clause provides that
notwithstanding anything contained in sub-clause ( 1), where an
offence under the Act has been committed with the consent or
connivance of, or attributable to any neglect on the part of, any
director, manager, secretary or other officer or employees shall also
be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be
proceeded against and punished accordingly. The explanation to the
clause clarifies and explains the terms ‘company’ and ‘director’.
Clause 42.—This clause provides for directions by Central
Government. Sub-clause (l) of the said clause provides that the
Central Government may, from time to time, issue to the Authority
or other regulatory bodies, such directions as it may think necessary
in the interest of the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security
of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order,
decency or morality or in public interest.
Sub-clause ( 2) of the said clause provides that without
prejudice to the foregoing provisions, the Authority shall, in exercise
of its powers or the performance of its functions, be bound by
such directions on questions of policy as the Central Government
may give in writing to it from time to time. However, the Authority
shall, as far as practicable, be given an opportunity to express its
views before any direction is given under this section. Sub-
clause ( 3) of the said clause provides that the decision of the
Central Government whether a question is one of policy or not shall
be final.
Clause 43.—This clause provides for Members, officers and
employees of Authority to be publish servants. It provides that the
Chairperson, Members, Secretary, officers and other employees of
the Authority shall be deemed, when acting or purporting to act in
pursuance of any of the provisions of the Act, to be public servants
within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code.
Clause 44.—This clause provides for bar of jurisdiction. The
said clause provides that no civil court shall have jurisdiction in
respect of any matter which the Authority or other regulatory bodies
are empowered by or under the Act to determine.
Clause 45.—This clause provides for obligations as to fidelity
and secrecy. The said clause provides that every Chairperson,
Member, adviser, consultant, Secretary, officer or any other
employee of the Authority or other regulatory bodies shall, before
entering upon his duties, make a declaration of fidelity and secrecy
in the form set out in the First Schedule.

62
Clause 46.—This clause provides for protection of action
taken in good faith. It provides that no suit, prosecution or other
legal proceedings shall lie against the Central Government or the
Authority or any Member, officer or other employees thereof for
anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done under
the Act or the rules and regulations made thereunder.
Clause 47.—This clause provides for cognizance of offence.
The said clause provides that no Court inferior to the Chief Judicial
Magistrate shall take cognizance of an offence under the Act except
upon a complaint in writing made by the Authority or any officer of
the Authority duly authorised by it where the offence relates to an
act falling within the jurisdiction of the Authority or the Central
Government or any officer of that Government duly authorised by
it in respect of any other offence.
Clause 48.—This clause provides for power of Central
Government to supersede Authority. Sub-clause ( 1) of the said
clause provides that the Central Government may, by notification,
supersede the authority for such period not exceeding six months,
extendable for a further term not exceeding six months, in certain
circumstances such as ( a) that the Authority has acted in a manner
inconsistent with the provisions of this Act or rules and regulations
made thereunder; or ( b) that on account of circumstances beyond
the control of the Authority, it is unable to discharge the functions
and duties imposed on it by or under the provisions of this Act; or
(c) that the Authority has persistently made default in complying
with any direction issued by the Central Government under this Act
or in the discharge of the functions and duties imposed on it by or
under the provisions of this Act and as a result of which default,
the financial position of the Authority has suffered or the
administration of any radiation or nuclear installation has
deteriorated; or ( d) that circumstances exist which render it
necessary in the public interest so to do. However, only after giving
reasonable opportunity to the Authority to showcause as to why it
should not be superseded and considering explanations and
objections, if any of the Authority.
Sub-clause ( 2) of the said clause provides that on
supersession of the Authority, the Chairperson and other Members
shall vacate their offices and al1 powers, functions and duties of the
Authority be exercised and discharged by the Central Government or
such authority or persons as the Central Government may specify
in this behalf.
It also provides that all properties owned or controlled by the
Authority shall, until it is reconstituted, vest in the Central
Government.
Sub-clause ( 3) of the said clause provides that on the
expiration of the period of supersession specified in the notification
issued under sub-section ( 1), the Central Government may
(a) extend the period of supersession for such further term not

63
exceeding six months, as it may consider necessary; or ( b) re-
constitute the Authority by fresh appointment and in such case the
Chairperson and other Members who vacated their offices under
clause ( a) of sub-section ( 2) shall not be deemed disqualified for
appointment. However, the Central Government may, at any time
before the expiration of the period of supersession, whether as
specified under sub-section ( 1) or as extended under this sub-
section, take action under clause ( b) of this sub-section.
Sub-clause ( 4) of the said clause provides that the Central
Government shall cause a notification issued under sub-section ( 1)
and a full report of any action taken under this section and the
circumstances leading to such action to be laid before each House
of Parliament at the earliest.
Clause 49.—This clause provides that application of other
laws not barred. The said clause provides that the Act shall be in
addition to and not in derogation of, the provisions of any other law
for the time being in force. It further states that nothing in the Act
shal1 affect the provisions of the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and save
and except as otherwise provided, the provision of the Act shall be
in addition to and not in derogation of that Act.
Clause 50.—This clause confers upon the Central
Government the power to make rules for carrying out the provisions
of the Act. Sub-clause ( 2) of this clause enumerates the various
matters in respect of which such rules may be made the matters
specified in the said clause.
Clause 51.—This clause confers upon the Authority the
power to make regulations consistent with the Act and the rules
made thereunder to carry out the provisions of the Act. Sub-
clause ( 2) of this clause enumerates the various matters in respect
of which such regulations may be made by the Authority.
Clause 52.—This clause provides that every rule and
regulations made under the Act shall be laid before each House of
Parliament.
Clause 53.—This clause provides for amendment to certain
enactments. It provides that the specified in the Second Schedule to
this Act shall be amended in the manner specified therein and such
amendments shall take effect on the date of establishment of the
Authority.
Clause 54.— This clause provides for power to remove
difficulties. The said clause provides that if any difficulty arises
in giving effect to the provisions of the Act, the Central
Government may, by order published in the Official Gazette,
make such provisions, not inconsistent with the provisions of the
Act, as appear to it to be necessary for removing the difficulty.
However, no such order can be made under this section after
expiry of three years from the date of commencement of the Act.
It further provides that every order made under this section shall,

as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before each House
of Parliament.
The First Schedule to the Bill sets out the form of making
declaration of fidelity and secrecy.
Part-I of the Second Schedule provides for amendments to

provides for amendments to the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and

FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM
Sub-clause ( 1) of clause 8 of the Bill provides for the
establishment of an Authority to be called the Nuclear Safety
Regulatory Authority by the Central Government. Sub-clause ( 3)
thereof provides that the head office of the Authority shall be at
such place as the Central Government may consider necessary. Sub-
clause ( 4) thereof enables the Authority to establish, with prior
approval of the Central Government, its offices at such other places
as may be considered necessary.
2. Sub-clause ( 1) of clause 9 of the Bill provides that the
Authority shall consist of a Chairperson, two whole-time Members
and part-time Members not exceeding four to be appointed by the
Central Government. Sub-clause ( 3) of clause 11 of the Bill provides
that the Chairperson and Members of the Authority shall be entitled
to such salary and allowances and other terms and conditions of
service as may be specified by rules made by the Central
Government.
3. Sub-clause ( 1) of clause 17 provides that the Authority
may appoint a Secretary and such number of other officers,
employees, consultants or experts as it considers necessary for the
efficient discharge of its functions and exercise of its powers. Sub-
clause ( 2) thereof provides that the salaries, allowances and
pensions payable to and other terms and conditions of service of the
officers and other employees of the Authority shall be such as may
be specified by regulations.
4. Clause 18 of the Bill provides that on and from the
establishment of the Authority, the existing Atomic Energy
Regulatory Board shall stand dissolved and the Chairman and
Members of the said Board shall stand transferred to the Authority
to function as its Chairperson and Members until the Chairperson
and Members of the Authority are appointed in accordance with the
provisions of the Bill. Further, sub-clause ( 3) thereof provides that
on and from the date of commencement of the Act, every officer
and employee holding a post in the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board
before that date shall hold the post in the Authority by the same
tenure and upon the same terms and conditions of service for a
period of three years from the date of the commencement of this
Act. Therefore, there may not be any immediate significant increase
in the financial implication on constitution of the Authority or in the
near future.
5. Sub-clause ( 2) of clause 25 of the Bill provides that the
Central Government may, by an order in writing, establish one or
more regulatory bodies.

66
6. Sub-clause ( 1) of clause 35 of the Bill empowers the
Council to constitute an Appellate Authority to hear appeals. Sub-
clause ( 2) thereof  provides that the Appellate Authority shall consist
of a Chairperson and not more than two Members.
7. Clause 37 of the Bill provides that the Central Government
may, after due appropriation made by Parliament by law in this
behalf make to the Authority grants of such sums of money as are
required to be paid.
8. It is estimated that during the financial year 2012-2013, a
sum of rupees thirty-seven crores may be required for the
establishment of the Authority. In  addition, it is estimated that during
the Twelfth Plan, a sum of rupees one hundred and sixty-four
crores may be required for expanding and strengthening the
activities of the Authority. The said expenditure will be borne out of
the usual budget grants of the Department of Atomic Energy.
9. It is not practicable to make an exact estimate of the
expenditure both recurring and non-recurring at this stage as the
exact structure of the Council, other regulatory bodies and the
Appellate Authority would emerge later.

MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION
Clause 51 of the Bill confers power upon the Central
Government to make rules for carrying out the provisions of the Act.
The matters in respect of which such rules may be made relate inter
alia to (a) the salaries and allowances payable to and the other terms
and conditions of service of Chairperson and Members under sub-
section (3) of section 11; (b) the financial and administrative powers
to be exercised by the Chairperson under section. 12; (c) the manner
of maintaining books of account and other documents under sub-
section (3) of section 31; (d) the manner and fees for filing appeal
under sub-section (6) of section 35; (e) the form and time for
preparing the budget under section 36; (j) the form for annual
statement of accounts under section 38; (g) the form and manner of
furnishing returns under sub-section (I) of section 39; (h) the form
and time for preparing the annual report under sub-section (2) of
section 39; (i) any other matter which is to be, or may be,
prescribed, or in respect of which provision is to be made by rules.
2. Clause 52 of the Bill confers power upon the Nuclear Safety
Regulatory Authority to make, with the previous approval of the Central
Government, regulations consistent with the Act and the rules made
thereunder to carry out the provisions of the Act. The matters in
respect of which such regulations may be made relate inter alia to (a)
the time, place, procedure for transaction of business and the quorum
of the Authority under sub-section (I) of section 15; (b) the salaries,
allowances and pensions payable to, and other terms and conditions of
service of the officers and other employees of the Authority under
sub-section (2) of section 17; (c) the requisite qualifications and
training required to persons under clause (h) of sub-section (2) of
section 20; (d) the requirement of approval to, or the licensing of,
persons under clause (i) of sub-section (2) of section 20; (e) levy of
fee for issue, modification and renewal of consent under clause (f) of
sub-section (2) of section 20; (j) the form and manner of application
for consent, the fee and documents and information to accompany it
under sub-section (I) of section 28; and (g) any other matter which is
required to be, or may be, specified by regulations.
3. The rules made by the Central Government and the regulations
made by the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority shall be laid as soon
as may be, after they are made, before each House of Parliament.
4. The matters in respect of which rules and regulations may
be made or notification issued are generally matters of procedure
and administrative detail and it is not practicable to provide for them
in the Bill itself.
5. The delegation of legislative power is, therefore, of a
normal character.

2. At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Secretary, Department of Atomic Energy along
with his team of officials to the meeting of the Committee and informed that the meeting has been
convened to hear the views of the Secretary, DAE on “The Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority
Bill, 2011”. He also informed that the comments of the Department on the memoranda received
from the public has already been circulated to the Members.
3. The Secretary, highlighting the need for the Bill stated that the Atomic Energy Regulatory
Board (AERB) which is responsible for regulating the safety aspects of atomic energy, reports to
the Atomic Energy Commission. However, the AERB which has been formed by an executive order,
presently, does not have a statutory status. The Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority (NSRA) which
is proposed to be formed through this Bill, will have complete autonomy so far as its functioning
is concerned. In response to a query of the Chairman, regarding the autonomy of the Authority,
the Secretary, replied that though the Authority is completely autonomous, their policies will be
overseen by the Council and which shall have representatives of the concerned Ministries, headed
by the Prime Minister.
4. One of the Members pointed out that since the Chairperson of the Authority is not
represented in the Council, his views would not be reflected in the decisions of the Council. The
Secretary, clarified that the council will have three pronged function viz. formation of the Authority,
secondly, to overseeing and reviewing the policies and thirdly to create an appellate authority for
hearing appeal against NSRA.
5. The Secretary while further elaborating the objectives behind the creation of NSRA clarified
that the authority will examine all activities in Nuclear area including the reactor construction and
its setting up, fuel cycle activity including mining to reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel. He further
elaborated that clearance of a particular reactor design, site selection for setting up nuclear reactor
has to be given by the NSRA failing which no construction of nuclear plant can take place. This
means the regulatory authority will work as check point which will be imposed on the vendor from
the stage of construction of nuclear reactor to the stage of operation and each vendor will have
to undergo strict vigilance clearance at different levels of competence. He further added that Safety
Authority is not looking after the quantity of generation of electricity through nuclear power but
it will keep a strict vigilance over the safety aspect of the operation. If at any stage, any vendor
is found to have violated the stipulation laid down by the authority, the authority will take immediate
action against such erring vendor. At this stage, the Secretary further elaborated that India is in
constant touch with IAEA for taking feedback that India’s safety regulatory practice is in no way
falling short of the standing international best practices being followed in the field of nuclear safety
regulation.
6. While responding to some of the queries raised by the members of the Committee, the
Secretary clarified that the main function of the council is to hear people who will come to the
authority against any of its decisions which is the appellate part of the body. He also stated that
under clause 39 of the Bill there is provision regarding the annual reporting of the functioning of
the authority to the Parliament.
7. While responding to further queries, the Secretary, DAE informed the Committee that after
the Japanese accident, Prime Minister instructed that there should be a safety review and safety
audit of all nuclear plants in India and in response to that the NPCIL has divided the job of safety
review and audit into four independent committees which have given reports on the issue and the
same has been made public and recommendations of NPCIL in respect of safety audits is under
consideration. In the mean time, as told by the Secretary an independent assessment of safety audit
has been undertaken by AERB, NPCIL and the last one by BARC. All these assessments are in the
public domain. Secretary assured the Committee that the problem which the tsunami has caused
to Fukushima nuclear plant will not be possible in our system because additional cooling capability

is being incorporated in our plants with facilities of additional power supply etc. This will enhance

Fukushima plant.

in India and handling plutonium waste in terms of US safety measures is not good and America
is storing nuclear spent fuel in Yucca mountain which finally didn’t got clearance from environment

reduces the waste quantity to a very small portion. He also mentioned that high level radio active

2. At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members, the Experts, and representatives of the
Department of Atomic Energy to the meeting of the Committee. He gave a brief outline of the
salient features of the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority Bill, 2011. While pointing out the
objective of the Bill, he said that it sought to establish a ‘Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority’ to
ensure that the use of radiation and atomic energy was safe for the radiation workers, public, and
the environment. He asked the experts not only to apprise the Committee of their views in general
on the various provisions of the Bill, but also to express their views on the potency of the
regulatory framework sought to be put in place to ensure safety of public and environment from
radiation hazards. He, thereafter, requested Head, PRS Legislative Research to express his views on
the Bill.
3. The Head, PRS, Legislative Research, while referring to Clause 25(2) of the Bill, pointed
out that the status of the Other Regulatory Bodies, which the Central Govt. might establish, by an
order in writing was not clear. Since, those bodies were proposed to be established under delegated
powers they could not be considered Statutory bodies. In case, they were not statutory bodies,
there was no real need for this Clause to be added in the Bill as the Central Govt. had inherent
powers to establish such bodies the way Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) was established
earlier. Moreover, detailed provision regarding finance, accounts and audit of the Authority as
provided from Clause 36 to 39 had not been made applicable to the Other Regulatory Bodies that
provided them blanket immunity from Parliamentary scrutiny.
4. He, further, opined that there was an inherent conflict in the Bill. While the Bill proposed
to create an independent regulatory body to replace. AERB, inclusion of the Chairman, Atomic
Energy Commission (AEC), who was the promoter of nuclear energy, in the Council of Nuclear
Safety as an Ex-officio Member compromised on the independence of the regulatory body. The
.provision that the Council shall oversee and review policies with respect to radiation safety as
provided in Clause 7 with Chairman, AEC as an Ex-officio Member on the Council blurred the line
of separation between the implementer and the safety inspector/regulator.
5. He also drew the attention of the Committee to the fact that while the Minister for External
Affairs and Home were included as Members of the Council of Nuclear Safety, the Defence
Minister had not been given a representation in the Council. He also pointed that while explanation
to Clause 8 emphasized on the autonomy of the Authority notwithstanding anything contained in
Clause 7 which provided that the Council shall oversee and review the policies. Therefore, there
seemed to be some contradiction in the way it had been phrased and it would be useful to clarify
this and remove the contradiction.
6. He was further of the view that inclusion of Chairperson of the Authority in the Search
Committee for selection of Members might adversely affect the independent functioning of the
Authority. This issue became more important, particularly, because as per Clause 15(3) of the Bill

79
the Authority would take its decision by a majority vote. While commenting on Clause 35 of the
Bill, he drew the attention of the Committee to the wordings “as and when required” and contended
that the Appellate Authority would be an adhoc and not a permanent body. He wondered as to how
the appeal could be filed within a time limit of 30 days as provided in Clause 35(5) when there
was no Authority to receive the Appeal. Commenting on the qualification of Members of the
Appellate Authority as provided in Clause 35(4)(b), he stated that the eligibility condition – that the
person who had held the post of Secretary to the Govt. of India or any equivalent post, precluded
eminent scientists, Directors of National Laboratories under CSIR, as well as, professors from
leading institutes, such as IITs, Indian Institute of Science, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research,
etc., from being appointed as Members of the Authority as they did not hold the rank equivalent
to the post of Secretary to the Govt. of India. Lastly, he pointed out that the penalties prescribed
in Clause 40 were not proportional to the offences, if seen in the light of other laws in the overall
legal perspective.
7. Former Director, Safety Group, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research was of the view
that if the Chairman, Atomic Energy Commission was going to be an Ex-officio Member of the
Council of Nuclear Safety, the Chairperson of the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority should also
be included as an Ex-officio Member in the Council. Suggesting modifications in Clause 9(2)(b),
he desired that Experts from the field of electronics, computer science and Information
Technology, might be considered eligible for being Chairperson of the Authority. He stated that it
was desirable to include among the Members of the Authority, one Expert with life sciences
background and another with social sciences background. He was further of the view that the
explanation (ii) to Clause 20(c) was not needed as it might create an impression among the NGOs
that Government was hesitant to provide information to the public. He further desired that a
National Body of Experts needed to be established to look at radiation protection by constantly
reviewing the development of radiation effects on human and environment and advise the NSRA.
A separate body to look at radiation protection existed in Germany, France, U.K. and U.S.A. Taking
exceptions to Clause 20(2)(h) which provided that the Authority shall specify the hours of work,
minimum leave, etc., he stated that this was an antiquated prescription and was no more in practice
in any part of the world. Therefore, he suggested their deletion from the Clause. His other
suggestions included extending medical examination of the employees beyond their service period,
constant dialogue between the NSRA and the National Disaster Management Authority, even during
normal times, dialogue between the NSRA and the Claims Commissioner as provided in the Civil
Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, making the Appellate Authority a permanent body, creation of a
health data base in every district where there was a nuclear plant with the help of Ministry of
Health & Family Welfare.
8. Representative from Delhi Science Forum was of the view that the Cabinet in any case
oversaw and reviewed policies. There was therefore, no reason why under Clause 7, the powers
to oversee and review policy should again be vested in virtually a body which was a sub-body of
the Cabinet itself. Taking objections to the provision of an Appellate Authority to review the
decision taken by the Authority, he stated that there should not be any Appellate Authority. He was
of the view that safety was paramount and there should not be any Appellate Authority set up on
what was a decision regarding safety.
9. For bringing transparency and building faith and credibility in the domain of general public,
he added that in multilingual India, interaction of the Regulatory Authority with the public should
be done not just in English and Hindi but also in the vernacular languages so that, the rural people
also get the requisite information. Updated information put on website would be very useful in that

10. Consulting Fellow, IDSA was of the view that Clause 35 of the Bill, dealing with setting

hear. Explaining the rationale behind the Appellate Authority to be headed by a Judge of the

scientists, due to scientific nature of the issue.
4. In response to a query of the Chairman, regarding the autonomy of the Authority, the
Secretary, replied that though the Authority was completely autonomous, its policies would be
overseen by the Council of Nuclear Safety with the Prime Minister as its Chairperson and, the
Union Ministers as its members, the Cabinet Secretary and the Chairman, Atomic Energy
Commission as ex-officio Members of the Council and such number of eminent experts as may
be nominated by the Centre to the Council as Members. As per the present status, the Atomic
Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) responsible for regulating the safety aspects of Atomic Energy,
reports to the Atomic Energy Commission. The AERB has been formed by an executive order and
do not have a statutory status where as proposed the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority (NSRA)
would be an autonomous body in its function with a statutory status.
5. He, further, elaborated that the in twenty eight years long history of AERB only one appeal
was filed against it that precisely was the reason why Appellate authority was not made a
permanent body. While elaborating on the NSRA, he mentioned that the Authority would be a
technical organisation in which the decision-making would not only be based on pure debate but
also be backed by research and detailed calculation as those things could not be done by a Judicial
body alone. The NSRA could always review the process, giving its consent only when the certain
conditions were fulfilled. Since NSRA would give its consent only after fulfilment of a long list
of conditions to be complied by the applicant, there would not be much necessity to go to the
Appellate Authority.
6. While commenting on composition of the Council, Secretary, Department of atomic Energy
clarified that the Council had three pronged functions viz. overseeing and reviewing of policies,
having a Search Committee to identify the Chairman and other Members and creating an Appellate
Authority for hearing appeals against NSRA depending on the type of appeal. On being asked by
the Chairman about the life of the appellate authority he clarified that once a particular appeal was
over, the authority that heard the said case also ceases to exist.
7. One of the members pointed out that the basic reasons behind having an authority, was
redressal of grievance against the authority and maintenance of transparency. He wanted to know
about the content of report prepared by nuclear experts appointed by the PM after the Fukushima
Disaster in Japan about the existing safety standards in nuclear plants of India. While commenting
on the composition of council, he asked the Secretary to compress the number of experts to be
nominated by the Executive in the Council of Nuclear Safety to a smaller number as a lengthy
oversized council would make it difficult to function.
8. Commenting on Clause 9, one of the Members desired to know the reason behind keeping
part-time members in majority. He observed that the area of responsibility and accountability of the

83
part-time members would not be as much as that of the full-time members. He, further, added that
number of members of the Council should be specified. While commenting on clause 25(2) dealing
with additional Regulatory Bodies, he said provision regarding the number of regulatory bodies was
not specified. He, further, pointed out that offences and penalties were also not specified. The law
must have in its jurisdiction the quantum of membership and the areas in which they were
supposed to be.
9. Commenting on the structure of the Bill, it was said that there were five stages - the
Council, the search committee, the authority, the appellate authority and the regulatory bodies
which had made the intended Authority’s structure a cumbersome structure.
10. He opined that the powers given to the Executive to supersede, to give directions to the
authority and under Clause 27, power to take over the responsibility for the purpose of National
Defence and security and carry out those functions in relation thereto indicated that the ultimate
responsibility, impartiality and freedom of the authority would be compromised.
11. While replying to query raised by the Members, the Secretary highlighted the fact that
safety was something which was constantly evolving to a higher and higher level. Commenting on
avoiding Fukushima like disasters in India, he said that all reactors in India were backed up by
what was known as the passive safety system using thermo siphon technique which did not require
electrical power.
12. Assuring the committee, he said that a very detailed evaluation both in the design aspect
and physical inspection was done by a Committee and existing Nuclear Plants qualified that test.
In addition to that, further, stipulations from time to time were given by Atomic Energy Regulatory
Board and were being implemented by the Nuclear Power Corporation. All those measures prove
that Indian Nuclear Plants were safe.
13. The Secretary welcomed any suggestion given by the Committee on specified number of
members in search committee. Replying to a query on status of part time members he clarified that
full time people were actually employees of the NSRA drawing their salaries from it. In order to
have independent members on the body, it was always better that salaried employees should not
have majority in the authority and non-salaried employees should not be a part of NSRA. He further
added that, though, part time members were in advisory capacity but their authority was at par
with full time members.
14. The members of the committee raised a number of questions about nomenclature, quantum
of responsibility and accountability on the part of part time members. Many alternatives such as
‘Special Members’/’expert members’ were suggested. The Secretary said that suggestion from the
members was welcome. On the number of members in Search Committee, he clarified that power
to decide the number of search committee lied with the ‘Council of Nuclear Safety’.
15. The Chairman observed that Search Committee was a livewire because it was authorised
to decide the members of the Authority and there should be clarity about the number of members
of the Search Committee responsible for preparation of panel. It was suggested by the members
to specify the number of members to ‘Five’ or ‘seven’ an odd number. The Secretary was in
favour of seven. While commenting on the question about setting up of one or more regulatory
bodies, the Secretary replied that the entire nuclear activity had two components: one was
nuclear power production; non-power plant application of nuclear energy in agriculture, health,
food preservation, and the other was strategic activities. The NSRA would look after all aspects
relating to the nuclear power production and the non-power application of radiation and nuclear
energy. However, strategic side was to be dealt by a separate authority under the National
Security Advisor (NSA).

16. Under the new arrangement, different Safety authorities would be converged into a
single body which was to be notified soon. After passage of the NSRA Bill, body for strategic
sector might be brought in the new law. He said that it was the reason behind the provision
for keeping one or more bodies. Basically, two bodies would be set up under the new law: one
under the strategic side and one for the reaming part and there could not be umpteen numbers
of bodies.
17. While commenting on provision of the criminal offences, he explained that it was a kind
of normal provision which was present in many other  legislations of similar nature, including the
existing Atomic Energy Act.
18. Replying to issue of empowering the authority by Central Government by issuing directions,

Government could take over and whether executive had enough mechanism and structure to take

Replying to a query raised by the Member, Secretary said that the implementing authority would
be the Government department, laboratories such as BARC and not the NSRA. NSRA would not
be an implementing type authority. Implementation would be done by Technical Support
Organizations (TSOs)
19. While elaborating on provisions regarding transparency, the Secretary said that there was a
mechanism for transparency with regard to all decisions as well as information which were put
on the website. Clarifying doubts of one of the members that whether NSRA was under the control
of council, he explained three functions of NSRA. Further elaborating the point he added that in

and functions and clause 7 did not conflict with such autonomy. Council of Nuclear Safety would
ensure that the safety policy devised by the NSRA did not conflict with the overall national policies,
and not opposed to general public policy. According to him, drafting was done to ensure that the
NSRA was totally autonomous authority.
20. The committee desired to know about the conflict resolution mechanism in case of any
conflict or difference of opinion. The members were apprehensive that under clause 48 of the Bill,

independence of the Authority.
21. One of the Members said that ‘public interest’ was a vague term and liable to be misused.
Allaying the fears, the Secretary replied that Clause 48 of the Bill was essentially for any
unforeseen situation.
22. It was suggested by the members that Authority needed to be strengthened. One of the
members of the committee wanted to know whether there was any dichotomy or not in a situation
when decision of the Appellate Authority was challenged in a court of law, replying to the query,

a higher level in status compared to the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority.
23. It was suggested by one of the Members that as the decision were to be taken in the light
of scientific facts the search Committee was to be headed by a scientist rather than a High Court/

make it a higher authority in status compared to NSRA.

3. Presenting his views before the Committee, Dr. Gopalakrishnan emphasised that there was
a close connection between the independence of the AERB and transparency to attain public safety.
He said that India was aspiring to move forward in the nuclear sector like all advanced countries
in the world and hence it was expected that we not  only emulated the technologies of other
countries but  also their practices in regulation. According to him, there was a serious dichotomy
between what was given in the Bill and what other countries like USA, Canada and France were
practicing. He further stated that the exact nature of practices in these countries might differ but
we should aim for the similar levels of transparency, independence and freedom of action but these
were totally missing from the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority Bill. He added that the Authority
being created through this Bill would be a much more constrained and a much more captive
organisation of the Government even compared to AERB.
4. He said that broadly his comments on the Bill were in two areas – it was a question of
autonomy and independence on the one side and on the other side, it was lack of transparency and
openness. Commenting on the composition and functions of the proposed ‘Council of Nuclear
Safety’ he said that it was doubtful as to what extent, focused guidance required for safety of a
nuclear system which was highly technical and a techno-managerial affair would be available in
such a group. He added that looking at the subsequent actions of the Council, it was clear that
it would be used more as a controlling agent to keep the regulator in line. He, therefore, suggested
that this Council should be altered to be a Council on Civil Nuclear Policy. He suggested that the
Clause 7 of the Bill be changed to read as, “The Council of Civil Nuclear Policy shall frame and
establish policies and directions for the civilian nuclear activities in the country including matters
related to nuclear power and its safety and security. The Council shall oversee and support
autonomous functioning of the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority and facilitate its independent
decision making in nuclear radiation and safety related matter”.
5. He appreciated that the Bill intended to create separate regulatory agencies for defence
related nuclear facilities which had hitherto been directly under the Department of Atomic Energy
and not under AERB. He, however, felt that it should be made clear as to which facilities Nuclear
Safety Regulatory Authority would be responsible for. He, therefore, suggested that the facilities
which were currently under the AERB’s purview and supervision, should be transferred to the
proposed Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority. He added that if civilian and defence facilities were
mixed together in a bucket and only one agency was looking after them, level of overall
transparency and openness would be reduced.
6. Thereafter, expressing his views on the appointment and removal of the Chairperson of the
NSRA, he suggested that after having completed the selection process, there was a - need to have
concurrence of Parliament on the lines of USA and Canada. When one of the Members pointed out
that, we did not have a system where appointment of Chairperson of various bodies was presented
to the Parliament for ratification and as such, this suggestion would entail a drastic change in the
system of governance in the country. To this, Dr. Gopalakrishnan averred that if it, seriously
violated practices and provisions in our Constitution, he would leave it to the Committee. However,
he asserted that his concern arose out of the fact that there seemed to be a certain level of
arbitrary power in the hands of the executive to appoint and remove the Chairman and Members
of the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority.
7. Commenting on the explanation to Clause 20(1) of the Bill, he drew the attention of the
Committee to the words ‘The functions of the Authority shall, in no case, extend to the function
or any other matter which the Central Government was required to discharge under the Atomic
Energy Act, 1962’. He elaborated that it was .somewhat vague because setting up a new power
station, etc., came under the Atomic Energy Act and this provision basically debarred the Authority
to get involved in the safety aspect of the new facility. That was really not a workable preposition

95
because having created a Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority, the Authority should have the
freedom to examine and advise the Government on purchasing of new reactors or new systems.
He cited the example of Westinghouse Reactor, an American reactor, which was put through a 3
year detailed examination by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, because it was the first of its
kind reactor and they wanted it to be absolutely sure that it was safe and only after their clearance,
Government could buy that reactor.
8. He wanted to know as to why our regulator should not have the authority of looking at
the safety of system before they were purchased. When asked to clarify as to what exactly he
wanted to be included in the Bill, he stated that “In case the Operator or the Government intends
to introduce, install or commission a new, first of its kind nuclear facility system, a major sub-
system or component, which could potentially have serious safety-related adverse consequence,
shall be first subjected to a National Design Certification and preliminary safety approval by the
Authority before permission is granted for initiation of any associated site activity and facility
creation. Such a design certification and safety approval by the Authority shall be mandatory
notwithstanding any certifications or safety approvals granted by a foreign nuclear safety regulator
or Government”.
9. Commenting on Clause 20(2) (e) of the Bill regarding interaction of the Authority with
international organisations, etc., with prior approval of the Central Government, he was of the view
that the Authority should not directly interact with the foreign entities only on the policy related
matters and not on the technical matters. He, therefore, suggested to add policy related matters to
the proviso of Clause 20(2) (e).
10. Submitting his view on Clause 20(2)(q) of the Bill, he stated that it was somewhat vague to
put the onus on the Authority that it should discharge its powers and functions consistent with
international obligations of India. With such a provision, questioning any international obligation
from the safety point of view could become difficult. He, therefore, gave the following suggestions
to modify Clause 20(2)( q) “the operator shall bring to the attention of the Authority any
international obligation or treaty, which they, or, the Government are likely to enter into or have
entered into, and, the Authority shall then examine the consequences thereof from the stand point
of impact of acceding to that obligation the safety of the public and the environment. Once the
Authority completes this assessment, it shall advise the Government of their comprehensive views
in writing on the safety consequences of having entered into or entering into such international
obligation. Thereafter, the Authority shall discharge its functions as directed by the Government.
However, in case, the Authority considers that the final Government decision is not in the best
interest of public safety, health and environment, the authority shall prepare and place on record
their dissenting note before the Council with a request to forward the same to both Houses of
Parliament and include the same in their Annual Report”.
11. However, the Committee felt that the above suggestions would set a precedent for others
at various levels and it would be an unending process with other organisations also coming up with
similar demands. Intervening in the matter, National Security Advisor stated that the assumptions
on which the discussion was being held, was not true. He made it clear that before entering into
any agreement with foreign countries, three conditions were made very clear. Firstly, that they
would have to be competitive with other sources of energy in India, secondly, that they could not
sell reactors which had not been certified in their respective countries and thirdly that the reactor
would go through our regulatory procedures and safety procedures. So the assumption through out
in all the agreements was that in India, the law of India applied.
12. On Clauses 21 and 42 of the Bill, he wondered how an Authority selected by a selection
committee appointed by a Council headed by the Prime Minister and senior Cabinet Ministers could
be indecent and would single handedly overthrow the sovereignty and integrity of India. He was

96
of the view that these two Clauses were superfluous and did not add any value to the Act. He,
therefore, suggested that these Clauses should be dropped. Commenting further on Clause 42, he
added that it was not clear in the Bill on which aspect Government felt the necessity to give
directions to the Authority. He suggested inclusion of two Clauses in the Bill ill case Government
felt it necessary to retain Clause 42 in the Bill. His suggestions read as follows:
(i) In case the Authority, upon a thorough evaluation of the implications of following a
Government directive, finds no potential adverse impact could arise on public safety or
environment, they may document the entire matter and proceed with implementing the
Government directive.
(ii) If they found that unacceptable and adverse impact could thereby arise on public
safety or the environment, the Authority shall document the entire matter along with
the detailed reasons for their conclusion and submit these to the Council for a
reconsideration of the directive given by the Government. The Authority shall prepare
a dissent note and then submit it to them.
13. National Security Advisor clarified that the need to give direction came from the incident
of radiation leak at Mayapuri, when the Government felt that it had to ask Atomic Energy
Regulatory Board (AERB) not only to look into the incident but also to devise an operating
procedure and do a census of all radiation sources, etc. The purpose, therefore, was positive and
it was not to tell the AERB not to do this or that. Former Chairman, AERB, however, asserted that
the directives for morality, decency, public interest, etc. should be dropped from Clauses 21 and
42.
14. Thereafter, he suggested that Clause 48(1)(d) was a vague statement and hence needed to
be dropped. He further suggested that if the Authority was superseded or Chairman or Members
of the Authority were thrown out, they could not be denied the principles of natural justice to
approach the courts. He remarked that it was all the more necessary in view of Clause 46 of the
Bill which provided that no legal proceedings against the Central Government or the Authority could
lie for anything which was done in good faith. However, it was brought to the notice of
Dr. Gopalakrishnan that the Constitution of India gave the right to writ jurisdiction and if any one
was dissatisfied or had any grievance he could go to a court and challenge that.
15. Emphasizing on the need for transparency and openness, he suggested three areas where
we could improve. One area was putting such information on the website on which considered
decision had been taken like minutes of the meeting or summaries of the action taken, summary
of the site selection process, etc. He asserted that this should be used as a means for building up
trust which was lacking in India with the atomic energy establishment in spite of their excellent
technological capability. The second area was of public hearings, whereby certain opportunities
were given to  the public to  put questions face to  face and these were answered after giving them
certain written material and the third aspect was creation of small local level committees having
representatives, from Panchayats, local college professors, etc., which would meet at least once
in three months and interact with the local people.
16. Chairman thanked Dr.  Gopalakrishnan for presenting his views before the Committee.
The witness, then, withdrew.
A verbatim record of the proceedings was kept.
17. The Chairman, thereafter, informed the Members that National Security Advisor shall apprise

it was to be regulated after the enactment of the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority
Bill, 2011.

Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred Twenty Second Report of the Committee. This
Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2012-2013) of the Department of Atomic

of the Department of Atomic Energy gave an overview of the various activities of the Department
