soon as possible and therefore such programmes should be actively pursued and adequately
funded.
19.5 The Committee after examining the various aspects of the Demands for Grants
(2012-13) of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry
through its various schemes/programmes is providing a wide range of meteorological
services to people, besides carrying out high end research in meterological and polar
sciences. The Committee is therefore of the opinion that the programmes of the Ministry
of Earth Sciences should be properly and adequately funded, to provide the necessary
impetus to the core and critical programmes, Ministry has envisaged for the year 2012-13.

16
SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
1. The Committee feels that without any financial and administrative powers, the Earth
Commission will hardly be effective in performing its role and functions and the very
purpose of setting up of Earth Commission would be defeated. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that immediate steps be taken to provide necessary financial and
administrative powers to the Earth Commission so that it may carry out it assigned role
effectively. (Para 5.3)
2. The Committee notes with satisfaction that Result Framework Document (RFD), has
been adopted by the Ministry to review and monitor physical and financial progress/
achievements of major activities with respect to agreed targets fixed for each programme,
in addition to its internal monitoring mechanisms. The Committee is of the opinion that an
effective monitoring mechanism is imperative for ensuring that the various projects are
completed as per the projected schedule and timely action taken to overcome problems that
may arise in the implementation of the projects. The Committee hopes that with potent
monitoring mechanisms, the Ministry would be able to complete its projects in time.
(Para 6.3)
3. In this connection the Committee would like to invite the attention of the Ministry
to its 204th Report (page 3, para 5.1) on the Demands for Grants (2010-11), wherein it has
been stated that as per information furnished by the Ministry, the total initial Budgetary
allocation of Rs. 7004.00 crores for the XIth Five Year Plan was revised to Rs. 6637.00
crores at the mid term appraisal stage. In comparison to this, the Committee has observed
from the foregoing para, that the projected amount has been increased by almost three
times during XIIth Plan with outlay proposed by the Ministry at Rs. 18,824.00 crores. The
Committee also notes that for focused attention and securing effective implementation,
Ministry has reoriented its 76 projects into 15 major programmes for XIIth Plan. The
Committee hopes that with increased allocations and more focused attention, the Ministry
would be able to achieve capacity for reliable weather forecasts at par with the highest
international standards and would be able to develop technologies needed for effective
exploitation of marine resources for the socio-economic development of our people during
the XIIth Plan period. (Para 7.3)
4. The Committee also notes that two projects viz. Multi-channel Seismic System on
board Sagar Kanya and National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) extension centre in
West Bengal, could not be completed during the XIth Plan period. The Committee would
like Ministry to make all possible efforts to complete these programmes as soon as possible
and well before the expiry of the first year of the XIIth Plan. (Para 7.4)
5. The Committee observes that the Ministry has received a plan outlay of Rs.1281.00
crores, which is Rs. 369.00 crores less than the amount of Rs 1650.00 crores, projected by
the Ministry. The Committee, however, notes with surprise and concern that XIIth Five
Year Plan of the Ministry is yet to be finalised and the Ministry is not certain about some
of the new initiatives that it had proposed during the Plan period. The Committee
recommends that all possible efforts may be made to finalise the XII Five Year Plan of the
Ministry at the earliest so that future roadmap of the Ministry’s action Plan becomes
certain and it can vigorously pursue the Plan targets and achieve them. (Para 8.2)
16

17
6. The Committee notes that various ongoing projects/activities and proposed new
initiatives have been integrated into 15 broad major restructured programmes to carry out
the research activities in a more focused way. The Committee hopes that the new initiatives
does not lead to less focused monitoring or neglect of some of the programmes vis-a-vis the
position existing so far when these programmes were assigned individual budgetary
allocations. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should carry out a
review, after a suitable interval, to see if the new system has helped achieve improved
meeting of physical and financial targets and appraise the Committee of the finding of such
a review. The Committee would, however, like Ministry to ensure that despite amalgamation
of a large number of projects/schemes in a programmes, individual focus and attention
continues to be provided to each schemes and project of the Ministry. (Para 9.3)
7. The Committee has always stressed upon the need for greater application of
technologies for socio-economic development of common masses. The Committee, therefore,
commends the initiative of the NIOT in using technology i.e. ‘Low Temperature Thermal
Desalination (LTTD)’ to solve the drinking water problem in two islands of Lakshadweep,
by setting up two LTTD plants. The Committee is also happy to know that NIOT, also
proposes to set up six more plants in other islands of Lakshadweep, through public-private
partnership mode. The Committee is of the opinion that such technologies needs to be
popularized and such plants should also be established in Andaman and Nicobar Islands as
well and other coastal regions of the country, which face a scarcity of fresh drinking water.
It also feels that the adoption of the public-private partnership model would make the
establishment of such plants more cost effective, and enable the Ministry to commission a
larger number of plants in the coastal regions of the country in a short time. (Para 10.4)
8. The Committee commends the efforts of the Ministry in augmenting the scientific
and technological capabilities of the INCOIS, in respect of predicting cyclones and tsunami,
since accurate and advance warnings about these natural hazards give sufficient time to
disaster management agencies to gear themselves better to minimise the loss of property
and lives. The Committee is also happy to note that the Indian Tsunami Warning System,
has been entrusted the responsibility to function as Regional Tsunami Service Provider by
UNESCO and have started its operation for the Indian Ocean Rim countries. The
Committee commends the Ministry for making accurate predictions on recent earthquake
that hit certain parts of India and saving the country from unnecessary anxiety and fear.
The Committee appreciates the fact that the technological capabilities of the INCOIS have
been recognized internationally and hopes that, in future, the Centre would forge
collaborations with similar scientific organizations of the advanced countries, to provide
ocean information and advisory services to society, industry, Government agencies and
scientific community through sustained ocean observations, information management, and
focused research. (Para 10.8)
9. The Committee is aware of NCAOR’s good performance in conducting scientific
expeditions to polar regions. The Committee hopes results of scientific studies being done
in polar regions would find useful application in glaciers of Himalayas, forecasts and control
relating to monsoons and in other areas and a better understanding of climate change would
emerge from these studies. (Para 10.11)
10. The Committee notes the importance of the useful research being done by the IITM
and hopes that the Institute would successfully provide research backup needed for raising
the accuracy levels of our weather and climate forecasts to the highest international
standards well before the end of XIIth Five Y ear Plan and the Committee recommends
adequate budgetary support during the period be provided to the Institute to achieve this
task. (Para 10.14)

18
11. The Committee is of the opinion that research in the field of cloud physics should
be accorded high priority as it would not only help in right selection of clouds for seeding
but would help master its other aspects as well including development of cost effective
techniques for successful cloud seeding, which may go a long way in helping the country
solve the problems of drought and water scarcity in certain parts of the country. Such
research may also provide greater insights in understanding the dynamics of global
warming. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that Ministry should make all
out efforts to strengthen the special laboratory which has been set up at Mahabaleshwar to
study all kinds of clouds from precipitation point of view so that cost effective techniques
for artificial precipitation could be developed and for that, if needed, adequate funds should
be made available. (Para 11.2)
12. The Committee is happy to note that allocations made for R&D activities of IMD and
for the programmes ‘Research, Training, Education and Outreach’ taken together are
sufficient and hopes that a strong research backup would be available for the Ministry to
complete its various programmes and achieve its objectives during the year 2011-12.
(Para 12.3)
13. The Committee fully understands that though it may not humanly possible to
completely control the forces of nature like earthquake, yet through technological
interventions the massive destruction and financial losses it causes can certainly be
minimized. The Committee, therefore, feels that, intensive efforts towards scientific
research are needed to fully understand the various aspects of earthquakes. It is therefore,
imperative to establish a separate institutional mechanism to effectively deal with
earthquake related issues in the country, so as to minimize the damage in future due to
earthquakes. (Para 13.5)
14. The Committee also notes that presently, various aspects of seismology related
research are being carried out in a fragmented way by several research, academic and State
and Central Government institutions in the country. In view of the extreme killer and
destructive potential of earthquake as a natural phenomenon, the Committee fully endorses
the proposal of the Ministry to set up a separate research institute of the nature of
‘National Centre of Seismology’ which is exclusively devoted to study of the mechanics of
earthquakes, geo-tectonic movements and all other aspects of earthquake so as to avoid/
minimise the loses of life and property, a field which is yet to by mastered by the human
mind. (Para 13.6)
15. The Committee is of the opinion that the agricultural economy of the country is
immensely affected by the vagaries of nature. However, this effect can only be minimized
with the through scientific inputs, through the installation of state-of-the-art weather
observation systems throughout the country and utilizing them for providing accurate and
advance information to the farmers pertaining to the weather and climatic conditions. In
this connection the Committee appreciates the Ministry for initiating the ‘Agro-
meterological services’ to provide advance information to the farmers pertaining to wind,
temperature, rainfall, humidity and soil moisture and helps them to plan the cultivation and
harvesting of various crops and in issuing district-level bulletins to 560 districts across the
country. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Government intends to increase the
coverage of farmers under the agro-meteorological services from the current level of 10%
to around 40%. (Para 14.7)
16. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should develop Atmospheric
Observations Systems Network and Atmospheric Processes and Modelling and Services
throughout the country in a time bound manner so as to improve weather and climate

19
forecasting services. The Committee further recommends that agro-meteorological advisory
services should be extended to cover all districts of the country. The Committee further
recommends that crop and location specific information to farmers be disseminated in a
more farmer friendly manner and its reach extended to cover all farmers in a time-bound
manner, so that even small and marginal farmers could take full benefit of these services.
(Para 14.8)
17. The Committee appreciates the good initiative of the Ministry in providing the
fishermen advance advisories, which have led to reduction of search time and increase in
the catch per unit effort, resulting in an increased net profit from 1.5 to 2.5 times and fuel
savings upto 30%. The Committee also notes the proposal to increase the user base of
these advisories from the existing 65% to 90% of the fishermen across the country, by the
end of the Plan period. The Committee desires the Ministry to make concerted efforts to
achieve this target. (Para 15.3)
18. The Committee feels that the above discussion itself shows the urgent need for
making concerted efforts to improve the accuracy of our weather and climate services. In
a country like India, where a large section of population is dependent on agriculture for its
living, correct and reliable weather prediction well in advance, will prove a boon for the
farmers. The Committee, therefore, feels that instead of putting a distant plan of achieving
the US level of accuracy, in climate and weather forecasting in the next five years, the
Ministry should make all out efforts to improve our weather and climate prediction services
and bring them at par with the highest international standards of accuracy within the next
three years. (Para 16.3)
19. The Committee acknowledges the significance of the Indian polar missions as the
climatic conditions in these regions have a direct bearing on the monsoons, which is the
lifeline of the agriculture in our country. The Committee commends the setting of the
Indian polar stations which would increase the base of data collection regarding polar
processes. The Committee hopes that Bharati station would be commissioned as per
schedule and start its operations during the 2012-13, which will give significant boost to
India’s polar research programme. The Committee’ recommends that the continuing long
term approved scientific projects which are the proposed activity under the “Polar Science
and Cryosphere”, should be pursued diligently and in a well-planned and strategic manner
and the data collected from its scientific expeditions must be analyzed and a serious
endeavor made to use the results to predict the Indian monsoons more accurately.
(Para 17.5)
20. The Committee, notes with concern that there was a shortfall in utilisation of
allocated funds by the Ministry, to the tune of Rs. 1.24 crores in the year 2009-10 and
Rs. 2.54 crores in the year 2010-11; which is evident from the difference in B.E. and Actual
allocations for the said years. The shortfall in utilization, is even more apparent for the
year 2012, where the B.E. allocation stood reduced from Rs. 18.00 crores to Rs. 2.00 crores
only, i.e. a drastic reduction of about 90 per cent of allocated budget. The Committee takes
a serious view of the under utilisation of funds in last few years by the Ministry, which
shows that the Ministry is not seriously persuing this important programme. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry must actively pursue this
programme and the programme must be carried forward with full vigour, for exploitation of
the mineral resources in our vast Exclusive Economic Zone to enhance availability of
sufficient mineral resources required for our industrial growth. (Para 18.4)
21. The Committee observes that as regards the detection and quantification of gas-
hydrates, major portions of the deep-water regions have remained unexplored and available

20
data is inadequate for the assessment of gas-hydrates. The Committee therefore
recommends that evaluation and quantification of gas-hydrates must be intensified in the
EEZ region of the country to fully explore this resource specially in view of its potential as
clean fuel resource. The Committee is of the opinion that to meet the ever increasing
demand of energy in the country, it is imperative to explore alternate sources of energy as
soon as possible and therefore such programmes should be actively pursued and adequately
funded. (Para 19.4)
22. The Committee after examining the various aspects of the Demands for Grants
(2012-13) of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry
through its various schemes/programmes is providing a wide range of meteorological
services to people, besides carrying out high end research in meteorological and polar
sciences. The Committee is therefore of the opinion that the programmes of the Ministry
of Earth Sciences should be properly and adequately funded, to provide the necessary
impetus to the core and critical programmes, Ministry has envisaged for the year 2012-13.
(Para 19.5)

2. At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members of the Committee, Secretary, Ministry
of Earth Sciences and his team of officials. He informed that the Committee proposed to discuss
the functioning and Demands for Grants for the year 2012-13 of the Ministry of Earth Sciences.
The Committee while noting that polar studies have been thrust area of the Ministry of Earth
Sciences since 2008, desired to know the societal bebefits received so far from Indian Scientific
Expeditions to Antarctica. Besides the Committee desired to know about the progress made in some
important programmes of the Department such as Poly metallic Nodules Programmege, Gas
Hydrates Exploration, Development of Drugs from Oceans etc. The Committee also asked the
Secretary to brief the Committee about the budgetary allocations, initiatives for the year 2012-13
and whether the allocations were sufficient to implement the programmes of the Ministry.
Thereafter, the Chairman asked the Secretary to start his presentation.
3. In reply to a query regarding the activities of the Ministry, the Secretary stated that
preliminary studies had been carried out on a sample basis to detect the presence of rare-earths
on the sea bed. Besides the Ministry had prepared a wind potential atlas to locate coastal areas,
where wind energy can be generated and on the basis of the atlas specific areas in Tamil Nadu
and Gujarat-Maharashtra coast had been located with potential for off-shore wind farming.
4. The Chairman of the Committee desired to know whether there was any collaboration
among the Department of Space and the Ministry as regards weather forecasting. The Secretary
clarified that while the responsibility of weather forecasting lies with the Ministry, the Department
of Space, which launches the satellites, provides data, which is wholly used by the organisations
under the Ministry such as IMD, NCMRWF and INCOIS for various purposes.
5. The Committee also enquired about the existence of a separate research institute to study
the science behind earthquakes. The Ministry, in response, mentioned that it had already proposed
to set up a separate body in this regard, under the nomenclature ‘National Centre of Seismology’.
The Committee welcomed the initiative of the Ministry and directed them to provide a detailed note
in this regard so as to recommend the setting up of such an institute to the Government.
6. During its deliberations, the Committee took up the issue of the application of Numerical
weather modeling for the purpose of weather forecast. The Ministry informed that USA is more
advanced as regards meteorological predications than India, as it not only uses a more advanced high
speed computing system than India to frame weather models but also have sufficient trained people
to run and understand those models which India, at present lacks. Therefore the Ministry proposes
To establish schools to train people in the field of meterology so that the country can attain the US
level efficiency in the next five years. While explaining the efficiency of Numerical Weather Modeling,
the Ministry stated that it represents atmospheric conditions, through a set of equations solved
through high speed computers, through which the prediction period in advance could be increased
from two to five days. He further apprised the Committee that Numerical Modeling is very important
to generate initial weather conditions based upon which future predictions are made.
7. In response to another query regarding level of accuracy in forecasting raised by the
Committee, the Ministry replied that Numerical Weather prediction, will bring India at par with US

25
in terms of accuracy in prediction, in the next five years and forecast improvement will take place
in terms of accuracy upto five days. The Ministry also stated that there is an acute shortage of
scientists in this field and the Ministry is making efforts to attract the best talent, especially those
scientists who have worked in USA and Japan, to work in the country.
8. A query was thereafter raised by the Committee regarding differences of opinion among
scientists on the cloud seeding programme in different States. Citing a particular case, it was
pointed that the programme under Andhra Pradesh Government had resulted in improved rainfall,
while in case of Karnataka Government no such improvement in rainfall was observed. The
Ministry apprised the Committee that doing cloud seeding randomly on any cloud will not yeild rain
and understanding the nature of the cloud is a must before seeding. The Ministry further informed
the Committee that selecting a right type of cloud before seeding helps to enhance the precipitation
ratio. The Ministry further pointed out that lack of availability of correct data leads to the difficulty
in seeding the right type of cloud for yielding precipitation. An aircraft was hired two years back
to measure cloud behaviour, but as the study was sporadic the complete understanding of cloud
physics is still to be achieved. The Ministry further apprised that a special laboratory to study
clouds has been established at Mahabaleshwar.
9. In reply to a query regarding the studies being done by the stations in Antarctic and Arctic
regions and the justification for increasing the number of such stations, the Ministry informed the
Committee that an increased number of research stations in the Polar regions would increase the
base of data collection regarding polar processes which affect the monsoon and would also
facilitate climate change studies. Moreover, as most of the glaciers in the polar regions occur at
the sea level, one can go directly to the glacier and observe them and do scientific studies, which
yield meaningful results; while at the Himalayas the Glaciers are at the height of 10,000ft and
above, where studies are difficult and any results obtained from glacial studies at polar regions
could also be applied in Himalayan regions of the country.

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science
and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present
the Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred Twenty Seventh Report of the Committee.
This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (2012-2013) of the Department of
Scientific and Industrial Research (Ministry of Science and Technology) (Demand No. 86).
2. In its meeting of the Committee held on the 13
th April, 2012 the Secretary and other
Officers of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research gave an overview of the various
activities of the Department and the Members sought clarifications on various aspects of the

REPORT
The progressive development of science and technology since Independence reflects the
saga of a large developing nation struggling to establish an equitable society with reasonable quality
of life standards for its people within a stable democratic set-up. While, the focus during 1950-
1970 was on self-reliance, it shifted to technology denial driven science and technology during the
period 1971-1999 and post 1991 endeavor has been for IP generation and global competitiveness.
In the coming two decades, focus would be on attaining global leadership in science and
technology at organizational, as well as, individual level. During the ancient times, India was fairly
developed in the field of science and mathematics. Scientists such as Aryabhata, Sushrut, Charak
and Brahmagupta were some of the prominent figures of ancient India who contributed to the
advancement of ancient Indian science. However, advances made during the ancient times got
somehow lost in the medieval ages and during the British Colonial Rule.
1.2 Although, scientific development was initiated in 1942 with the establishment of CSIR,
major steps in our march towards revitalisation of the scientific traditions of ancient India were
taken by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru for whom science was not only a tool for economic development
but also a means of emancipation of man, and the scientific temper represented true religion which
alone could lead to the qualitative transformation of a stagnant society and a tool to solve the
problems of hunger and poverty. A number of specialized national laboratories under CSIR were
opened which after seventy years have now grown into a large network of 37 national laboratories,
39 Outreach Centers, 6 units and 3 innovation complexes carrying out industrial research in diverse
scientific disciplines dealing with a wide variety of technologies.
1.3 Developments since Independence have no doubt had a significant impact on the nation’s
techno-economic growth with scientific and technological research organisations playing major role
in it. The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research is one of the three Departments of
Ministry of Science and Technology, formed in 1985 with a view to promote industrial research,
technology development, transfer and its utilization. DSIR has two autonomous organizations viz.
Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and Consultancy Development Centre (CDC)
and two public sector undertakings viz. National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and
Central Electronics Limited (CEL). The Department also provides institutional host facilities to Asia
Pacific Centre for Transfer of Technology (APCTT).
1.4 The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology,
Environment and Forests considered the detailed Demand for Grants (2012-13) of the Department
of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) on 12
th April, 2012.
2. MANDATE
2.1 The primary endeavour of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is
to encourage industry to increase their share in R&D expenditure, support a larger cross section
of small and medium industrial units to develop state-of-the-art globally competitive technologies of
high commercial potential, catalyze faster commercialization of lab-scale R&D, enhance the share
of technology intensive exports, strengthen industrial consultancy and technology management
capabilities and establish user friendly information network to facilitate scientific and industrial
research in the country. The Department also acts as an administrative link between the
Government of India and the CSIR society.

2
2.2 The allocation of business of the Department is as under:–
(i) All matters concerning the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research;
(ii) All matters relating to National Research Development Corporation;
(iii) All matters relating to Central Electronics Limited;
(iv) Registration and Recognition of R&D Units;
(v) Matters relating to UNCTAD and WIPO;
(vi) National Register for Foreign Collaborations; and
(vii) Matters relating to creation of pool for temporary placement of Indian Scientists and
Technologists.
3. MECHANISM TO MONITOR AND REVIEW THE ONGOING SCHEMES
3.1 The Committee has been informed that progress of projects of the Department is monitored
at various levels. At the external level the Department has been reviewing the progress of on-going
schemes by involving an external agency or outside experts at the beginning of the Five Year plan.
The external Monitoring Committees review progress at Head Quarter level. Director General, CSIR
further reviews the overall progress of the projects from Head Quarters from time to time. During
the mid-term appraisal of Eleventh five year plan, CSIR started the Cluster concept of participative
planning and participatory monitoring and proposes to continue with the same in the Twelfth Five
Year Plan. The dynamic mode of project operation is also in place to ensure that all programmes
can be repositioned and reoriented to meet the desired objectives. Compilation of comprehensive
knowledge base information on Clusters; and project-wise white papers for appropriate
benchmarking are additional features for the monitoring of the schemes during the Twelfth Five
Year Plan.
3.2 Department’s performance has been measured through a third party review set up by the
Performance Management Division of the Cabinet Secretariat through a mechanism of Results
Framework Document (RFD), since its inception in 2009-10. Schemes, programmes and activities
are defined in quantitative terms and achievements made get reviewed by Ad hoc  Task force
consisting of former Secretaries of Government of India. The Committee has been informed that
the Department has achieved high composite value scores of 95.84% in 2009-10 and 95.97% in
2010-11.
3.3 The Committee is happy to note that the Department has put in operation a
monitoring mechanism which has helped it to make almost full utilisation of allocated
funds. The Committee appreciates the fact that the Department achieved a very high
composite value scores of 95.84% and 95.97% consecutively in two years with Excellent
grade which reflects the degree to which the DSIR has been able to accomplish success in
its programmes and schemes. The Committee, however, hopes that the Department
continues and maintains this performance in future as well.

4.4 The Committee is surprised to note that while the Plan outlay earmarked for the Department
for the Eleventh Five Year Plan was Rs.9000.00 crores, the actual allocation made was curtailed
to Rs.6959.00 crores – a cut of Rs.2041.00 crores, more than the outlay for any one financial year
during the plan. The Committee observes that against the total outlay of Rs. 9000.00 crores for
entire plan allocation, the B.E. allocation was to the tune of Rs. 7150.00 indicating a shortfall of
Rs. 8150.00 crores. It is all the more surprising for the Committee because the Department has
been efficiently utilising the allocations made to it throughout the entire Plan period. The
Department was in fact able to utilise over 99 per cent of the allocated funds.
4.5 The Committee expresses its anguish over such a huge cut resorted to by the Planning
Commission in plan outlays of the Department charged with the onerous responsibility of
using scientific innovation and interventions for catalyzing the industrial growth making
possible provisions of affordable health care for all and improving the living standards of
people at the bottom of economic pyramid. The Committee is of the opinion that such a step
on the part of Planning Commission is not justified. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that such cut measures should be avoided in future and it must be ensured that the entire
outlay for the T welfth Five Year Plan is actually made available to the Department.

ACHIEVEMENTS OF CSIR
CSIR, informed the Committee that it has made major strides in terms of its contributions
in varied areas such as affordable healthcare, sustainable energy, development of technologies for
industrial competitiveness, providing knowledgebase for strategic sector, and finding holistic
solution for societal welfare, etc. The Committee was particularly informed of the following
achievements made by CSIR in various spheres of its activities:–
5.1.1  A. Research Papers and Awards
CSIR published 4433 research papers in Science Citation Index (SCI) journals of national
and international repute during 2010 contributing to average 12% of the National SCI
publications. The average Impact Factor per paper stood at 2.28 during 2009 and 2010. CSIR
scientists have also bagged prestigious fellowships. In 2011, 37 fellows of Indian National
Science Academy, 23 fellows of Indian Academy of Engineers and 34 Shanti Swarup Bhatnager
Awardees were from CSIR. CSIR has bagged award for “Highest number of Patents in the
Country” instituted by Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion (DIPP), Ministry of
Commerce and Industry, for an Indian institute securing highest number of Indian patents in the
year 2009. It has also won Thomson and Reuters Innovation Award 2010 for “Most Innovative
Hi-Tech Academic Institution in the Country”. CSIR was granted 1282 foreign and 1507 Indian
Patents during the Eleventh Plan.
5.1.2 While the Committee lauds CSIR winning a number of prestigious awards at the
national level, the Committee desires that CSIR scientists should strive hard to make their
presence felt even at the international level by winning prestigious international awards as
well. The Committee further desires that with a good number of patents, CSIR should make
efforts to help Indian Industry develop more and more globally competitive products, for
that alone will determine usefulness of patents developed by CSIR scientists.
5.2 B. CSIR Technologies for National Capacity Building
5.2.1 CSIR has developed certain useful technologies for National Capacity Building namely
CNM5 (a five seater all metal civil aircraft designed and developed in Public-Private Partnership
mode with NAL and Mahindra Aerospace); Carbon Fibre Technology (an important strategic raw
material for the fabrication of advanced composite materials; Technology for recovery of Sulphate
of potash (SOP), a premium fertilizer with highest nutrient value of 68%; Head up Display
(a component of Cockpit Display). ATBS (Acrylamido Tertiary Butyl Sulfonic Acid) Technology,
etc.
5.2.2 CSIR has also significantly helped in building up of technology portfolio aimed at socio-
economic impact. Some notable successes in the field of Agriculture are development of tractors
Swaraj, Sonalika and now Krishi Shakti a 10 horsepower tractor for just Rs. One Lakh.
“RISORINE” for the treatment of tuberculosis, Prostalyn for the treatment and remedy of prostate
problem, Memory Enhancer, Caerulomycin, new contraceptives, Anti-malarial formulation,
Technologies for enhancing potability of Water, Streptokinase, Natural Streptokinase, Recombinant
Streptokinase, Clot-specific Streptokinase, Development of New-Generation Thrombolytic
Molecules, etc. are some of the important products developed in the field of healthcare. In addition

5
to this, CSIR Laboratories have developed significant knowledgebase on water, ranging from source
finding to mapping of water resources, from quality assessment to enhancing potability of water
and from recycling to waste water treatment.
5.3 C. Technology Transfer
Technology Transfer has been one of the focus areas of CSIR during the Eleventh Plan for
catalyzing the Industrial Growth. An outstanding example of Public-Private-Partnership that will
ultimately benefit the mankind is a unique deal with Nostrum Pharmaceuticals for world-wide
licensing of clinical development of new generation thrombolytic molecules. CSIR will be receiving
over 150 million US$ through various milestone payments and royalties. Other significant examples
are design and development of clot specific protein that displays plasminogen activation property;
new anti-ulcer drug; development of technology for Caerulmycin for its novel indication of immuno
suppression.
5.4 D. CSIR 800
Under CSIR 800, a programme which aims at improving the quality of life of the people
of India at the base of the economic pyramid through appropriate S&T interventions and developing
and providing innovative R&D based products and processes which would be affordable, CSIR has
designed and developed an eco-friendly dual powered rickshaw named ‘Soleckshaw’, driven partly
by pedal and partly by electric power supplied by a battery that is charged from solar energy. A
novel variety of Ashwagandha with high root yield of 15 quintal/hectare has been developed and
released to farmers which would help farmers with more earnings. A high yielding cultivar of
Lavender developed by CSIR has proved to be an excellent alternate crop for cultivation by farmers
in the state of Jammu & Kashmir.
5.5 E. Other Achievements
Other significant achievements of the CSIR are setting up of Academy of Scientific and
Innovation Research (AcSIR), CSIR Tech. Pvt. Ltd. for valorizing CSIR intellectual Property. The
Open Source Drug Discovery (OSDD) is an innovative programmes. It is an alternative model of
innovation to make healthcare affordable to the common man. OSDD got appreciated in the
prestigious scientific journal ‘Science’.
5.7 F. Ayurgenomics
Ayurgenomics, an integrative approach of Ayurveda and Genomics for discovery of
predictive markers for preventive and personalized medicine has been opened by the CSIR as a new
line of research. CSIR has played a major role in protecting the traditional knowledge by creating
a Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL). The TKDL contains information in 5 international
languages, i.e. English, Japanese, Spanish, French and German in 34 million pages concerning 2.26
lakh medicinal formulations in Ayurveda, Unani and Siddha. TKDL is recognized globally as a model
for protection of traditional knowledge.
5.8 G . TAPSUN
A Mega Project TAPSUN has been conceptualized in partnership with Ministry of New and
Renewable Energy (MNRE), CSIR led R&D initiatives on solar energy with number of
complementary and complimentary approaches are being implemented under the umbrella
programme T echnologies and Products for Solar ener gy utilization through Networks (T APSUN).

6
5.9 H. CSIR Innovation Complexes
CSIR Innovation Complexes is a new initiative for setting up Innovation Complexes focused
at translational research in diverse domains equipped with the state-of-the-art facilities in plug and
play mode innovation complexes and would help catalyze innovation in their regions of operation.
5.10 I. Technopreneur Promotion Programme
Technopreneur Promotion Programme (TePP), India’s largest network programme
supporting independent innovators and start-up firms aims at providing opportunities to all the
innovators across the country. It tries to increase 34 outreach centres and a hundred innovation
managers network to newer locations/states. This helps innovators to take benefit from TePP
progrmme for nurturing their innovations to convert into workable models/prototypes.
5.10.1 Achievements of TePP in 2011 were providing support to 400 projects of individual
innovators; commercialization of TePP Innovations; herbal medicine for treatment of Asthma; A V AZ,
an augmentative and alternative device for children suffering from Cerebral Palsy and development
of environment friendly Printing Ink, etc.
5.10.2 The Committee appreciates achievements of the Department both in high-end technology
and technologies for the societal benefits particularly in affordable healthcare during the
Eleventh Five Year Plan. The Committee, however, feels that a lot more needs to be done if
the country is to emerge as a technology driven economic superpower. The Committee,
therefore, desires that the Department should further intensify and galvanise its efforts during
the Twelfth Plan to make India a truly technology and innovation driven society.

8.2 An analysis of the amount allocated shows that there exists a yawning gap between demand
projected and amount allocated to the Department. The amount allocated to DSIR schemes (Plan
& Non Plan) against the demand projected is 18.90% and for CSIR schemes it is 56.42%.
8.3 The Committee notes with concern, drastic cuts imposed in the proposed demands of all
schemes. In particular, the cut in Plan scheme PRISM (Rs. 25 crores allocated against the
projected demand of Rs.220 crores); National Laboratories (Rs. 1316 crores allocated against the
projected demand of 2704 crores); CSIR 800 (Rs. 50 crores allocated against the projected demand
of 120 crores); National Civil Aircraft Programme (Rs. 10 crores allocated against the projected
demand of 500 crores), is surprisingly very severe. When the Committee enquired as to whether
the funds allocated were sufficient to carry out the activities of the Department, it was stated that
the projected demand of the Department for 2012-13 was Rs. 6612.06 crores and actual allocation
made was Rs. 3484.00 crore (2013.00 crore for Plan and Rs. 1471.00 crores for Non-Plan). All
in all, there is a reduction of 47% in the allocation. The Committee was informed that less
allocation would affect the four new schemes proposed by DSIR as lesser number of cluster
innovation centres, innovative proposals from MSMEs and common research facilities would only
be supported. CEL will not be able to upgrade its solar photovoltaic module manufacturing facility
from 10 Megawatt to 80 megawatt and initiate setting up of the National Silicon wafer production
facility. CSIR will not be able to setup all the five new institutions as proposed. Also, its new
schemes namely CSIR scheme for Open Innovation and CSIR initiative for Inclusive, Participative
and Collaborative Research & Development will have to be toned down. Apart from that, the
activities under on-going National Laboratories scheme will have to be down scaled in view of the
lowered budgetary outlay, while the new schemes will have to be largely down-scaled to that of
planned outlay. The National Civilian Aircraft Development (NCAD) programme would also get
affected.
8.4 The Committee is of the opinion that cuts would have an adverse effect on the
CSIR vision and strategies for 2022. Paucity of funds would compel the Department not
only to tone down targets set for the year but even adversely impact realisation of its long
term objectives. The shockingly high cuts indicate that scientific orgnisations are being
given step motherly treatment in allocation of resources. The Committee is of the opinion
that the axe of such a huge cut should not fall on scientific Departments as it adversely
affects Research and Development which is vital for the development and well being of
the nation.
8.5 The Committee hopes Government would, while allocating funds at RE stage and
for subsequent years, adopt a more rational and judicious approach in allocation of funds

11
and would ensue that for good schemes, adequate funds are made available. The
Committee feels that support to cluster innovation centres, innovative proposals from
MSMEs, upgradation of photovoltaic module from 10 to 80 MW are important initiatives
and making them suffer from financial crunch would not be in the national interest. The
Committee is of the view that considering that the conventional sources of energy like
coal and petro products are causing irreparable damage to the environment leading to
climate change, it is high time, that non-conventional sources of energy like Solar energy
are encouraged and enhanced, The Committee, therefore, recommends that Planning
Commission must ensure that crucial programmes like upgradations of photovoltaic
module are not starved of funds and adequate allocations be made to these programmes
at the R.E. stage.
8.6 The Committee also hopes that DSIR would make optimum use of funds made
available to it and provide to the people of the country best returns for funds invested in it.

RESEARCH (DSIR)
9.1.1 The Committee has been informed that Technology Promotion, Development and Utilization
(TPDU) Programme constituted one of the major plan programmes of DSIR during the Eleventh
Five Year Plan which aimed at promoting industrial R&D; development and commercialization of
technologies; acquisition, management and export of technologies; promotion of consultancy
capabilities; facilitation of technology information to support R&D, etc. It had four major sub
schemes viz.
(i) Industrial R&D Promotion Programme
(ii) T echnology Development and Demonstration Programme (TDDP)
(iii) T echnopreneur Promotion Programme (TePP); and
(iv) Technology Development Utilization Programme for Women.
9.1.2 When the Committee found that no budgetary allocation has been made for TPDU for the
year 2012-13, it enquired from the Department, whether the programme had been discontinued and
if so, what were the reasons for that?
9.1.3 The Department clarified that it had decided to discontinue the programme since it had
run for two plan periods i.e. Tenth and Eleventh Plan and the Department felt the need to
introduce innovative mechanisms for achieving significant outcomes in terms of establishment of
a large number of knowledge based enterprises and making the MSME Sector globally
competitive. TPDU has, therefore, been replaced by four new schemes in the T welfth Five Year
Plan focusing on nurturing innovations among individuals, startup companies, MSMEs and
industries for achieving inclusive growth in industry and economy. The most significant
component of TPDU i.e. TePP outreach centre activity would however continue as a part of the
new scheme called “PRISM”.
9.1.4 The Committee is aware that investment of over Rs. 10000 crores in R&D had been
reported under this programme and DSIR had reported innovations in various fields like
development of Fuel Cell Bus; E-waste Recycling & Precious Metal Recovery; Indigenous
Dialysis Device; Novel plant tissue culture medium from bio-waste – Fly Ash; Herbal
Medicine for treatment of Asthma; and A V AZ – Device for Cerebral Palsy through this
programme. The programme has now been scrapped as need for more innovative mechanism
was felt for achieving significant results. The Committee hopes that four new schemes now
introduced would be able to produce significant and much better results than obtained under
TPDU and for the purpose, the Committee recommends that Department should effectively
monitor these schemes so that money invested in these schemes is not only adequately
justified but also provides the desired results.

9.1.6 NEW SCHEMES OF THE DEPARTMENT
9.1.7 DSIR pro poses to pursue the following four new Plan Schemes during the Twelfth Five
Year Plan, namely:–
(i) Promoting Innovations in Individuals, Start-ups and MSMEs (PRISM),
(ii) Patent Acquisition and Collaborative Research and Technology Development (PACE),
(iii) Building Industrial R&D and Common Research Facilities (BIRD) and
(iv) Access to kn owledge for Technology Development and Dissemination (A2K +).
A brief analysis of the objectives, targets set and allocation made for the schemes for the
year 2012-13 is given below:–
(i) Promoting Innovations in Individuals, Start-ups and MSMEs (PRISM)
Under the scheme, innovative proposals of MSMEs shall be supported; CSIR – Cluster
Innovation Centres (CICs) promoted by National Innovation Council shall be supported for
providing innovative solutions; proposals from individual innovators/incubates shall be supported;
and support shall be extended to approved Technopreneur Promotion Programme (TePP) projects,
spilling over from the Eleventh five year plan.
Some of the significant objectives of the schemes include:–
• To create an innovation eco-system in India for growth of MSMEs;
• To create industry-CSIR Cluster Innovation Centres (CICs) for strengthening
competitive advantages of MSMEs;

14
• To support innovative proposals of innovators/researchers (students/scientists/
consultants/grassroots innovators) formulated by CICs;
• To convert innovative ideas or inventions into demonstrable working models/
prototypes/processes;
Targets envisaged under PRISM Scheme for 2012-13 are to establish 10 cluster innovation
centres and to support around 200 innovative proposals from MSME clusters; to establish 5 DSIR
Outreach Centres and to support around 75 innovative proposals; to identify and support 2 startup
companies in focused areas in collaboration with SIDBI; and to complete 40 ongoing TePP
projects. An allocation of Rs 25 crores has been made under this scheme as against the projected
demand of Rs. 220 crores. The Department, however, has informed the Committee that it would
have to significantly tone down these targets in view of reduced allocation made for the scheme.
(ii) Scheme on Patent Acquisition and Collaborative Research and Technology Development
(PACE) –
This scheme aims at providing support to Indian industries to acquire Intellectual Property
at early stage from overseas or within the country and add value to the acquired IP and focus on
Public-Private-Partnerships (PPP) to create enabling environment for collaborative research between
Industry and Universities/Public Funded Research Institutions.
Some Significant Objectives of this scheme are:–
• To focus on Public Private Partnership (PPP) and create enabling environment for
collaborative research between Industry and Universities/Public Funded Research
Institutions;
• To develop a dynamic database on existing expertise and IPs available in the
Universities/Public Funded Research Institutions to facilitate tie-ups with industry for
PPP;
• To promote commercialization of lab scale technologies of the Universities/Public
Funded Research Institutions;
• To strengthen tie-ups between Universities/Public Funded Research Institutions and
Industry to formulate collaborative projects for development of new products and
processes;
Main targets to be achieved under this scheme are to support 3 collaborative projects of
industry and institutions; to assist industry in acquiring one technology and adding value for
development and demonstration. An outlay of Rs 10 crores has been allocated against the projected
demand of Rs. 160 crores under this scheme. The Committee was informed by the Department
that in view of reduced allocation under the schemes, targets have to be toned down.
(iii) Building Industrial R&D and Common Research Facilities (BIRD)
BIRD scheme aims at recognizing and encouraging in-house R&D units of industry as well
as NGOs, Universities and other institutions (designated as Scientific & Industrial Research
Organisations) through various support mechanisms and implementing fiscal incentives announced
by the Government from time to time.
Some of the significant objectives of the scheme include:–
• To promote and nurture research and development in industry with a view to enhance
industry‘s share in national R&D expenditure;

15
• To establish at least 10 privately operated facilities for industrial R&D;
• To cover areas where Indian industry will be required to compete internationally in the
next 10 years;
The criteria for granting recognition to in-house R&D of industry and SIROs, which include
research publications and patents, shall focus on commercialization of patents into useful products
and services.
Some major targets to be achieved under this scheme include processing of around 240
applications for grant of recognition and registration to new in-house R&D units; Scientific and
Industrial Research Organisations (SIROs); Public Funded Research Institutions (PFRI)and around
775 applications for renewal of recognition and registration to in-house R&D units, Scientific and
Industrial Research Organisations (SIROs); Public Funded Research Institutions (PFRI); and to
initiate the process of setting up at least one common facility centre.
Under the scheme, Rs 25 crores has been allocated against the projected demand of 60.50
crores. Lower allocations, the Department informed the Committee, shall have an adverse impact
on the outcomes of the schemes.
(iv) Access to Knowledge for Technology Development and Dissemination (A2K+) –
Under this scheme, Science, technology and innovation related international journals from
major publishers shall be made accessible to 1500 in-house R&D units of industry and 600 SIROs
and techno-entrepreneurs.
The specific objectives of the scheme would be to subscribe to science, technology and
innovation related international journals and make it accessible to in-house R&D units of industry, SIROs
and techno-entrepreneurs; to sponsor industrial technology related studies and disseminate them widely;
and to organize, support and participate in national and international conferences, seminars &
workshops, exhibitions etc. to share the knowledge and success stories with stake-holders.
Main targets envisaged under A2K+ Scheme for 2012-13 are to initiate the process of
subscription to international science journals and making them accessible to in-house R&D units
and SIROs, to initiate 5 technology related studies and organize 5 conferences/exhibitions and to
support ongoing Technology Development and Demonstration Programme (TDDP) Projects. An
allocation of Rs 24.50 crores has been made against the projected demand of Rs. 56.50 crores.
The Committee was informed that targets set for 2012-13 under the schemes would be lowered
in view of significant reduction in allocation under the scheme.
9.1.8 The Committee feels that in view of budgetary constraints, there is a need for the
Department to devise innovative ways for funding these schemes. Public Private Partnership
(PPP) model, levy of appropriate user charges, funding from other beneficiaries, sharing of
profits arising from commercial exploitation of patents funded under scheme, etc. are some
of the known ways in which requisite funds for implementation of scheme can be generated.
The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to devise innovative ways of
funding the scheme and achieve the targets set for 2012-13 under these schemes. The
Committee, however, feels that Government should, to the extent necessary, provide
adequate funds for these schemes at RE stage, so that target set for 2012-13 under these
schemes get realised in toto .

I. NATIONAL LABORATORIES SCHEME
The Scheme Covers R&D projects in suprainstitutional Network, Inter-agency and facility
creation modes. CSIR, during the Twelfth Plan, proposes to set up five new institutions either in
the physical or in virtual mode, namely CSIR-Institute of Synthetic and System Biology (CSIR-
ISSB); CSIR- Fourth Paradigm Institute (CSIR-4PI); CSIR-Institute of Bio-Mimetic Materials
(CSIR-IBMM); CSIR-Network Institute of Solar Energy (CSIR-NISE); and CSIR-Network Institute
of Manufacturing Technology (CSIR-NIMT).
It also proposes to undertake R&D programmes across the biological, chemical,
engineering, information and physical science clusters. Different categories of projects include
supra-institutional projects (involving individual laboratories),network projects (involving multiple
CSIR laboratories), supra-institutional network projects (involving as well the non-CSIR
participation in identified set of projects), large mission projects, cross-cluster projects (that are
formulated to overarch multiple clusters) and facility creation projects. In addition, few mega
projects have been proposed.
The Department has informed that under this scheme, for 2012-13 it has set a target of
developing 10 advanced products/technologies either singly or in trans-cluster mode through
biological, chemical, engineering, information and physical sciences clusters. Establishment of five
new institutions and formulation of projects and securing relevant approvals for setting up of CSIR
outreach centres and CSIR special centres; operationalization of new projects under the EMPOWER
and RISK programmes; and augmenting core competency in identified R&D areas, appropriate
steps to augment R&D infrastructure in CSIR laboratories and to develop energy efficient green
campuses etc. are other targets under the scheme.
The Committee observes that National Laboratories scheme has been allocated an
outlay of Rs. 2146.00 crores for 2012-13 as against the projected demand of Rs. 2312.68
crores were allocated to this scheme at B.E. Stage in 2011-12 which was reduced to
Rs. 2225.91 crores at R.E. stage. The Committee finds that 2012-13, outlay under this
scheme is lower by Rs. 166 crores as compared to B.E. 2011-12 and by Rs. 79.91 crores
vis-à-vis  R.E. 2011-12. The Committee apprehends that this reduction might be because of
the fact that the Department failed to fully utilise the allocated outlay last year with
underutilisation being to the tune of Rs. 86.77 crores. However, when the Committee
enquired about the reasons for lesser allocation this year as compared to the last year,
the Department clarified that the decrease is due to overall low allocations during
2012-13 and initiation of new schemes for the T welfth Five Year Plan for which, though,
desired allocations have not been made, some budget had been diverted, from National
Laboratories to new schemes.
The Committee, in its 208
th report, had recommended that the network of National
Laboratories should be extended to all the states of the country, with at least one laboratory
in each state so that there is equitable scientific progress in each state. The Committee had
also recommended that though the National Laboratories are doing a lot of ingenious work
as regards Research and Development in various scientific spheres but most of its
achievements are not reaching the common man. In fact, the Committee had felt that the
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research could justify an increase in the budgetary
allocation only if substantial benefits reach the common man and had accordingly
recommended that the Department should focus towards transfer of technology from the
National Laboratories to the society.

17
The Department, however, in its Action Taken Note defended its stand by saying that
CSIR transferred its developed technologies regularly to industries through its constituent
laboratories. Some technology transfers at that time included improved process for
centchroman (a non-steroidal oral contraceptive); treatment of Bio refractory wastewater
without sludge and odor emission. While the Committee appreciates the fact that transfer of
some technologies had taken place but transfer of just few technologies is not going to make
the desired impact. The CSIR, with a large scientific manpower at its command, needs to
transfer innovative technologies in a large number so as to help common man improve his
living standard. The CSIR must pay rich dividends to the common citizen of this country by
way of transfer of appropriate technologies for every rupee invested in its schemes.

number of bright students not opting science subjects for higher studies in view of
attractive opportunities that have emerged in other disciplines and which in turn is leading
to shortage of scientific personnel in the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that there is a need for further increasing the number of scholarships as also for making

fair and objective criteria be devised for awarding these scholarships so that meritorious

Indian Technology Leadership Initiative (NMITLI) has created a brand image and is viewed today
as a benchmark of PPP schemes which is being emulated by various other government
departments. The partners especially from the industry were of the view that industries, which
collaborated NMITLI projects, have highly benefited not only in terms of the hard objectives and

seamless team between industry and publicly funded institutions. It has further been informed that
the Department proposes to broaden the NMITLI scheme in the Twelfth Plan as per the Cabinet

The Committee is of the view that the Department should take necessary steps to
dispel the apprehensions about PPP mode and make sincere efforts to ensure success of this

V. CSIR-800 SCHEME
Twelfth Five Year Plan goal of CSIR 800 is to measurably augment the incomes and
improve the quality of the lives of one million rural citizens geographically spread across the
country, in accordance with stated Government of India targets and relevant UN-Millennium
Development Goals. Strategic implementation of the program will focus on CSIR’s new initiative
of 24 geographically distributed CSIR Technology-enabled Villages (TECHVIL) chosen because of
their high proportion of families living below the poverty line.
Following are the main Objectives of the schemes:–
• Transform life in TECHVIL [24 CSIR Technology-Enabled Villages].
• Showcase TECHVIL to enroll 1 million citizens in adjoining communities to the benefits
of technology.
• Formalize TECHVIL experiences into a spectrum of replicable small entrepreneurial
business models to cover the remaining 800 million citizens at the base of the Indian
economic pyramid.
Stating the targets for 2012-13, the Department has informed that the CSIR-800 would have
three phases REACH-TECH, DEMO-TECH, INNO-TECH. These phases would be initiated after
formulation of appropriate projects and securing necessary statutory approvals. An allocation of
Rs. 50 crores has been made against the projected demand of Rs. 120 crores amounting to
decrease of 58.4% from the projected demand.
Introduction of Soleckshaw, development of a novel variety of Ashwagandha, Cultivar of
Lavender in Jammu and Kashmir and development of Post Harvest Technology Centres in Aizawl
(Mizoram) and Pashighat (Arunachal Pradesh) under CSIR 800 schemes to some extent had helped
poor and needy.
The Committee notes an allocation of Rs. 50 crores to CSIR 800 scheme. The
Committee, however, feels that to make real impact on the lives of the poor people,
hundreds of such institutions/initiatives are required. The Committee hopes that the
Department would gear itself to meet this challenge and recommends that Government
should extend adequate financial support to the Department to meet it.

The Committee desired to know the details of CSIR Scheme for Open Innovation, Initiative
for Inclusive, Participative and Collaborative Research and Development. The Department informed
that CSIR launched an Open Source Drug Discovery (OSDD) programme which has emerged as
a new platform for innovation in the domain of affordable healthcare. The Department has informed
that CSIR is building up open innovation as a key vehicle for delivering at affordable costs S&T

that the OSDD programmes would be taken up at higher levels of activity. Drug discovery in open

th report, that OSDD programme is about two to two
and a half years old and in these small annals of time it has achieved a lot in the field of drug

innovation which aims to provide affordable medicines for common man diseases has seen

This ambitious programme has been initiated to reduce India’s total dependence on imports
for procurement of civil aircrafts and associated services with a token allocation of Rs.10 crores

for the programme and that explains token provision for the programme. Under the Design Bureau

set up by CSIR as part of the feasibility study for National Civil Aircraft Development Programme,
CSIR has constituted two committees to further develop the programme. The Committees are Joint

sufficient funds be made available to this programme so that our own indigenous 90 seater
aircraft becomes a reality in a short time from now.
VIII. INTERACTION BETWEEN INDUSTRY AND CSIR
The Committee raised the issue of interaction between the industry and CSIR and desired
to know the action taken on the Abid Hussain panel report especially on the recommendation
regarding interaction between the industry and CSIR. The Department informed that all the
recommendations of the Abid Hussain Committee have been implemented. CSIR has put in place
enabling mechanisms for contract research, consultancy, joint (collaborative) research, loan of
equipments and facilities and personnel exchange, etc.
The Committee is happy to learn that CSIR has implemented all the
recommendations of Abid Hussain Committee. The Committee notes that share of public
funding for R&D at 2-3 per cent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is at par with
international norms. However, the share of private funds for R&D at only 3 per cent of
GDP in our country is very low as compared to international norms of 1.3-1.4 of GDP. In
France, Industry performs over 63 per cent (of all R&D) and funds around 54 per cent
projects while this figure is 69 per cent in Japan. In India, contribution of industries is
estimated at around 25 per cent of national R&D expenditure which needs to be enhanced
to at least 50 per cent in the Twelfth plan. The Committee feels that the Department should
give more and more incentives and form more partnerships with the private sector
companies of India in order to infuse more funds in R&D sector. In this regard, the
Committee fully supports the recommendations of the Planning Commission in its ‘approach
paper on Twelfth Five Year Plan—Faster, Sustainable and More Inclusive Growth’ wherein
it has suggested on interaction of Public S&T Institutions with CSIR at large.
10. AUDIT OBJECTIONS
10.1 The Committee observes from Annual Report 2009-10 that activities of Central Glass and
Ceramic Research Institute, Kolkata show that although during the period from 2003-2008, six
technologies were transferred to industries by it, premium and royalty earned was not
commensurate with the cost of development of those technologies. The Comptroller and Auditor
General, therefore, observed that project management in CGCRI was deficient as a result of which
project objectives remained unachieved in case of many important projects.
10.2 Commenting on the activities of Institute of Mineral and Materials Technologies (IMMT),
Bhubaneswar, CAG pointed out that the said CSIR lab failed to transfer and commercialize even
a single technology. Moreover, Intellectual fees and service tax amounting to Rs. 29.20 lakhs was
interchanged in a number of consultancy projects which indicated lack of internal controls. Delays
in the range of 6 to 63 months were noticed in installation and commissioning of 26 imported

23
equipments. Management Council did not meet for the mandated number of times and monitoring
at higher levels was inadequate.
10.3 Y et another CSIR lab namely, Central Electro Chemical Research Institute, Karaikudi failed
to transfer technologies in nine disciplines of major R&D programmes to industries due to non-
existence of demands from that sector, thus, rendering expenditure of Rs. 3.72 crores useless.
10.4 The Committee taking serious note of the above observations made by the CAG
recommends that these deficiencies need to be addressed by the Department in right
earnest as such cases bring bad repute to CSIR and this does not put DSIR in right stead.
The Committee, further, recommends that the Department should strengthen its monitoring
mechanism so that misuse of funds could be prevented.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS
1. The Committee is happy to note that the Department has put in operation a
monitoring mechanism which has helped it to make almost full utilisation of allocated
funds. The Committee appreciates the fact that the Department achieved a very high
composite value scores of 95.84% and 95.97% consecutively in two years with Excellent
grade which reflects the degree to which the DSIR has been able to accomplish success in
its programmes and schemes. The Committee, however, hopes that the Department
continues and maintains this performance in future as well. (Para 3.3)
2. The Committee finds that the BE total allocation of Rs.13044.00 crores for the
Department of Eleventh plan was enhanced to Rs.13,198.75 crores at R.E. stage implying an
additional availability of funds to the extent of Rs.154.75 crores and is happy to note that
the Department was able to utilise an amount of Rs.13,I77.45 crores thus leaving only
Rs.21.3 lakhs unutilised. The Committee hopes that even in future the Department would
continue making all out efforts to gainfully utilise the allocation made to it. (Para 4.2)
3. The Committee expresses its anguish over such a huge cut resorted to by the
Planning Commission in plan outlays of the Department charged with the onerous
responsibility of using scientific innovation and interventions for catalyzing the industrial
growth making possible provisions of affordable health care for all and improving the living
standards of people at the bottom of economic pyramid. The Committee is of the opinion
that such a step on the part of Planning Commission is not justified. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that such cut measures should be avoided in future and it must be
ensured that the entire outlay for the Twelfth Five Year Plan is actually made available to
the Department. (Para 4.5)
4. While the Committee lauds CSIR winning a number of prestigious awards at the
national level, the Committee desires that CSIR scientists should strive hard to make their
presence felt even at the international level by winning prestigious international awards as
well. The Committee further desires that with a good number of patents, CSIR should make
efforts to help Indian Industry develop more and more globally competitive products, for
that alone will determine usefulness of patents developed by CSIR scientists. (Para 5.1.2)
5. The Committee appreciates achievements of the Department both in high-end
technology and technologies for the societal benefits particularly in affordable healthcare
during the Eleventh Five Year Plan. The Committee, however, feels that a lot more needs
to be done if the country is to emerge as a technology driven economic superpower. The
Committee, therefore, desires that the Department should further intensify and galvanise
its efforts during the Twelfth Plan to make India a truly technology and innovation driven
society. (Para 5.10.2)
6. The Committee finds it quite surprising that even when the T welfth F ive Year Plan has
started, Planning Commission is yet to finalise the T welfth Plan allocations. The Committee
feels that such a delay could affect not only the planning and distribution of resources of the
Department but also the physical and financial targets set by the Department. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that Planning Commission should finalise the allocations
for the T welfth five year plan without any fur ther delay so that the Department is clear on
its long term and short term targets to be achieved during the plan period. (Para 7.2)
24

25
7. The Committee is of the opinion that cuts would have an adverse effect on the CSIR
vision and strategies for 2022. Paucity of funds would compel the Department not only to
tone down targets set for the year but even adversely impact realisation of its long term
objectives. The shockingly high cuts indicate that scientific orgnisations are being given step
motherly treatment in allocation of resources. The Committee is of the opinion that the axe
of such a huge cut should not fall on scientific Departments as it adversely affects Research
and Development which is vital for the development and well being of the nation.
(Para 8.4)

subsequent years, adopt a more rational and judicious approach in allocation of funds and
would ensue that for good schemes, adequate funds are made available. The Committee
feels that support to cluster innovation centres, innovative proposals from MSMEs,
upgradation of photovoltaic module from 10 to 80 MW are important initiatives and making
them suffer from financial crunch would not be in the national interest. The Committee is
of the view that considering that the conventional sources of energy like coal and petro
products are causing irreparable damage to the environment leading to climate change, it
is high time, that non-conventional sources of energy like Solar energy are encouraged and
enhanced, The Committee, therefore, recommends that Planning Commission must ensure
that crucial programmes like upgradations of photovoltaic module are not starved of funds
and adequate allocations be made to these programmes at the R.E. stage. (Para 8.5)
9. The Committee also hopes that DSIR would make optimum use of funds made available
to it and provide to the people of the country best returns for funds invested in it. (Para 8.6)
10. The Committee, however, feels that a higher allocation of plan funds for scientific
departments is absolutely essential for realisation of vision of making India a knowledge
based economy by the end of second decade of twenty first century. The Committee,
therefore, recommends higher overall availability of funds (as % share of plan) for
scientific organisations. (Para 8.8)

reported under this programme and DSIR had reported innovations in various fields like

was felt for achieving significant results. The Committee hopes that four new schemes now
introduced would be able to produce significant and much better results than obtained under

monitor these schemes so that money invested in these schemes is not only adequately
justified but also provides the desired results. (Para 9.1.4)

(PPP) model, levy of appropriate user charges, funding from other beneficiaries, sharing of
profits arising from commercial exploitation of patents funded under scheme, etc. are some
of the known ways in which requisite funds for implementation of scheme can be generated.
The Committee hopes that the Department would be able to devise innovative ways of
funding the scheme and achieve the targets set for 2012-13 under these schemes. The
Committee, however, feels that Government should, to the extent necessary, provide
adequate funds for these schemes at RE stage, so that target set for 2012-13 under these
schemes get realised in toto . (Para 9.1.8)

improve his living standard. The CSIR must pay rich dividends to the common citizen of
this country by way of transfer of appropriate technologies for every rupee invested in its
schemes.

REPORT
The Department of Biotechnology, celebrated the Silver Jubilee of its existence in the year
2011-12. Initially set up in 1982 as an Independent Board, it became a full-fledged Department
under Ministry of Science and Technology in 1986. Biotechnology developments, in last 25 years,
experienced five distinct phases: initial foundation phase followed by capacity building; Research
and Development; institution building and promotion of innovation and excellence. The mission of
the Department inter-alia includes accelerating the pace of research, innovation, development, and
technology transfer to advance biotechnology as strategic area by taking India’s strengths in
foundational sciences to globally competitive levels and expanding the application of biotechnologies
for overall growth of bio-economy within the framework of inclusive development.
2. MANDATE
2.1 The main mandate of the Department of Biotechnology is as under:–
(i) To evolve policies and integrated programmes in biotechnology and ensure their
implementation and monitoring.
(ii) To identify specific programmes of Research and Development and manufacturing in
biological and biotechnology and oversee the initiation in pursuit of related research
and manufacturing activities;
(iii) To identify, set up and support Centres of Excellence for Research and Development
in biotechnology and ensure proper dovetailing of their activities as per national
priorities and objectives;
(iv) To create biotechnology tools and technologies that address the problems of
agricultural productivity, food production, nutrition security, health care and
environmental sustainability by providing new and emerging products and services at
affordable prices, generate employment opportunities and make India globally
competitive in the emerging bio-economy;
(v) To evolve safety guidelines for biotechnology Research and Development and
manufacturing in India;
(vi) To act as the central agency for the import of genetically manipulated materials,
culture, cells, specimens, tissues and biotech products including DNA and RNA of
any type or size and for promoting their production in the country;
(vii) To serve as the inter-ministerial and interagency nodal point for all specific
international bilateral and multilateral Research and Development collaborations and
agreements in the area of biotechnology; act as the nodal point for all technology
transfers in the area of biotechnology;
(viii) To manufacture and ensure application of recombinant, cell-based and DNA vaccines,
diagnostics and other biotechnological products;
(ix) To evolve programmes for Human Resource Development in the area of biotechnology;
(x) To serve as an administrative and implementing Department of agencies,
commissions, boards, etc. specifically formed by the Government for fulfilling the
national objectives in biotechnology and also to serve as the nodal point for Bio-
informatics including training and creation of infrastructure, collection, dissemination
and exchange of information relating to biotechnology;
