Recommendation (19.4)
In such a situation, the Committee feels that there is an urgent need to develop strong and
impartial regulatory mechanism which could inspire confidence in the public, so that, decision taken
by it enjoy credibility of all the stakeholders.
Action taken by Government
(i) India has one of the oldest regulatory frameworks which address the issue of biosafety
associated with Genetically Modified Organisms (GMOs). GMOs and products thereof
including GM crops are regulated product in India under the Rules for Manufacture,
Use/Import/Export and Storage of Hazardous Micro Organisms/ Genetically Engineered
Organisms or Cells, 1989 (Rule 1989) promulgated under the Environment (Protection)
Act, 1986 to ensure safety of environment & human health. These rules and
regulations commonly referred as Rules 1989 cover areas of research as well as large
scale applications of GMOs and its products. These rules and regulations are
implemented by the Ministry of Environment and Forests, Department of Biotechnology
(DBT) and the state governments through various committees. Rules 1989 are
supported by several biosafety guidelines.
(ii) These rules define the competent authorities and composition of such authorities for
handling of various aspects of the rules. Presently there are six Competent Authorities
i.e.  The Recombinant DNA Advisory Committee (RDAC), Institutional Biosafety
Committee (IBSC), Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation (RCGM), Genetic
Engineering Approval Committee (GEAC), State Biotechnology Coordination Committee
(SBCC), District Level Committee (DLC). While RDAC has an advisory role, IBSC,
RCGM and GEAC are involved in regulations and SBCCs and DLCs are involved in
monitoring. The compliance of the regulatory procedures during GM crop field trials
is also monitored by the Monitoring Committees set up by the RCGM/GEAC.
(iii) Under the Rule, 1989, Government of India follows the policy of case by case event
based approval of Genetically Modified (GM) crops. Evaluation of the safety of GM
crops and regulatory approval process takes place right from the research stage. The
development of GM crops at the laboratory stage, confined multi-location trials for
generation of biosafety data known as biosafety research trials – I and biosafety
research trials-II (BRL-I and BRL-II) require prior approval of the RCGM and the
GEAC set up in DBT and MoEF, respectively under the Rules, 1989.

26
(iv) Recognizing that regulation is a dynamic process and safety assessment of GM plant
is the most important regulatory step, these guidelines and protocols along with the
regulatory framework are being regularly reviewed/updated through a consultative
approach and following the international norms prescribed by the Organization for
Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), CODEX Alimentarius Commission
and International Plant Protection Convention (IPPC). V arious bio-safety guidelines
which are regularly updated keeping in tune with the international practices and
developments in biotechnology are:
a. Recombinant DNA Safety Guidelines, 1990 and 1994
b. Revised Guidelines for Research in Transgenic Plants and Guidelines for Toxicity
and Allergenicity Evaluation, 1998
c. Guidelines and SOPs for the conduct of Confined Field Trials of Transgenic Plant,
2008
d. Guidelines for the Safety Assessment of GM Foods, 2008 developed by Indian
Council of Medical Research (ICMR)
e. Protocol for Safety Assessment of Genetically Engineered Plants/crops, 2008.
(v) The GEAC takes into consideration the findings of the biosafety and agronomic studies
as well as recommendations of the RCGM before according approval for environmental
release. Only those transgenic crops which are found to be safe for human
consumption as well as the environment are recommended for environmental release.
(vi) Further, taking into account apprehensions received from various State Governments
and other stakeholders in recent time; and recognizing the fact that agriculture is a
State subject, GEAC during its 111
th meeting held on 6.7.2011 made ‘No Objection
Certificate’ (NOC) from State Government a prerequisite for issuance of approval letter
by GEAC for field trials of GM crops in the State.
(vii) A draft Bill to establish Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) as an
autonomous and statutory agency to regulate the research, transport, import,
manufacture and use of organisms and products of modern biotechnology under DBT
is under consideration. The safety aspects including both environmental safety and
food safety with respect to genetic manipulation are proposed to be regulated by BRAI.
Accordingly, all GM foods (living as well as processed) shall be cleared by BRAI with
respect to introduced genetic modification. The bill has been prepared through a
consultative process involving interdisciplinary and inter-ministerial experts, State
Governments and Stakeholders. The Cabinet Committee has approved the note for
introduction of Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) Bill, 2010 on 18
th
November 2010. On necessary legislative procedure, the BRAI Bill, 2011 has been
submitted to Lok Sabha Secretariat for introduction in parliament. No specific time
frame can be given for setting up the authority at this stage.
(viii) Moreover, India being a party to Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety adopted under
Convention on Biological Diversity, several measures has been taken to implement
obligations under the Protocol in order to ensure safe handling, transport and use of
living modified organisms (LMOs) resulting from modern biotechnology that may have
adverse effects on biological diversity taking also into account risk to human health.
Comments
The Committee takes note of the reply.

PROJECT TIGER : APPROACH PAPER TO TWELFTH PLAN
1. Background
1.1 “Project Tiger”, now ongoing as a Centrally Sponsored Scheme, was launched by the
Government of India in 1973 in nine reserves of different States (Assam, Bihar, Karnataka,
Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal) over an

33
area of approximately 14,000 sq. km. Since then, the project coverage has expanded
considerably to 40 tiger reserves (TR), encompassing an area of around 46,388.22 sq.km.
in 17 tiger States with 32578.78 sq.km. of notified core/critical tiger habitats in 16 tiger
States. Further, in-principle approval has been accorded for creation of 6 new tiger
reserves, besides advising the States for 6 additional areas which are important for tiger
conservation.
1.2 The Project has saved the tiger from the brink of extinction. Due to ongoing conservation
efforts under the Project in designated tiger reserves, India has the maximum number of
tigers along with its source areas amongst the 13 tiger range countries in the world.
1.3 Project Tiger has a holistic, ecosystem approach. Its core–buffer strategy, protection and
development initiatives gave a new perspective to the concept of wildlife management in our
country and has been “role model” for conservation.
2. Present status of tiger, co-predators, prey and habitat
2.1 The second countrywide assessment of the status of tigers, co-predators and their prey was
released in March, 2011. This assessment of 2010 is the second such countrywide
assessment using the refined methodology as recommended by the Tiger Task Force. The
findings indicate a countrywide 20% increase in tiger numbers in 2010 with an estimated
number of 1706 (1520-1909). The 2006 estimation was 1411 (1165-1657 tigers). A decline
of 12.6% in tiger occupancy from connecting habitats has also been reported. This has
occurred in peripheral and dispersal areas having low densities outside tiger reserves and
tiger source populations.
2.2 The increase in tiger numbers is due to the fact that tiger populations in Uttarakhand, Tamil
Nadu, Maharashtra and Karnataka have shown an increase in tiger density. The inclusion of
Sunderbans, some portions of North East and parts of Maharashtra have also contributed
to the increase.
2.3 Tiger occurrence and density were dependent on availability of habitats that were remote,
with minimal human disturbance and having a high availability of large wild prey (chital,
sambar, gaur, and wild pig).
2.4 Tiger occupied forests in India were classified into 6 landscape complexes : (a) Shivalik
Hills and the Gangetic Plain, (b) Central India (c) Eastern Ghats, (d) Western Ghats,
(e) North-Eastern Hills and Brahmaputra Plains, and (f) Sunderbans.
2.4.1 In Shivalik-Terai Landscape tigers occupied 6712 km
2 of forested habitats with an
estimated population of 353 (320 to 388) in five separate populations.
2.4.2 Central Indian Landscape  (inclusive of Nagarjunasagar Srisailam of the Eastern Ghats)
tiger presence was reported from 39,017 km 2 with an estimated population of 601 (518 to
685) distributed in 20 tiger populations with a few other sporadic occurrences.
2.4.3 Western Ghats Landscape  was 29,607 km 2 and registered a decline of about 11.5%
compared to that of 2006. The current tiger population was estimated at 534 (500 to 568)
registering a rise of about 32% since 2006.
2.4.4 T iger occupancy of 4,900 km
2 and population numbers between 118 to 178 tigers should
be considered as minimal for the North East  since systematic coverage of the entire
landscape was not done.
2.4.5 Population estimation of the Sundarbans tigers was done with a combination of camera
trapping and satellite telemetry. A tiger density of 4.3 (se 0.3) tigers per 100 km 2 was

34
estimated. The total population for the Indian Sundarbans was estimated to be between 64
to 90 tigers.
2.4.6 Currently, only a few populations Nagarhole-Bandipur-Mudumalai-Wayanad-Moyar-Segur,
Corbett population, Sundarbans (India and Bangladesh) and Kaziranga-KarbiAnglong
populations have the required population size for long term survival without immigration.
The remaining tiger populations require habitat connectivity for genetic and demographic
viability.

4. General reasons for tiger decline in areas outside tiger reserves
The reasons for tiger decline in areas outside tiger reserves/protected areas are as below:
(i) Degradation of forest status outside Protected Areas/Tiger Reserves owing to:
(a) human pressure
(b) livestock pressure
(c) ecologically unsustainable land uses
(ii) Fragmentation leading to loss of gene flow from source populations
(iii) Loss of forest quality in terms of prey biomass
(iv) Tiger deaths due to man-animal conflict
(v) Tiger deaths due to poaching
(vi) Loss of reproduction owing to disturbance on account of heavily used infrastructure
like highways, etc
(vii) Lack of adequate protection in outside areas
(viii) Insurgency/law and order problems
5. Present approach to tiger conservation
Owing to habitat fragmentation on account of ecologically unsustainable land uses, biotic
pressure and poaching, the following approach is imperative:
5.1 Consolidating/strengthening the “source” population of tiger and its prey in tiger
reserves, protected areas and tiger bearing forests
This involves the following active managerial interventions:

40
(i) Protection/antipoaching operations/intelligence networking
(ii) Strengthening of infrastructure within tiger reserves
(iii) Creation of inviolate space through relocation
(iv) Capacity building of frontline staff/local people and officers (including strengthening
of training centres and training in related fields, viz. enforcement, intelligence
networking, tourism activities, etc.)
5.2  Managing the “source-sink dynamics” by restoring habitat connectivity
This involves the following managerial interventions:
(i) Actively providing incentives to local people for the eco-system services/corridor
values provided by them by not degrading the forest (payment for eco-system
services)
(ii) Incentives to local people for taking up plantations and protecting natural root stocks
besides preventing free grazing
(iii) Encouraging stall feeding of cattle and fostering marketing of dairy products
(iv) Providing subsidized gas connection to local people for reducing their dependency on
forest towards fuel wood collection
5.3 Mainstreaming tiger/wildlife concerns in the landscape through smart practices with
other sectors to prevent/address man-tiger conflicts (sectors: forestry, agriculture, welfare
activities through the district Collector sector, tourism, fisheries, tea-coffee estates, road/rail
transport, industry, mining, thermal power plants, irrigation projects, temple tourism and
communication projects operating in the landscape).
6. Milestone Initiatives taken for strengthening tiger conservation
Several milestone initiatives have been taken in the last few years to strengthen tiger
conservation in the country. The urgent recommendations of the Tiger Task Force constituted by
the National Board for Wildlife under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister have been
implemented. The important ones are indicated below:
Legal steps
1. Amendment of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 for providing enabling provisions for
constitution of the National Tiger Conservation Authority and the Tiger and Other Endangered
Species Crime Control Bureau.
2. Enhancement of punishment in cases of offence relating to a tiger reserve or its core area.
Administrative steps
3. Strengthening of antipoaching activities, including special strategy for monsoon patrolling,
by providing funding support to Tiger Reserve States, as proposed by them, for deployment of
antipoaching squads involving ex-army personnel/home guards, apart from workforce comprising of
local people, in addition to strengthening of communication/wireless facilities.
4. Constitution of the National Tiger Conservation Authority with effect from 4.09.2006, for
strengthening tiger conservation by, interalia, ensuring normative standards in tiger reserve

41
management, preparation of reserve specific tiger conservation plan, laying down annual audit
report before Parliament, constituting State level Steering Committees under the Chairmanship of
Chief Ministers and establishment of Tiger Conservation Foundation.
5. Constitution of a multidisciplinary Tiger and Other Endangered Species Crime Control
Bureau (Wildlife Crime Control Bureau) with effect from 6.6.2007 to effectively control illegal trade
in wildlife.
6. The in-principle approval has been accorded by the National Tiger Conservation Authority
for creation of four new tiger reserves, and the sites are:, Pilibhit (Uttar Pradesh), Ratapani
(Madhya Pradesh), Sunabeda (Orissa), Mukundara Hills (including Darrah, Jawahar Sagar and
Chambal Wildlife Sanctuaries) (Rajasthan), Kudremukh (Karnataka), and Kawal (Andhra Pradesh).
Besides, the States have been advised to send proposals for declaring the following areas as Tiger
Reserves: (i) Bor (Maharashtra), (ii) Suhelwa (Uttar Pradesh), (iii) Nagzira-Navegaon (Maharashtra),
(iv) Satyamangalam (Tamil Nadu), (v) Guru Ghasidas National Park (Chhattisgarh), and (vi) Mhdei
Sanctuary (Goa).
7. The revised Project Tiger guidelines have been issued to States for strengthening tiger
conservation, which apart from ongoing activities, interalia, include funding support to States for
enhanced village relocation/rehabilitation package for people living in core or critical tiger habitats
(from Rs. 1 lakh/family to Rs. 10 lakhs/family), rehabilitation/resettlement of communities involved
in traditional hunting, mainstreaming livelihood and wildlife concerns in forests outside tiger
reserves and fostering corridor conservation through restorative strategy to arrest habitat
fragmentation.
8. A scientific methodology for estimating tiger (including co-predators, prey animals and
assessment of habitat status) has been evolved and mainstreamed. The findings of this estimation/
assessment are bench marks for future tiger conservation strategy.
9. An area of 32578.78 sq. km. has been notified by 16 Tiger States (out of 17) as core or
critical tiger habitat under section 38V of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, as amended in 2006
(Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya
Pradesh, Maharashtra, Mizoram, Orissa, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and
West Bengal). The State of Bihar has taken a decision for notifying the core or critical tiger habitat
(840 sq.km.).
Financial steps
10. Financial and technical help is provided to the States under various Centrally Sponsored
Schemes, viz. Project Tiger and Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats for enhancing the
capacity and infrastructure of the States for providing effective protection to wild animals.
International Cooperation
11. India has a Memorandum of Understanding with Nepal on controlling trans-boundary illegal
trade in wildlife and conservation, apart from a protocol on tiger conservation with China.
12. A Global Tiger Forum of Tiger Range Countries has been created for addressing
international issues related to tiger conservation.
13. During the 14 th meeting of the Conference of Parties to CITES, which was held from
3rd to 15 th June, 2007 at The Hague, India introduced a resolution along with China, Nepal and the
Russian Federation, with directions to Parties with operations breeding tigers on a commercial
scale, for restricting such captive populations to a level supportive only to conserving wild tigers.

42
The resolution was adopted as a decision with minor amendments. Further, India made an
intervention appealing to China to phase out tiger farming, and eliminate stockpiles of Asian big cats

14. Based on India’s strong intervention during the 58
th meeting of the Standing Committee of

8. Field strategies with sub-activities
(a) Stepping up protection: (antipoaching squad/Tiger Protection Force deployment)
The antipoaching operations in Tiger Reserves are site specific. However, the following

(b) Deciding inviolate spaces for wildlife and relocation of villagers from core or critical
tiger habitats in Tiger Reserves within a timeframe and settlement of rights:
The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, as well as the Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional
Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006, require that rights of people (Scheduled
Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers) recognized in forest areas within core/critical tiger/wildlife
habitats of tiger reserves/protected areas may be modified and resettled for providing inviolate spaces
to tiger/wild animals. This requires payment of compensation (rights settlement in addition to the
relocation package offered under the CSS at present). Chapter IV of the Wild Life (Protection) Act,
1972 (Section 24) provides for acquisition of rights in or over the land declared by the State
Government under Section 18 (for constituting a Sanctuary) or Section 35 (for constituting a National
Park). Sub-section 2 of Section 24 of the Wild Life (Protection) Act, authorizes the Collector to
acquire such land or rights. Therefore, payment of compensation for the immovable property of
people forms part of modifying/settling their rights which is a statutory requirement.
The ongoing study and the analysis of the available research data on tiger ecology indicate
that the minimum population of tigresses in breeding age, which are needed to maintain a viable
population of 80-100 tigers (in and around core) require an inviolate space of 800-1200 sq. km.
Tiger being an “umbrella species”, this will also ensure viable populations of other wild animals
(co-predators, prey) and forest, thereby ensuring the ecological viability of the entire area/habitat.
Thus, it becomes an ecological imperative to keep the core areas of tiger reserves inviolate for the
survival of source populations of tiger and other wild animals.
The proposed package has two options:
Option I – Payment of the entire package amount (Rs. 10 lakhs per family) to the family
in case the family opts so, without involving any rehabilitation/relocation process by the
Forest Department.
Option II – Carrying out relocation/rehabilitation of village from protected area/tiger reserve
by the Forest Department.
(c) Strengthening of infrastructure within Tiger Reserves:
The following activities, inter alia , would form part of reinforcing the infrastructure of
Tiger Reserves (including support to new tiger reserves):

46
• Civil Works (staff quarters, family hostels, office improvement, patrolling camp, house
keeping buildings, museum, culverts).
• Maintenance/creation/upgradation of road network.
• Maintenance/creation of wireless tower.
• Maintenance/creation of fire watch tower.
• Maintenance/creation of bridges, dams, anicuts.
• Maintenance/creation of firelines/firebreaks.
• Maintenance/creation of earthen ponds.
• Procurement/maintenance of vehicles (Gypsy, Jeep, Truck, Tractor).
• Habitat improvement works.
• Procurement of hardware, software/GIS.
• Procurement of compass, range finder, GPS, camera traps.
• Procurement of satellite imageries for management planning.
• Map digitization facility for management planning.
(d) Habitat improvement and water development:
These, inter alia , may include:  weed eradication, removal of gregarious plant growth from
grasslands, grass improvement, water retention structures and the like. These initiatives would
increase the forage and browse values of the habitat for wild animals.
(e) Addressing man-animal conflict (ensuring uniform, timely compensation for human
deaths due to wild animals, livestock depredation by carnivores, crop depredation by wild
ungulates) (compensation for crop loss is a new component):
This would involve:
• Payment of compensation for cattle lifting, death of human beings and crop
depredation due to wild animals.
• Creation of crop protection structures.
• Procurement/deployment of traps, cages to catch problematic animals.
• Procurement of tranquilizing equipments, rescue vehicles and drugs.
(f) Co-existence agenda in buffer/fringe areas:
The fringe areas around Tiger Reserve have corridor value, and their ecological
sustainability is important to prevent the area from becoming ecological sinks on account of over
use of resources and unwise land use. This calls for delineation of buffer zone around a tiger
reserve to incorporate such fringe areas so that it can fulfill the following objectives:
• Providing ecologically viable livelihood options to local stakeholders for reducing their
dependency on forests.
• Conserving the forest area through restorative inputs involving local people for
providing habitat supplement to wild animals moving out of core areas.

47
(g) Rehabilitation of traditional hunting tribes living around tiger reserves:
There is an urgent need to launch a rehabilitation and development programme for the
denotified tribes and tribes involved in traditional hunting, living around tiger reserves and tiger
corridors. The following denotified tribes/communities are involved in traditional hunting of wild
animals : Behelias, Ambalgars, Badaks, Mongias, Bavariyas, Monglias, Pardhi, Boyas, Kaikads,
Karwal Nat, Nirshikaris, Picharis, Valayaras, Yenadis, Chakma, Mizo, Bru, Solung and Nyishi. While
this list is not exhaustive, around 5,000 such families are required to be taken up under a welfare
programme (forming part of NTCA initiatives) during the Plan period. The rehabilitation/welfare
package should be evolved in a site specific, consultative manner with livelihood options, to include :
wages for such people towards their deployment in foot patrolling for protecting wildlife, providing
agricultural land with irrigation, basic health care, housing and related community welfare inputs
and basic education facilities. The experience gained in the past for settling denotified tribes by the
salvation army is required to be considered dispassionately while structuring the programme.
(h) Research and field equipments:
The All India tiger estimation using the new methodology approved by the Tiger task Force
has resulted in a permanent monitoring protocol for the field units. The Phase-IV tiger reserve level
would be launched to monitor the source populations of tiger. Further, assistance would be
provided for fostering field oriented research and to equip the staff with facilities like GPS, camera
traps, night vision, range finder and related accessories including hardware and software.
(i) Staff development and capacity building:
This would involve:
• Capacity building/training.
• Providing project allowance and special incentives.
• Specialized training in the use of GIS, antipoaching operations.
• Specialized training in jurisprudence and wildlife forensics.
• Study tours for appraisal of good practices in other reserves.
• Dissemination workshops.
• Specialized training in park interpretation.
• Specialized training in management planning.
The above inputs are extremely important for enhancing the skill of field staff. Several
instances of poaching occur for want of specialized training in crime detection and related skills.
(j) Mainstreaming wildlife concerns in tiger bearing forests and fostering corridor
conservation through restorative strategy involving locals to arrest fragmentation of
habitats:
This would involve:
• Redressing man-animal conflict.
• Capturing problematic/aberrant wild animals.
• Monitoring of wild animals.
• Antipoaching operations.
• Habitat improvement measures.

48
(k) Safeguards/Retrofitting measures in the interest of wildlife conservation:
Several Tiger Reserves are affected on account of heavily used infrastructure like roads, railway
tracks and others. The high tension electric lines passing through many reserves cause mortality of wild
animals due to electrocution by poachers. In the interest of wild animals several safeguards as well as
retrofitting measures may be required, which would be supported on a site-specific basis.
(l) Providing basic infrastructure/Project Tiger Headquarter expenditure for consultancy,
all India tiger estimation/continuous monitoring of tigers outside tiger reserves,
strengthening of NTCA at the Center. The following are envisaged:
• Creation of office space at Delhi for National Tiger Conservation Authority.
• Carrying out All India Tiger Estimation, monitoring.
• Support to research work.
• Contractual arrangement for special studies.
• International/National Workshops.
• Contractual arrangement for data entry, analysis.
(m) Independent monitoring and evaluation of tiger reserves:
The second round of independent monitoring has been completed using globally accepted
indicators. This would be further refined and continued.
(n) Establishment and development of new Tiger Reserves:
‘Project Tiger’ has a holistic ecosystem approach. Though the focus is on the flagship
species ‘tiger’, the project strives to maintain the stability of ecosystem by fostering other trophic
levels in the food chain. This is essential to ensure an ecologically viable population of tiger, which
is at the ‘apex’ of the ecological food chain. The community pressures on forests are ever on the
increase in developing countries, and India is no exception. As a sequel, the tiger habitat has
become fragile and weak at several places, warranting a focused conservation approach. Our
protected areas/Tiger Reserves are analogous to “islands” in an ocean of the other-use patterns.
Empirical evidences from ‘island biogeography’ indicate that “isolated” reserves lose their species
rapidly owing to ‘ecological insularization’. Further, apart from fragmentation, the situation is
aggravated by degraded forest cover owing to biotic pressure, dislocated prey – predator ratio,
absence of effective measures to ensure the desired level of protection and lack of eco
developmental initiatives for the fringe dwelling stake holders to reduce their dependency on forest
resources. Since ‘Project Tiger’ would go a long way in redressing the above situation, the
Steering Committee of Project Tiger in its meeting held on 23.1.2003 recommended inclusion of
new Tiger Reserve areas so as to increase the total area of Project Tiger from existing 37761 sq.
kms. to 50,000 sq. kms. during the Tenth Plan period.
(o) Provision of Project Allowance to staff of Project Tiger:
The tiger States would be supported (100%) for Project Allowance to staff of Tiger
Reserves.
(p) Staff welfare activities:
Staff welfare inputs like residential accommodation for the children of frontline staff in
nearby towns/villages, supply of kerosene, medicine, field kit, mosquito net, torch and the like
would be supported.

49
(q) Fostering Eco-Tourism in Tiger Reserves:
‘Ecotourism’ in the context of Tiger Reserves is ecologically sustainable nature-tourism,
which is emerging as an important component of tourism industry. It is distinct from ‘mass
tourism’, having sustainable, equitable, community based effort for improving the living standards
of local, host communities living on the fringes of Tiger Reserves. Ecotourism is proposed to
be fostered with financial support to the host community through ‘soft loans’ from
Ecodevelopment Committees, in accordance with site – specific ‘Ecotourism plan’ and carrying
capacity of Tiger Reserves in the buffer areas. The core/critical tiger habitats would not be used
for any form of tourism, and the ongoing tourism activities in such areas should be phased out
in the fringe/buffer areas, without affecting its corridor value. The development of tourism
related facilities within the buffer zones of Tiger Reserves would continue with inputs under
Project Tiger. The opportunities for stakeholders would include management of low cost
accommodation for tourists, providing guide services, providing sale outlets, managing
excursions, organizing ethnic dances and the like.

1
REPORT
The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Space on
the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred and Twenty Fifth Report of the Department-
related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests on
the Demands for Grants (2012-13) of the Department of Space, which was presented to both the
Houses of Parliament on 18
th May, 2012. There were fifteen recommendations in the Two Hundred
and Twenty Fifth Report of the Committee. Action Taken notes on the recommendations of the
Committee were received from the Department on 5 th September, 2012.
The Committee’s recommendations, action taken thereon and comments of the Committee
on the Action Taken by the Department of Space are set out in the succeeding paragraphs.
MONITORING MECHANISM FOR ONGOING SCHEMES
Recommendation (Para 5.3)
The Committee is of the view that an effective monitoring mechanism is vital to ensure that
the various projects are completed as per the schedule and there is no time or cost overruns. In
this context, the Committee appreciates the adoption of the Result Framework Document (RFD)
by the Department, which aims towards an effective appraisal of the actual physical and financial
progress/achievements in implementation of policies/programmes in comparison to the projected
targets for each programme. The Committee, in view of strengthening of monitoring mechanism,
hopes that the Department would, in future, be able to ensure timely completion of projects and
optimum utilization of funds.
Action Taken by Government
The views of the Committee are noted. The Department will continue to put an effort to
ensure timely completion of projects with optimum utilization of funds.
Comments
The Committee hopes that the Department will make a critical review of its
monitoring mechanism and plug the gaps, wherever necessary, so as to preclude any scope
of time and cost overruns.
ELEVENTH PLAN ACHIEVEMENTS AND TWELFTH FIVE YEAR PLAN
Recommendation (Para 6.2)
The Committee appreciates the achievements made by the Department during the Eleventh
Plan, notably the Chandrayaan-1 Mission and progress made in the field of Launch Vehicle
Development, Earth Observation and Satellite Communication Systems. However, it notes with
concern that some of the missions such as Radar Imaging Satellite (RISAT-1), Advanced
Meteorological satellite INSAT-3D, Multi-wavelength X-ray astronomy satellites ASTROSAT,
SARAL, GSAT-9, GSAT-10, GSAT-6/6A, GSAT-11 and IRNSS could not be completed as per
schedule and shall spill over to the Twelfth Plan period due to technological developmental
complexities, difficulties in sourcing the critical supplies and mission contingencies. The Committee
hopes Department would make all possible efforts to tide over these difficulties and projects would
be completed as per the revised schedule.

2
Action Taken by Government
Noted. It is brought to the notice of the Committee that Radar Imaging Satellite (RISAT-1)
has already been launched on 26 th April, 2012. GSAT-10 satellite is scheduled to be launched in
September, 2012. As recommended by the committee, the Department will make all possible efforts
to complete the remaining spill-over missions as per the revised schedule.
Comments
The Committee congratulates the Department on the successful launch of the RISAT-
I and hopes that the Department will make all out efforts to launch its remaining spill-over
missions during the Twelfth Plan period.
Recommendation (Para 6.5 and 6.6)
The Committee notes that in the Twelfth Five Year Plan (2012-17) the major thrust of the
Indian Space programme will be to carry forward and strengthen the already established space based
services aimed at socio-economic development of the country. The Committee hopes that, apart from
the ongoing space programmes and its efforts for developing advanced launch vehicles, the
Department should also strive for mastering critical technologies, so as to reduce the chances of
failure of important missions. The Committee is of the opinion that the next stepping stone of the
Department should be to strive towards sending a Manned Mission to Space, which naturally follows
from its successes obtained in sending launch vehicles which can carry higher payloads to space.
Action Taken by Government
Noted. Department has taken up activities for development of critical technologies required
for the advanced missions such as Re-usable Launch V ehicles, Manned Spaceflight, advanced
communication satellite, sub-meter resolution remote sensing satellites and planetary exploration.
The Department is also actively pursuing the development of the heavy lift launch vehicle, the
GSLV-MkIII.
Recommendation (Para 6.6)
The Committee also recommends that Department should also strive to increase its global
market share in space services by developing more innovative and competitive space services on
commercial lines and the revenue generated from marketing of these services, should be used for
further growth and development of space technology in the country. This will also increasingly
reduce the dependence of our space programme on budgetary resources.
Action Taken by Government
Noted. Department is pursuing the commercial activities through Antrix Corporation Limited.
Space Services in the global market is provided by Antrix in the areas of Remote Sensing Data,
Value Added Services, Communication Transponders, design and development of custom-built
satellite, PSLV Launch Services and Ground Station Services. The Annual Revenue of Antrix has
grown from Rs. 940.26 crores in 2007-08 to Rs. 1179.92 crores (provisional) in 2011-12. Antrix
has plans to further expand its activities to increase its share in space services in the global market
in the coming years.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply of the Department and hopes that Antrix would be
able to secure a respectable share in global market in space services in the near future.

3
MANNED MISSION INITIATIVE
Recommendation (Para 8.3)
The Committee notes with concern that a programme initiated in the year 2006 and having
target date of 2014 as its completion, is yet to get a final approval even for its Phase 1
programme. It shows that the Department is either not serious in timely completion of the project
or has casually fixed a schedule for its completion. It also reflects a lack of proper planning and
effective monitoring, as also absence of adequate research and technological support for timely
execution of the project. The Committee, however hopes that the pre-project activities would be
expeditiously completed and approval for Phase 1 of the programme obtained, so that the project
is completed as per schedule in the year 2014.
Action Taken by Government
Noted. After a careful consideration of the magnitude of efforts, investments and
technological complexities involving development of a host of new technologies in diverse areas,
it was decided to take up the Manned Mission Programme in a phased manner focusing on the
development of critical technologies in the initial phase. Accordingly, the pre-project activities in the
areas of Crew module development, Environmental Control and Life Support System etc. are
progressing satisfactorily.
Comments
The Committee finds that the Department in its reply has  neither advanced any
reason for the delay nor underlined the efforts made by them to complete its pre-project
activities. The Committee,  therefore, reiterates that the pre-project activities for the
mission may be completed within a fixed time-frame.
CHANDRAYAAN-2 AND MARS ORBITER MISSION
Recommendation (Para 9.5)
The Committee after going thoroughly through the aforesaid reply of the Department is of
the opinion that preparation of an optimistic schedule for missions like Chandrayaan-2 and Mars
Orbiter Mission, alone is not sufficient but what is required is the will and dedication to complete
the mission target within the time schedule. If time schedule does not inspire the confidence of
the team and is seen by it as an unrealistic target, it will hardly serve any purpose. The Department
should therefore, fix time schedules in a more realistic way, rather than fixing time schedules
which are not to be adhered. The Committee feels that failure to adhere to programme schedule
sends a wrong message to the public and lowers their confidence in our capability to take our
space programme to new heights. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
schedule for all missions including complex missions should be prepared only after taking into
account all ground realities, so that a realistic schedule meant to be adhered by all, rather than that
being violated with impunity, is prepared.
Action Taken by Government
Noted. Department prepares schedules for the project taking into account the development
time required for the key/new technologies and the lead time required for fabrication, assembly,
integration and testing activities. The Department has also implemented a Project Management
Structure involving multi-level periodical reviews of the project progress to ensure that the projects

4
are realized within the targeted schedule. Chandrayaan-2 was approved in September, 2008 as an
Indo-Russian joint mission with an objective of carrying out in-situ Lunar surface studies using
Moon Lander and Rover. Russia had the responsibility of developing the ‘Moon Lander and Rover’,
while India had the responsibility of developing the ‘Moon Orbiter’ and launch by Geo-synchronous
Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV).
However, based on the suggestion from Russian side, technical configuration of
Chandrayaan-2 mission was revised in February 2010. As per the revised plan, Russia took the
responsibility to realize the ‘Moon Lander’ and ISRO took up the responsibility to realize the Rover
and module.
Subsequent to the failure of the Russian interplanetary mission Phobos-Grunt, Russian side
has proposed for a shift in approach for Chandrayaan-2 mission in a recent meeting held at
Bangalore on May 12, 2012. As per the communication, Russia wants to increase the reliability of
their planetary missions by incorporating additional redundant systems. As a result, the mass of the
proposed ‘Moon Lander’ is likely to increase and the Lander will be made available only during
2014. These recent inputs from Russia have called for a programmatic realignment for
Chandrayaan-2 mission which is being examined by the Department. However, the Department
would continue to strive hard and spare no efforts in meeting the project time schedules.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
INDIAN INSTITUTE OF SPACE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
Recommendation (Para 10.3)
The Committee commends the initiative of the Department in setting up of the Indian
Institute of Space Science and Technology (IIST) for developing high quality man power required
for our space programmes and research. The Committee is further happy to note that it is Asia’s
first Space Institute to offer the complete range of courses related to space sciences. The
Committee hopes that the Institute would turn into a centre of excellence imparting high quality
space education and producing highly skilled and proficient space scientists and technologists. The
Committee is happy to note that a large numbers of students are competing for admission to the
IIST, which indicates growing popularity and importance of the institute.
Action Taken by the Government
Noted. From the current academic year, the institute has started four Post Graduation
programmes in the areas of RF and Microwave Engineering, Aerospace Propulsion Engineering,
Optical-Engineering and Digital Signal Processing. Moreover, the Institute is offering doctoral
programme in various areas of research which are relevant to Space and advanced technology areas
which would enable IIST to become a centre of excellence.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply of the Department.
OCEANSAT AND RESOURCESAT PROGRAMMES
Recommendation (Para 11.5)
The Committee observes that for both the Oceansat 2 and 3 and Resourcesat 2 and 3

5
programmes, there has been a trend to seek substantial budgetary allocations at B.E. stage without
making an extensive and critical assessment of the actual requirements. The Committee feels that
budgetary demands should be sought by the Department only after comprehensive analysis of the
actual fund requirement for the programme. Scarce resources should not be blocked by asking for
ambitious allocations and not utilizing them subsequently. These instances are also a reflection on
the capacity of the Department to plan its projects, efficiently, set realistic targets and its
determination to achieve the targets set.
Action Taken by Government
Noted.
Comments
The Committee expresses its displeasure that the Department has not initiated any
action in pursuance of the observations of the Committee and has simply noted it. The
Committee hopes that the Department would, in future, make extensive and critical
assessments of its actual requirements.
TELE-MEDICINE
Recommendation (Para 12.4)
The Committee feels that Telemedicine is a very useful programme pursued by the
Department for providing societal benefits by use of space technology to the common masses. The
Committee is aware that to provide even the basic healthcare facilities in all the villages of the
country, would require a huge capital investment, both in terms of manpower and resources. The
Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that this is a very cost effective method for providing
quality healthcare facilities in the rural and remote areas of the country. The Committee
recommends that the telemedicine network should be expanded in a time-bound manner to cover
the backward, remote, inaccessible or disease-prone areas, left out so far.
Action Taken by Government
Noted. Since 2001, ISRO has been providing Telemedicine nodes in a phased manner. It
covers remote regions of the country including J&K, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep
islands and most of the mainland States.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply of the Department and presumes that the
Department will spread their telemedicine programme over to other left out places soon.
Recommendation (Para 12.5)
The Committee also notes that due to the failure of the launch vehicle carrying the
GSAT-5P satellite, the expansion of telemedicine network work was adversely affected. The
Committee is happy to note that with the successful launch of GSAT-12, the telemedicine activities
are being restored. The Committee hopes that the migration of telemedicine network to GSAT-12
satellite, which is currently in progress, will be completed soon and the expansion of the facility
will be pursued with vigour.

6
Action Taken by Government
Noted. Two transponders in GSAT-12 satellite are allotted by INSAT Coordination
Committee (ICC) for tele-medicine programme. Out of 382 tele-medicine nodes, 190 tele-
medicine nodes were planned to be migrated to GSAT-12 satellite and rest of the nodes are to
be operated through INSAT-3A, INSAT-3C and INSAT-4A satellites. Against the 190 nodes that
are scheduled for migration, 165 nodes have already been migrated and actions are taken to
migrate the remaining nodes. In order to ensure the effective utilization of all the tele-medicine
nodes, steps are taken up by DOS/ISRO to enter into an appropriate maintenance agreements and
for monitoring activities.
Comments
The Committee applauds the Department for migration of 165 nodes out of 190 and
hopes that the migration of the remaining nodes would be done soon.
DISASTER MANAGEMENT SUPPORT SYSTEM
Recommendation (Para 13.3)
The Committee is of the view that natural disasters such as floods, droughts, cyclones,
earthquakes and landslides are a recurring phenomena and every year widespread economic
devastation and loss of human lives is caused on account of these natural calamities. The
Committee is of the opinion that the services of Virtual Private Network (VPN) which has been
set up for networking the State and district level emergency control centres for natural disasters
management must be optimally utilized for rapid dissemination of information to lessen the human
and economic loss.
Action Taken by Government
Noted. Presently, the satellite based Virtual Private Network set up under the Disaster
Management Support (DMS) Programme offers connectivity to the following:
(i) 20 State Emergency Operation centres (Andhra Pradesh, Andaman and Nicobar
Islands, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Delhi, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala,
Maharashtra, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Orissa, Sikkim, Tamil
Nadu, Tripura, Uttarakhand, and West Bengal)
(ii) 5 observation nodes (Prime Minister Office, Prime Minister residence, National
Disaster Management Authority, Delhi, Cabinet Secretariat, Delhi, and Control Room
North Block)
(iii) 10 primary nodes (National Remote sensing Centre, Hyderabad, National Remote
Sensing Centre, Shadnagar, Indian Meteorological Department, Central Water
Commission, Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services, Geologlcal
Survey of India, New Delhi, Space Application Centre, Ahmedabad; NESAC, Shillong;
Master Control Facility, Hassan and National Institute of Disaster Management, Delhi)
The Virtual Private Network which was earlier functional through INSAT-3E satellite is re-
established to its full capacity by allotting a full transponder in GSAT-12 and all the nodes are now
re-aligned with GSAT-12. To further optimize the usage of the network, periodical meetings of the
nodal officers from the States and the data providing nodes will be organized.

7
Comments
The Committee is happy to hear that Virtual Private Network (VPN) has been re-
established to its full capacity by allotting a full transponder in GSAT-12 and reiterates that
efforts may be made to link State and district level emergency control centres through VPN.
SPACE INDUSTRY PARTNERSHIP
Recommendation (Para 14.3)
The Committee is of the opinion that active involvement and effective participation of more
and more Indian industries in providing quality products and services needed for our Space
programme will lead to self-reliance and would decrease our dependence on foreign industries for
space equipments and technologies. The involvement of Indian industries in production of
aggregates/systems for the Indian Space programme would augment the technical expertise of the
Indian industry and would also lead to employment generation. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Department of Space should make concerted efforts in this direction. The
Committee also desires that Department of Space should look forward to transfer more and more
technologies which may be useful for civilian applications to Indian Industries so as to make them
globally competitive.
Action Taken by Government
Noted. Department has been progressively increasing the participation of Indian Industries
in the Space Programme. The focus has been to upgrade the Indian Industries from mere supplier
of parts/components/subsystem to system level integrator. The Indian Industries are also supported
with transfer of ISRO developed technologies to make them globally competitive.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.
FAILURE ANALYSIS COMMITTEE (FAC)
Recommendation (Para 15.4)
After going through the replies of the Department of Space and findings of FAC, the
Committee is of the opinion that the Department should make efforts to develop our indigenous
cryogenic engines for GSLV and other advanced launch vehicles, as it would make us self reliant
in this important area. The Committee would however like the Department to ensure that every
possible care is taken while launching our satellite so that chances of failure are reduced to the
minimum. It should bear in mind that any failure of our missions, though failures are bound to
happen in such complex missions, not only results in loss of crores of rupees but also raises a
doubt in the mind of the people about the credibility of our space programme.
Action Taken by Government
Noted. Development of indigenous cryogenic engines for GSLV is a critical milestone for
making India’s launch vehicle programme self-reliant. Hence the development of indigenous
cryogenic is being taken up on priority basis. The recommendations of Failure Analysis Committees
(FAC) have been implemented in the realization of the indigenous cryogenic upper stage for the
next development flight of GSLV , i.e., GSLV-D5.
Comments
The Committee notes the reply.

MINUTES

11

PREFACE
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science
and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the
Report on its behalf, present this Two Hundred Thirty Sixth Report on the Action Taken by the
Ministry of Earth Sciences on the recommendations contained in Two Hundred Twenty Sixth

2. The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Earth Sciences
on the recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Twenty Sixth Report of the Department-
related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests on
the Demands for Grants (2012-2013) of the Ministry of Earth Sciences which was presented to
the Rajya Sabha on 18
th May, 2012.
3. There were twenty two recommendations contained in the Two Hundred Twenty Sixth
Report of the Committee. Action Taken Notes on the recommendations of the Committee were
received from the Ministry on 27
th July, 2012.

Taken Report and adopted the same.
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY
