12.6 The Committee, however, would like to see such benefits extended further to 
cover more and more scheduled castes  and scheduled tribes population and 
accordingly, recommends that the Depa rtment should further expand this 
programme.  
13. MODERNISATION OF MAPPING ORGANIZATIONS (SoI AND 
NATMO) 
13.1 The National Atlas and Thematic Mappi ng Organization set up in 1956 primarily 
aims at preparing National Atlas of India.  Subsequently, its scop e and activities were 
extended to new fields of geographical research, themat ic mapping covering all the 
academic and applied aspects of geography and allied subject.   
13.2 Survey of India, the National Survey  and Mapping Organisation of the country 
under the Department of Science & Tech nology, is the oldest organisation of 
Government of India, set up in 1767.  As the Nation’s principal mapping agency, SoI 
bears special responsibility to ensure that  the country’s domain is  explored and mapped 
suitably to provide base maps  for expeditious and integrated development and that all 
resources contribute their full  measure to the progress, pros perity and security of our 
country now and for generations to come.  Th e Department is undertaking infrastructure 
modernization and technical skill developmen t of Survey of India (SoI) and National 
Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organi zation (NATMO) under the programme 
“Modernization of Mapping Organizations”.  
13.3 So far as the Budgetary allocations are concerned, the Committee finds that 
programme for Modernisation of Mapping Or ganisations was allocated   350.86 Crores 
at B.E. 2012-13 which was reduced to Rs 333.0 7 crores at R.E. 2012- 13 i.e. a reduction 
of  17.79 crores. However, the Department could utilise an amount of  276.36 crores 
by 22
nd February,2013 thus showing underutilisa tion of 66.71crores.  At B.E. 2013-14, 
allocation has been incr eased to .348.62 crores i.e. an increase of about 15.55 crores 
over R.E. 2012-13, despite the fact that both SoI and NATMO failed to fully utilize the 
B.E. allocation. When asked about the reas ons for underutilisation of fund, the 
Department replied that the curtailment of funds at RE 2012-2013 stage was mainly 
attributable to 10% cut imposed on Non-Plan  expenditure by Ministry of Finance.  
Further, from the ‘Salaries’ head of SoI, .11.47 crores was curtailed due to non-
proportionate expenditure.   Hence the allocati ons of both organizations were reduced by 
.17.79 crores at R.E. 2012-13.   

13.4 The Committee desired to know as to  what measures were taken for 
modernization of SoI and NATMO.  Informin g about the schemes for modernization of 
NATMO & SoI, the Department informed th at during the financial year 2013-14, both 
SoI and NATMO proposed to initiate certain schemes and measures for modernization.  
Survey of India proposed to take up the following Plan Schemes : 
(i) Formation of Geospatial Data set fo r National Geospatial Information System 
(NGIS) 
(ii) Redefinition of India Vertical Datum 
(iii) Creation of National Topogra phical Database on 1:10,000 scale 
(iv) Modernization of Tidal Gauge Network 
13.5 Through these Schemes, efforts would be made to mode rnize/upgrade the 
equipments, hardware and software availa ble in SoI; Introduce new technological 
innovation in the field e.g. Advance methods  of Data Capturing, Digital Aerial 
Photography, Digital Photogramme tric Processing, Data storage and Dissemination, etc.  
Capacity building of the human resources by  upgradation of techni cal skills; and up 
gradation and modernisation of the office buildings and other estates. 
13.6 NATMO proposed to mould its activities towards the path forward into the Geo-
spatial space by way of using geo-spatial te chniques in preparation of Micro, macro and 
meso-level maps in NATMO.  Software, Ha rdware, Computer peripherals, Geospatial 
Information system (GIS), Global Positio ning System (GPS) gadgets were being 
procured by NATMO.  NATMO is using GIS,  GPS and Remote Sensing techniques and 
their utilities for catering to geo-spatial data  and other utilities which could be used for 
planning and development by the government bodies as well as the common people of 
the country. The Rashtriya Atlas Bhavan of NATMO is going to be completed very soon 
which will house a special Geo-spatial laboratory.   
13.7 The Committee notes that the Department  is undertaking modernisation and   
upgradation of infrastructure and techni cal capabilities of SoI and NATMO under 
the programme “Modernisation of Mappi ng Organisations”.  The Committee, 
however, notes that in the year 2012-13, Department failed to fully utilise funds 
made available to it under this programme .  Modernisation of infrastructural 
facilities and upgradation of data capturing and processing capabilities and 
technical skills of these organisations a re  essential for efficient exploration and 
mapping of the country's domain and to ensure that all resources  available in the 
country contribute their full measures to the progress, prosperity and security of 
our country.  The Committee, therefore, expresses its displeasure that the 
Department has not even been able to fu lly utilise funds meant for upgradation of 
infrastructure of its two important or ganisations and recommends that the 
Department should take all necessary measures to ensure early and successful 
implementation of this programme.   
14. DISHA PROGRAMME FOR WOMEN SCIENTISTS 
14.1 The Department informed the Committee that during the year 2012-13, under this 
programme 20 new projects to benefit women had been sanctioned. Apart from this, 176 
projects under Women Scient ists Programme (WOS)-A schol arship scheme; 29 projects 
under WOS-B scholarship scheme and 100 sc holarships for training in IPR under WOS-
C scheme were sanctioned by the Department during 2012-13.  
14.2 The Department further informed that ‘DISHA’ for women science and 
technology professionals have been re-looked and redesigned in a holistic manner. New 
initiatives have also been incorporated to address the mobility issue among the women 

scientists and to use the women scientific pool available to work and address societal 
issues through technological solutions and effective science communication.  
14.3 Coming to budgetary allocations to the programme the Committee finds that at 
BE 2012-13, the DISHA programme was allocated . 49 crores and have been enhanced 
by . 4 crores i.e. . 53 crores during the current fiscal 2013-14.   
14.4 The Committee notes that DISHA Programme has been launched by the 
Department to encourage women to pursue a career in science research as also for 
augmenting the pool of women scientists in the country and is a socially useful 
programme.  The Department has funded projects and provided scholarship to 
women scientists under this programme.  Th e Committee, further, notes that there 
has been a marginal increase in the funds allocated to the programme in the current 
fiscal year and hopes that Department will make efficient use of funds allocated in a 
transparent  and objective manner so th at objectives of the programme are 
achieved. 
15. SCHOLARSHIPS FOR RETAININ G RESEARCH TALENT AND 
PROMOTION OF SCIENCE IN THE COUNTRY 
15.1 The Committee desired to know the de tails of efforts being made by the 
Department for retaining research talent in  the Country and initia tives announced in the 
new Science, Technology and Innovation Policy, 2013  to check brain-drain. Replying to 
the query the Department informed that Ministry of Science and Technology is 
implementing several initiatives including the fellowship scheme to attract and retain 
Indian scientists who have se ttled in various part s of the world for pu rsuing research in 
India in their respective field of  expertise as well as in home country research programs.  
These initiatives include:-  
(i)  “Ramanujan Fellowships” seeks to attract brilliant scientists and engineers from all 
over the world to take up scientific research  in India. The Ramanujan Fellows can work 
in any of the scientific institutions and universities in the country and they are eligible for 
receiving regular research grants through the extramural funding schemes of various S&T 
agencies of the Government of India. Sin ce its inception, 184 Indian origin scientists 
working abroad have been offered this “Fellowship”  
(ii)    “ Innovation in Science Pursuit for Insp ired Research (INSPIRE)” Faculty 
Award under ‘Assured Opportunity for Research  Careers (AORC)’ scheme initiated in 
July, 2011 provides opportunity to the scie ntists under 32 years of age who have 
completed their doctoral research from any recognized university/ academic institution in 
the world. Each “INSPIRE Faculty Awardee”  receives a consolidated amount equivalent 
to the scale of the Assistant Professor of an IIT as Fello wship amount with .7 lakh per 
year as Research Grant for 5 years.   
(iii) Collaborative projects with Scientists  and Technologists of Indian Origin (CP-
STIO): The programme seeks to attract the Scientists and Technologists of Indian Origin 
for strengthening institutional and human capacity building.  
(iv)    Young Investigator Meet (YIM): It is organized every year in India and overseas 
to create awareness amongst scientists working in overseas laboratories.  
15.2 The Department has further informed  that with stagnation of R&D funding 
systems in developed economies and improveme nts in R&D funding pattern in India, 
there are indications of reversal  of flow of researchers at this time especially after the 
implementation of 6
th pay commission recommendations. There are also indications of 
attracting talent from manu facturing sector within th e national employment market. 
While international experience in research is  to be welcomed, bleeding-out of talent for 
research for want of opportunities in India needs to be avoided.  

15.3 Informing about the initiatives take n in the new Science, Technology and 
Innovation Policy 2013 the Department apprised that the Policy envisages making careers 
in science, research and innovation attractiv e enough for talented and bright minds. It 
also envisages, establishing world class infrastructures for R&D; creating an environment 
for enhanced private sector participat ion in R&D and creating a robust national 
innovation system that will be conducive to stop the brain drain.    
15.4 The Committee commends the measures taken by the Department to attract 
and retain Indian scientists who have se ttled in various parts of the world for 
pursuing research in India in their respectiv e field of expertise as well as in home 
country research programs and notes with satisfaction that measures taken have led 
to reversal of flow of researchers.  The Committee recommends that further 
measures be taken to make career in sc ience, research and innovation lucrative 
enough to attract best talent available in the country.   
16. NEW PROGRAMMES PLANNED DURING THE XII PLAN        
16.1 The Department of Science and Technology has started two major new 
programmes namely “Building National Capaci ty and Capability for High Performance 
Computing” and “National Geospatial Informat ion System” (NGIS) in the XII Five Year 
Plan. These are large nationally coordinate d projects with super-ordinate goals and 
expectations.  
16.2 These two programmes have been a llocated budgetary support amounting to 
.100.00 crores and .200.00 crores respec tively at B.E. 2013-14.  The Committee 
desired to know the aims and objectives of these new programmes and the roadmap 
drawn under National Geographic Informati on System (NGIS) to enable smooth 
transition of the country from e-governance to geo-spatial governance.  A brief account 
of aims and objectives of these two schemes provided by the Department is given below:-  
16.3 SUPER COMPUTING FACILITY AND CAPACITY BUILDING : 
The Planning Commission has drawn a Na tional Supercomputing Roadmap in the 
XII Plan which covers seve ral aspects of supercompu ting, namely, architecture, 
supercomputing grid resting on National Know ledge Network and the million core cloud 
supercomputer.  The aim of the scheme is  to undertake projected development of high 
capacity petascale (over 1,000,000,000,000,000 flops) supercomputers and technologies 
that may create an opening lead ing to building Exa-scale (over 
1,000,000,000,000,000,000 flops) supercomputing capability.  It also aims at capacity 
and capability development in the area of hardware and more in the area of application 
software to meet the demands of the scientif ic community from all disciplines. The DST, 
the Department of Electronics & Information Technology (Deity) in consultation with the 
Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru and Center for Development of Advance 
Computing (C-DAC), Pune, are preparin g the strategies for implementing the 
Programme. 
16.4  NATIONAL GEOGRAPHIC INFORMATION SYSTEM (NGIS) 
The NGIS has been set up with the objectives of establishing a “National GIS” as a 
Decision Support GIS-platform with a systematic nation-wide, seamless GIS Asset and to 
realise an organisational stru cture of Indian National GIS Organisation (INGO) that will 
be responsible for National GIS system, maintaining and operating the GIS Platform. 
16.5 The NGIS Mission will also organise the GSIS Asset-GIS database for the whole 
country for the first time.  The Mission woul d also develop National GIS Applications 
software suite required fo r different Ministries for governance. According to the 
Department, the Major elements of the Na tional GIS platform include creation of 

National GIS infrastructure, GIS portal development, National GIS standardization and 
process definition would be a key for success of National GIS.   
16.6 An innovative mission struct ure is planned for implem entation of National GIS, 
which would take care of overlaps and integration and alignment of all efforts to National 
GIS. The apex body of NGIS will be the National GIS Advisory Board (NAB) to provide 
overall policy-direction, advi ce/guide, and review to a ssess performance and suggest 
improvements and fine tuning of Mission and also function as the think tank for NGIS.  
16.7 DST has also constituted a High Power Governing Council (HPGC), with 
Secretaries of Department of Space, the Department of Electronics & Information 
Technology (Deity) and Ministry of Earth Scie nces as Co-Chairs.  A full time Mission 
Director would also be selected with a small and nimble NGIS Mission Directorate. 
16.8 The Committee feels that the above programmes are of great national 
importance and hence recommends that the Department should make every possible 
effort to successfu lly implement them in a time bound manner.  The Committee, 
further, recommends that the Department must ensure that the allocated outlays for 
these two schemes are fully utilized. 
17. The Committee hopes that Department of Science & Technology shall make 
prudent utilisation of funds allocated to it under Demand No. 85 for the year 2013-
14 having due regard to the recommendations made by the Committee and 
efficiently implement its various programmes and schemes in the year 2013-14.

REPORT 
INTRODUCTORY 
 Environment, over the years, has emerged as a key component a nd all pervading theme 
on the broader contours of economic growth w ithin sustainable development framework.  
Environmental concerns in the process of developmental philosophy have, however, 
sharpened further in the recent years with  the consequences of the environmental 
degradation manifesting in numerous ways su ch as global warming, scanty and scattered 
rainfall, changing weather pattern, depleting glaciers, receding water flow in major rivers, 
poor and pathetic state of e nvironmental resources – land, ai r & water and their adverse 
impact on human health, etc. also known as climate cha nge on the one hand and with 
blatant, brazen and reckless exploitation of natural reso urces resulting in massive 
deforestation and degeneration of green covers on the other.  As recently as on 18th April, 
2013, Supreme Court, in its landmark judgment,  decreed that environment & ecology are 
national assets, they are subject to interg enerational equity a nd the principle of 
sustainable development has been  rendered as part of Articl e 21 of the Constitution of 
India.  Yet, the national commitment to a clean and healthy environment as enshrined in 
Articles 48(a) and 51(a)(g) of the Indian Constitution and the aspiration that human 
beings should be able to enj oy a decent quality of  life remains a far cry.  The reasons are 
not far too difficult to find out.  The fact is that the reas ons are both obvious and opaque.  
An evolving and expanding society, such as  ours, in desperate pursuit of economic 
prosperity for poverty alleviation, livelihood secu rity and restoration of  greater justice to 
those deprived is bound to c onfront environmental challe nges.  Secondly, exponential 
population growth, inappropriate  technology, consumption choi ces, paradigm shift in 
amicable and harmonious relationship of co-existence between people and ecosystem, 
proliferation of polluting indus tries, unplanned urbanisation, etc. have prominently and 

routinely been attributed to be the chie f drivers of environmental degradation and 
ecological imbalances.  But there are certain ot her latent yet potent contributory factors 
which need attention and focus too.  These ar e institutional failures resulting in lack of 
enforcement of rights of access to and use of  environmental resources, failed and flawed 
regulatory regime, governance constrains in environmental management, policy lacunae, 
disincentivising  environmen tal conservation, to mention a few.  The widely 
acknowledged fact that not much could be done to manage the former category of 
prominent factors catapults us to concentrate more on the latter ones as to how best we 
can overcome them.  Sooner or later, this ha s to be done in recogni tion of the axiomatic 
fact that environmental resources play pivot al role not only in pr oviding livelihoods but 
also in securing life supportin g ecological services to all forms of life – human, animal 
and plant.  But, the sooner done is better because environmental damages beyond a 
certain degree, become irreparable and irreversible.   
2. It, therefore, becomes imperative for al l of us to gear and galvanize all the 
resources at our disposal to minimize if not  altogether eliminate the possibilities of 
collateral damage done to the environment, ecology, forests and wildlife. 
3.  Environment is universal, ubiquitous and all pervasiv e comprising of entities – 
natural or manmade, external to oneself and their interrelationships, which provide value 
now or perhaps in the future to mankind.  Mana ging such a vast and wi der rather infinite 
spectrum of challenges, is undoubtedly a daun ting task entrusted to  the Ministry of 
Environment & Forests as a nodal agency in the administrative setup of the Govt. of 
India.  The ministry, since its inception on 4
th January, 1985 has been, through thick and 
thins of overriding and pres sing priorities, sometimes c onflicting and contradictory 
engaged in trying to strike a fine bala nce by planning, promoting, coordinating and 
overseeing environmental, ecological forestry and wildlife programmes and policies.  The 
main activities of the Ministry involve prot ection of the environment; conservation and 
survey of existing forests, wildlife, aqua tic bodies, water resources and eco-systems 
including biodiversity and ot her resources particularly in eco-sensitive zones for 
identification of new species of flora and fauna; afforestation and regeneration of 
degraded areas; prevention and control of pollution (air, water, noise, industrial); 
management of hazardous substances; mitigation and adaptation to climate change 
through adoption of cleaner technologies; pr omotion of sustainable development and 
better environmental governance; ensuring welfare of animals; capacity building; training 
and research in classical and molecular taxonomy; etc.  Apart from these national 
activities, the Ministry is also engaged in promoting in ternational cooperation through 
regional, bilateral and multilateral initiatives in the arena of environment and ecology.  
Issues relating to regional bodies like Economic and Social  Council for Asia & Pacific 
(ESCAP) and South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) and 
multilateral bodies such as the Commission on Sustainable Development (CSD); Global 
Environment Facility (GEF) have been entruste d to the Ministry.  Besides, the Ministry 
also serves as the nodal agency for the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), 
South Asia Cooperation Environment Programme  (SACEP) and Intern ational Centre for 
Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMD) , as well as, for follow up on the United 
Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED).  
4. Institutional Setup
 
4.1 The Institutional setup of the Minist ry includes a number of Directorates, 
Divisions, Regional Offices, Subordinate Offi ces, Boards, Autonomous Institutions and 
one Public Sector Undertaking, the details of which are as follows:-

various Zones of the country.  The No rth Zone Regional Office is located 
at Chandigarh; the Central Zone at Lucknow; the Northeastern Zone at 
Shillong and Bhubaneswar; the South Zone at Bengaluru; the Eastern 
plateau or upper East at Ranchi and the West Zone at Bhopal.

5.1 In order to support, assist and guide the Ministry, attain its objectives of 
preservation, conservation and protection of  environment, it has the following main 
Legislations/ Policies:- 
(i) Indian Forest Act, 1927; 
(ii) The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980;

7. Monitorable Targets of XI Five Year Plan 
7.1  As per the Mid-term Appraisal Do cument of the Planning Commission, the 
following 4 monitorable socioeconomic target s in the Environment and Forests Sector 
had been emphasised in the XI Five Year Plan period: 
 To increase forest and tree cover by 5 percentage points; 
 To attain WHO standards of air quality in all major cities by 2011-12; 
 To treat all urban waste water by 2011-12 in order to clean river waters; and 
 To increase energy efficiency by 20 per cent by 2016-17. 
 7.2  When the Committee enquired from the Ministry about the achievements in 
respect of the above targets,  the Ministry did not come out with specific and pointed 
reply.  Going through the replies, it is very  difficult to make out precisely the physical 
achievements.  In reply to the targets of in creasing forest and tree cover by 5 percentage 
points, the Ministry replied that in order to achieve the target of 5 per cent, an additional 
16.5 million hectares forest and tree cover ha d to be obtained by 2012.  But the tree 
planting during the Plan period was around 1.52 million hectare per year which if 
multiplied by 5, gives a figure of 7.6 million hectares during the Plan period, thus 
showing an overall shortage of plantation in  8.9 million hectares.  The Ministry further 
stated that given the constraints of land a nd financial resources, th e achievement of the 
target was ambitious.  With regard to the target of treating all urban waste water by 2011-
12 in order to clean river waters, the Ministry  stated that the primary responsibility of 
treating sewage was with the Municipalities.  The Ministry further added that maintaining 
cleanliness of rivers required minimum river water and it was the Ministry of Water 
Resources, which was the nodal Ministry to ensu re adequate water flow in rivers.  The 
Ministry thus had limited role to play in achie vement of this target.  On the target of 
attaining World Health Organisation standards of Air Quality in all major cities by 2011-
12, the Ministry had a very peculiar reply to offer.  The Ministry felt that the notified 
National Ambient Air Quality Standards in  India, based mostly on United States 
Environmental Protection Agency health Criteria (USEPA) documents and not WHO 
Guidelines would provide a more realistic and appropriate goal fo r achieving better air 
quality in India. Responding to  the monitorable target of en hancing energy efficiency by 
20 per cent points by 2016-17, the Mi nistry tossed the ball in th e court of the Ministry of 
Power stating that action on enhancement of energy efficiency and lowering energy 
intensity was the responsibility  of Ministry of Power.  The Committee feels that if the 
Ministry has to handle the socioeconomic mo nitorable targets given to it in such a 
casual and cavalier manner, the very purpo se of devising and deciding a target 
becomes meaningless.  The Ministry should  have, while or before fixing the target, 
thought as to whether the targets pertained to it or not.  But once the targets were 
set, the Ministry must have  made sincere and serious effo rts to meet them in close 
coordination and cooperation with the ot her concerned Ministries.  The Committee 
takes a very serious view on the way and the manner in which the targets given to 
the Ministry had been handled.  The Commi ttee feels that if the Ministry was not 
serious in trying to seriously pursue the ta rgets set, they must not have accepted 
these monitorable targets at all.  The Committee hopes that monitorable 
socioeconomic targets set for the XII Five Year Plan would not meet the same fate 
as the targets of the XI Five Year Pl an and therefore, recommends, that the 
Ministry should seriously and vigorously pursue the targets and goals set for the XII 
Five Year Plan so as to ensure that concre te achievements in re spect of each target 
are made.

9.4  The Committee enquired from the Mini stry whether the XII Five Year Plan 
allocation was in consonance with the obser vation made by the Pl anning Commission in 
its Mid-term Appraisal of the XI Five Year Pl an Document that an allocation of at least 5 
per cent of the Annual Central Plan Outlay for the Environment and Forestry Sectors 
separately needed to be ensured preferably by the XII Five Year Plan.  The Ministry of 
Environment & Forests stated that neither th e overall XII Five Year Plan allocation nor 
the Annual allocation of the Ministry were in  accordance with the above observations of 
the Planning Commission, despit e the fact that the Minist ry had been consistently 
highlighting the lowering of its relative prio rity in Plan outlay allocations over the 
various Five Year Plans to the Planning Commission, despite growing importance of 
environmental, ecological and forestry issu es over these years.  The Ministry also 
submitted a chart showing percentage share of Environment and Forests Sector in Central 
Plans which is given at Annexure-I.  
9.5  This shows that while the share of th e Ministry in the Central Sector Plan 
allocations was 0.83 per cent in the VII Five Y ear Plan, it came down to 0.48 per cent in 
the VIII Five Year Plan.  After registering some increase over the next two Five Year 
Plans, i.e., IX and X,  the percentage share came down sharpl y to 0.43 per cent in the XI 
Five Year Plan as compared to the 0.67 per cen t in the X Plan and in  the XII Five Year 
Plan, it has further come down to 0.41 per ce nt.  Over the last 4 Annual Plans, the 
declining trend continued unabated.  While in the year 2010-11, the share of Environment 
& Forests Sector in the Annual Central Outlays was to the exte nt of 0.42 per cent, it had 
consistently come down to  0.39 per cent in 2011-12, 0.37 pe r cent in 2012- 13 and this 
year, it has further gone down to 0.36 per cent.   

 
9.6  The Committee expresses its deep anguish  over the declining pe rcentage of share 
for the Ministry of Environment & Forests in the overall Central Plan outlay in the 
successive Five Year Plans/ Annual Pl ans despite increasing importance of 
environmental issues.  The Committee takes a ve ry serious note of the fact that while in 
the VII Five Year Plan, the percentage of share was 0.83 per cent, it has gone down by 
more than 50 per cent to 0.41 per cent in th e XII Five Year Plan.  The Committee is of 
the considered view that Planning Commi ssion must not consider Budgetary Support 
made to Environment & Forests as non-produc tive, non-priority and hence avoidable.  
The Planning Commission needs to understand  and realize that the damage done to 
environment, disturbance made to the ecologi cal balance can’t be easily repaired and 
restored.  It, therefore, becomes expedient that the very process of degradation and 
degeneration of environmenta l resources be contained and minimized to the possible 
extent through preventive and curative measures  before it is too late and it is possible 
inter-alia by mounting environmental surveillance and reinforcing monitoring mechanism 
– the task assigned to Ministry of Environm ent & Forests.  For doing all these sufficient 
monetary support is undoubtedly required.  The Committee, ther efore, recommends 
that the Planning Commission must act on its own observation of allocating 5 per 
cent of the Annual Central Sector Outlay to Environment and Forestry Sectors in 
right earnest.  The Committee also recomme nds that Ministry of Environment & 
Forests must not only forcefully and vigorously take up this matter with the 
Planning Commission but also apprise it of the details of response gathered from the 
Planning Commission in this regard.  The Committee also recommends that the 
Planning Commission must ensure full a llocation of the approved outlay during the 
XII Plan period and should not resort to an y cut at RE Stage in any of the Annual 
Plans unless Ministry itself is not in a positi on to utilise the full allocation.  In any 
case, full requirements of the Ministry of  Environment and Forests must be met.  
The Ministry must, at the same  time, make all out efforts to make full utilisation of 
allocated budgetary outlay so as not to  provide any alibi to the Planning 
Commission for reduction at RE Stage.

his budget speech.  The Ministry can justif y its demand for additional resources only 
when it is able to first utilise th e entire resources allocated to it.  The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that the Mi nistry of Environment & Forests must 
make sincere, serious and potent efforts by way of meticulous  planning, timely 
implementation and stricter monitoring of  schemes/projects and should not come 
out with the same lame and routine excuses for underutilization year after year.   
10.7  The Committee also notes that the Ministry has not been getting annual

Crores which is almost the half of the a nnual allocation during the XII Plan period.  The 
Committee taking a serious view in this ma tter, feels that by doi ng this, Planning 
Commission is making a mockery of a pproved outlay for the XII Plan period.  The 
Committee therefore, recommends that the Planning Commission must desist from 
such practices and allocate budgetary resources in the Annual Plans in proportion it 
is due to the Ministry or else the very pur pose of Five Year Plan allocations gets 
defeated and falsified.
