12.  Impact of lower allocation  
 12.1 The Committee has been informed that substantial reduction in the Plan Outlay 
for 2013-14 has resulted in reduction of allocation even for the key schemes such as 
Climate Change Action Programme, National River Conservation Plan, Indian Council of 
Forestry Research Education, National a fforestation Programme, Green India Mission, 
Biodiversity Conservation; National Coastal Ma nagement Programme and Project Tiger.  
Under the Climate Change Action Programme, the following proposed activities could be 
adversely affected due to reduced allocations: - National Carbonaceous Aerosol 
Programme; Long-Term Ecological Observ atory for Climate Change Studies; 
International Negotiations and Contributions; Capacity Building; National Institute for 
Climate Change Studies and Actions Projects , etc.  Under national Coastal Management 
Programme, the major activities proposed to be undertaken in 2013-14 included mapping, 
delineation of coastal hazard line for entire coast which could be affected because of 
grossly insufficient fund provided for the above mentioned programmes.  Similarly, other 
proposed activities under National River C onservation Plan, National Afforestation 
Programme, Green India Mission, etc. could be adversely affected due to insufficient 
funds. 
12.2  The Committee takes a very serious view on the drastic cut imposed on the 
proposed demand of the Ministry in the year 2013-14, which would adversely affect such 
important and crucial projects, such as climate change, National River Conservation Plan, 
National Afforestation Programme, Green Indian  Mission, Project Tiger, etc.  Making 
such a drastic reduction for such crucial programmes is not at all justified.  The 

Committee feels that the Ministry  was very much within its rights to ask the Plan Outlay 
of Rs. 4690.00 Crores which included the 1/5 th share out of the approved outlay of Rs. 
17874.00 Crores for the XII Plan period amounti ng to Rs. 3574.80 Crores plus the arrear 
of the last year allocation to the tune of Rs. 1144.80.  Besi des, aspects like strengthening 
of the institutions, such as, Central Pollution Control Board and its zonal offices, Wildlife 
Crime Control Bureau and Regional offices of the Ministry, National Green Tribunal, etc. 
are long overdue and need to be addressed urgently.  The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that Planning Commission mu st restore the projected demand of the 
Ministry at the RE Stage so that the Mini stry is able to carry on its proposed 
activities properly.  At the same time , the Committee also recommends that the 
Ministry of Environment & Forests should make all out efforts to spend the entire 
budgetary resources allocated to it.  
13.   Monetary Requirements of the Ministry 
 
13.1  The Secretary, Ministry of Environmen t & Forests while making his presentation 
before the Committee gave an overview of the fund requirements in respect of major 
schemes falling into three broad areas viz. Na tional River Conservation; Forestry and the 
Wildlife Management.  Starting with National River Conservation, it was stated that the 
approach of the Ganga and the Yamuna Ac tion Plan had been to treat waste water 
generated from Class-I and Class- II cities so that critically  polluted stretches falling the 
down streams of major cities on the river bank could be take n care of.  An amount of the 
order of Rs. 9000.00 Crores had been spent from the year 1985 onwards for creating 
treatment capacity of around 5000 Million Litre Per Day (MLD).  There was still a gap of 
around 26000 MLD between the sewage generated and the capacity of treatment created.  
In order to bridge the gap of treatment capacity of the order of 26000 MLD around 5 
times of what had been create d thus far at a cost of ar ound Rs. 9000 crores, the Ministry 
would be requiring money to the tune of approximately Rs. 50,000.00 Crores.  In the area 
of forestry, today we have tree and forest coverage of around 24 per cent, i.e., 78 million 
hectare of the geographical area of the country as against the target of 33 per cent.  To 
achieve the target of 33 per cent coverage  we needed to reach more than 100 million 
hectares from the present 78 million hectare.  Under Green India Mission, the objective is 
to increase forest/ tree cover of 5 million hectares of forest/ non-forest lands and improve 
the quality of forest cover on another 5 million hectares of forest land and the total cost of 
the Mission was Rs. 46,000.00 Crores spread over  ten years coinciding with the XII and 
XIII Plan periods.  Still the gap of 22 million hectares would be partly met and the rest 
almost 12 million hectares would remain to be covered at an estimated cost of around the 
same amount as earmarked for Green India Mission.  Similarly, for Wildlife 
Management/ Tiger Conservation, the appr oved outlay is somewhere around Rs. 300.00 
Crores while the magnitude of funds require d was much more.  There were 660 National 
Parks and sanctuaries, some of them exte nding to about 500 Sq. Kms. in size but the 
average allocation for them comes to about Rs. 0.5 Cror e per National Park/ Sanctuaries 
which is why the ever increasing man – animal  conflict had been on the rise.  For Tiger 
Conservation, there was a programme to relocate 40,000 families from core Tiger 
habitats under which a funding support of about 10 lakhs per family was to be provided 
for their rehabilitation.  The huge fund require d for the purpose can be easily imagined.  
Thus in broad terms, whether it be for ri ver cleaning, to achieve the desired tree and 
forestry coverage to 33 per cent of the to tal geographical area of the country or be it 
wildlife management, the fund requirement wa s pretty huge and the budgetary allocation 

made on an annual basis across these various schemes was pretty small in comparison to 
requirement. 
13.2  While the Committee takes note of the huge  gap between availability of fund vis-
à-vis its requirement, it feels that the entire required funding cannot be done by the Govt. 
of India, owing to budgetary constraints, although, it is of the c onsidered view that 
volume of funding from the Govt. of India must be reasonably raised.  In such a situation, 
the Committee feels that the Ministry should  explore the possibili ties of generating 
resources from sources other th an the Govt. of India.  These sources could be managing 
loans from the Asian Development Bank (ADB),  the World Bank or the Japanese aid.  
Yet another source could be strict enforcement of Polluters Pay Principle, so as to raise 
additional resources; making adequate provisio n for civil administrative adjudication to 
fast track levy of penalty, etc. by making enviro nment laws more stringent and effective.  
Integrating environmental elements/ factors into cost benefit analysis while making 
public, as well as, private investment decisions  for more prudent allocation of resources.  
The Ministry may also think in terms of pe rsuading Ministry of Finance to levy some 
green tax/ cess, on the lines of  Education Cess / service tax, et c.  The Ministry may also 
synergize its activities with projects/ programmes of those sectors of the economy which 
contribute to the volume of pollution the most , i.e., the Transport Se ctor, Energy Sector, 
Oil Sector, Mining Sector, etc. and require diversion of more forest land for non-forestry 
purposes.  One such effort has been made  in Visakhapatnam, where the local public 
sector Units have voluntarily undertaken the task of planting 40 lakh saplings in a span of 
five years and the progress of this experiment has been quite  satisfying.  Such initiative 
can very well be replicated in other such cities/ towns which are bearing the brunt of 
pollution because of Public Sect or/ Private Sector units loca ted there.  Over and above, 
the compensatory afforestation fund havi ng huge amount of money, i.e., Rs. 1718.20 
Crores (Approx.) as pr incipal amount as on 31
st March, 2012 and Rs. 384.59 Crores in 
the form of interest accrue d on the principal am ount put into the fund could also be 
utilised for the purpose of afforestation and regeneration of degraded forestland.  
Expenditure being incurred towards Corporate Social Responsibility by the Public Sector 
Undertaking, Banks, etc. may also be ch annelised towards forestry activities by 
persuading them to earmark certain amount of funds available for Corporate Social 
Responsibility (CSR) for this purpose.   
14.  Corporate Social Responsibility  
14.1 One of the major constraints of massi ve afforestation as emphasised by the 
Secretary, Ministry of Environm ent & Forests, is the non-availability of sufficient funds 
which certainly cannot be entirely met thr ough budgetary support.  As such, one of the 
potential sources for generating additional re sources for afforestation could be the fund 
earmarked under Corporate Social Responsibility towards which the Committee had been 
drawing the attention of the Mini stry time and again.  In its 210 th Report on Demand on 
Grants for 2010-11, 219 th Report on Action Taken by th e Govt. on the recommendations 
contained in its 210 th Report and once again in its 224 th Report on Demands for Grants 
2012-13, the Committee had been, through its recommendations, impressing upon the 
Ministry to proactively act in this direction so as to be able to manage a certain portion of 
CSR funds allocated by the Public Sector Undertaking towards afforestation.  Though, 
the Ministry of Environment & Forests had be en taking some steps but has not been able 
to make much headway.  In reply to a query as to whether the Mini stry has since been 
able to convene consultations with all the stak eholders to sort the issue of investment out 
of Corporate Social Responsibility for massive  afforestation, the Ministry stated that it 

had been consistently pursuing with the De partment of Public Enterprises to make 
provisions/guidelines to enhance the comm itted investment from Corporate Social 
Responsibility to 50 per cent for massive a fforestation.  However, response from 
Department of public enterprises had not been received either for convening stakeholders 
consultation or to facilitate information to Ministry of Environment & Forests to enable it 
to initiate dialogue with them .  The Ministry, however, asse rted that it was alive to the 
concern for the CSR investment for tree cover growth outside the forest areas.   
14.2  While, the Committee takes note of the efforts being made by the Ministry in 
this regard, it feels that concerted efforts must continue to be made in this regard so 
as to ensure that this additional source of funding becomes available for 
afforestation.  The Committee also recommends that since it is a policy matter to be 
decided at the higher level, the Ministry sh ould, besides taking up this matter with 
the Department of Public Enterprises, also  take this matter to the Cabinet for an 
early decision.   
14.3 The Committee understands The Compan ies Bill, 2012 mandates that any 
company having – (i) net worth of Rs. 500.00 Crores or more; (ii) turnover of Rs. 
1000.00 Crores or more; and (iii) net profits of  Rs. 5.00 Crores or more in a financial 
year, shall spend at least 2 percent of aver age net profits of the last three years in 
pursuance of Company’s Corpor ate Social Responsibility.  The Bill further lists the 
activity which may be included by Companies in their Corporate Social Responsibility 
Polices.  Ensuring environmental sustainability  has inter-alia been in cluded as one such 
permissible activity.  The said Bill is yet to be passed by the Parliament.  The Committee 
recommends that Ministry of Environmen t & Forests may take up the matter with 
the Ministry of Corporate Affairs for maki ng necessary amendments in the Bill to 
particularly provide for afforestation as  an activity which could be undertaken 
under CSR and further to make it mandatory that at least 50 per cent of the funds 
available for CSR shall be spent on afforesta tion.  By doing this, Ministry would be 
able to generate huge additional resources for massive afforestation.   
15.  Lack of Effective Monitoring/ Implementation of Environmental Laws
  
15.1 The Committee finds that despite what ever efforts made/ steps taken by the 
Ministry of Environment & Forests, the he alth of environment and the condition of 
natural resources is deterior ating day by day.  The problem of air, water and noise 
pollution, incidences of forest degeneration, man – animal conf lict, etc. are on the rise.  
Lack of enforcement of environmental laws/ absence of strong and effective monitoring 
to a large extent is responsible for all this.  One of the reasons for this lies in the fact that 
there has not been expansion of the Ministry in terms of staff strength and infrastructure 
commensurate to the manifold increase in its workload over the last two decades or so.  
Even worse is the fact that even existing sanctioned strength is not fully filled up.   
15.2  The Committee has been given to unde rstand that as against the sanctioned 
strength of 191, 285 and 392, the in position st rength is 175, 214 and 262 in Group ‘A’, 
‘B’ and ‘C’ posts respectively, meaning thereby that 16 Group ‘A’, 17 Group ‘B’ and 130 
Group ‘C’ posts are lying vacant in the Mini stry of Environment & Forests.  The 
Committee has been informed that out of the 6 existing regional offices of the Ministry, 5 
of them had been set up way back in 1986.  The 6
th regional office at Chandigarh was 
opened in 1988.  The number of regional offices increased to 7 in 1991, with a new 
regional office at Ranchi which could not be made functional due to financial constraints.  
The Committee understands that given the natu re of functions performed by the regional 
office of the Ministry which inter-alia in cludes monitoring and evaluation of ongoing 

forestry development projects and schemes with special emphasis on conservation of 
forest land and advising the State/Union Territories Gove rnments in preparation of 
proposals involving divergence of forestland for non-forest purposes under The Forest 
Conservation Act, 1980.  The capacities of the existing compliance and enforcement 
mechanism is fairly inadequate.  There has been manifold increase in their workload 
since their establishment.  The problem of the regional offices gets further aggravated due 
to shortage of adequate number of staff to man them.  
15.3 As per information furnished by the Mini stry, the Bengaluru regional office as on 
1
st March, 2013 has 22 in position staff strength as against the sanctioned strength of 31; 
Bhubaneswar office has 22 in position as agains t the sanctioned streng th of 32; Bhopal 
has 18 as against 29; Chandigarh 22 agains t 32; Lucknow 21 against 32 and Shillong as 
low as 16 against 32.  When the Committee enqu ired from the Ministry as to whether the 
regional offices with the motley strength of staff are able to do justice with the thorough 
scrutiny/ check before according environment and forestry clearances to the projects, the 
Ministry accepted that due to  lack of sufficient officers and staff to man the regional 
offices, at times, the scrutiny and checking of forests/ environmental clearance cases get 
affected adversely.   
15.4  Yet another serious problem,  that dogs the regional offi ces, is that on an average, 
one regional office has its jurisdiction over 6 States/ Union Territo ries with Shillong 
having the largest number, i.e., 8, followe d by Bengaluru region which has 6 States/ 
Union Territories under its jurisdiction.  A l ook at the statistics given by the Ministry 
regarding the monitoring activities undertaken, during the XI Fi ve Year Plan reveals that 
while Bengaluru regional office could monitor 601 projects as against the target of 750; 
the Bhubaneswar office could monitor only 85 against the target of 355; the Lucknow 
regional office could monitor 432 as against the target of 3103; Chandigarh regional 
office 294 as against the target of 760 unde r Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.  The 
position with regard to Environment (Protec tion) Act, 1986, does not appear to be any 
better either.  Bhubaneswar regional office monitored 509 projects as against the target of 
950, Bhopal office 430 as against the target of 950; and Shillong offi ce 222 out of 340.  
Responding to the query on the frequency of monitoring, the Ministry simply narrated – 
“the main parameters/conditions of formal approval for monitoring is as frequently as 
possible, at least once in a year.  At least once in 5 years, a comprehensive monitoring as 
to the effect of mining on air an d water pollution is also stipul ated to be carried out”.  It 
can be easily made out by the reply that, the Mi nistry has evaded the pointed and specific 
reply to the question, suggesting thereby th at the frequency of monitoring was not 
satisfactory.  A chart submitted to the Commi ttee by the Ministry in this regard is at 
Annexure-II. 
15.5  The Committee wanted to know the views of the Ministry on proposals to revamp 
the monitoring mechanism in view of the f act that monitoring/enforcing compliance of 
the conditions for environmental and forestry clearances was one of the grey areas which 
needed to be strengthened because gross vi olations of environmental norms had rendered 
industrial clusters in some of the States critically polluted.  The Ministry stated that it had 
decided to strengthen its 6 existing regiona l offices and also proposed to set up 4 new 
regional offices to make the monitoring of proj ect in the field more effective.  It was 
further added that the working of regional offices was reviewed recently in the Ministry 
and the following had been inter-alia, decided:  
  

 Notices for timely submission of si x monthly Compliance Reports by the 
Project Proponents may be issued by the Regional Offices to all the 
defaulting Units with a copy endorsed to Ministry of Environment & Forests; 
 At least 20 % of the cumulative ECs in the region should be monitored by 
the Regional Offices in a year with the emphasis on Red Category projects; 
 Regional offices to send progress repor t on monitoring of projects to the 
Ministry on quarterly basis; 
 Show Cause Notice/ directions under Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 
should be issued to the project proponents for non-compliance.   
15.6  The Committee notes that S upreme Court of India, had on 6 th July, 2011 while 
delivering its final judgment in Lafarge Umia m Mining Pvt. Ltd. directed for increase of 
regional offices of the Ministry from the pr esent strength of 6 to at least 10 at the 
locations to be decided in consultation with  the State/Union Territory Governments to 
facilitate more frequent inspections and in-d epth scrutiny and apprai sal of the proposals.  
After almost two years, the Expenditure Finance Committee, at its meeting held on 4 th 
March, 2013, has recommended strengthening of the regional offices, as well as, 
establishment of 4 new regional offices at Chennai, Dehradun, Nagpur and Ranchi.  As 
per the decision taken in th e meeting, each regional office would now have a total 
strength of 35 except for the regional office at  Shillong which would have the strength of 
39.   
15.7  The Committee expresses its serious con cern over the sorry state of affairs as 
regards monitoring/ reinforcement of forestry and environmental laws which has resulted 
in serious environmental and ecological probl ems badly affecting the inhabitants of the 
nearby areas.  Some of the industrial clusters have become so polluted due to reckless and 
blatant discharge of effluents and emissions that the residents are facing serious health 
hazards and even congenital problems.  If the situation is allowed to  go as it is, a time 
will come when people would be forced to ri se against the proposed projects and hamper 
their progress.  The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that before the situation 
goes beyond control and takes ug ly turn, the Ministry need s to act in a serious and 
sincere manner.  It, therefore, recommends  that the proposals for enhancing the 
number of regional offices of the Ministry  and strengthening the existing ones 
should be undertaken at the earliest, possibl y during this financial year itself.  The 
Committee also recommends that the Planning Commission/ Ministry of Finance 
should provide the Ministry with adequa te financial resources to enable the 
Ministry to achieve its desired objectives .  The Committee further recommends that 
apart from enhancing the number of regio nal offices and strengthening them, the 
Ministry should consider further devoluation of power and authority to the regional 
offices.    
15.8  In view of the fact that the magnanimity of po llution has been slowly, but 
certainly acquiring serious proportions, the Co mmittee, tried to extr act the views of the 
Ministry of Environment & Forests on the pe rception that protection of environment has 
not been accorded due priority by the State Govts., particularly because without their 
support and cooperation, it would not be possi ble for the Central Government alone to 
ensure environmental protection.  The Ministry of Environment & Forests evaded a direct 
reply and emphasised on the fact that the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowered 
the Central Government to take measures to  protect the environment which included the 
measures with respect to coordination of actions by the State G ovts. and such other 
matters as the Central Govt. deemed necessary or expedient for the purpose of securing 

the effective implementation of the provisions of the Act.  The Committee is of the 
considered view that it may not be practi cally feasible for the Central Ministry of 
Environment & Forests alone to fight and t ackle the menace of rapid rise in pollution 
witnessed all over – air, water, land, noise, etc. throughout the length and breadth of the 
country, it being a gigantic task.  Necessary cooperation and support from the State 
Govts. is definitely required in this regard.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that the Ministry of Environment & Fores ts should seriously think of including 
environment in the Concurrent List of the Constitution of India so as to help the 
State Govts. create their own institut ional mechanism like establishing a 
Department of Environment & Forests; en act, notify and enforce own laws and 
rules to ensure compliance of relevant en vironmental norms and take such other 
measures as deemed appropriate by the res pective State Govts.  Appropriate action 
should be taken by the Ministry in this  regard and the action initiated in this 
direction may be intimated to the Committee. 
16. Central Pollution Control Board 
 
16.1  Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) , a 100 per cent grants-in-aid Institution 
of the Ministry of Environment & Forests, in coordination with State Pollution Control 
Boards (SPCB)/ Pollution Control Commi ttees (PCCs) implements plans and 
programmes relating to abatement of pollution.  One of the mandates of the CPCB is to 
plan and cause to be executed a Nation wi de programme for prevention, control and 
abatement of water or air pollution.   
16.2  But the Committee finds that the institution of CPCB, although, enjoys 
autonomous status on paper, its autonomy is often found to be compromised in practice.  
The Committee finds that post of Chairman, CPCB has been lying vacant for the last over 
one year, and additional charge given to a se nior officer of Minist ry of Environment & 
Forests.  This is not the isolated incide nce of assumption of additional charge of 
Chairman, CPCB by officers of  the Ministry of Environm ent & Forests and it has 
happened in the past als o.  The Committee in its 192
nd Report on the Functioning of 
Central Pollution Control Board had recommended that the Chairman, CPCB should be a 
person having knowledge, experience and expertise in dealing with environmental issues.  
Moreover, such ad-hoc arrangements adve rsely impact functioning of CPCB.  When 
asked about the reasons for not filling up the vacancy on regular basis, the Ministry stated 
that the selection process of the post of Chairman has been kept under abeyance on 
account of the interim orders passed by the H on’ble High Court of Delhi in Nagin Nanda 
Vs. Union of India.  It was also assured th at the Ministry would undertake the process of 
screening the applications and interviewing the candidates after partial stay orders of the 
Hon’ble Court was vacated.  Ideally, the process of selection of suitable/ eligible 
candidate should be completed well before the date the Chairman is to demit the 
office and every effort made to appoint a professionally qualified person to man the 
post.  In a situation where for reasons be yond control of Ministry, the post cannot 
be filled up by the date the incumbent Chairman CPCB demits office, a practice 
may be adopted to give temporary charge to the seniormost Member of CPCB.   
16.3  But this is not the lone problem that the CPCB has been confronting.  The CPCB 
had also been facing acute shortage of scie ntific and technical manpower which had been 
coming in the way of effective functioning of the Board.  When the Committee asked the 
Ministry about the details of the main reco mmendations of and follow up action taken on 
the Study Report conducted by IIM, Lucknow fo r strengthening CPCB and the extent to 
which strengthening of CPCB, particularly, in terms of technical and scientific manpower 

in its headquarters and regional office had been made.  It was informed that IIM, 
Lucknow submitted its Report in Februar y, 2010 which inter-alia recommended 550 
additional posts; strengthening of laboratories; computerization; infrastructural 
development; provision of monitoring vehicles  to enhance environm ental surveillance, 
etc.  On the pointed and specific queries re garding follow up actions taken and the extent 
to which strengthening of  CPCB had been made in pursuance of the above 
recommendations, the Ministry did not come out with any specific reply and wrapped up 
the matter by saying that the proposals we re presently under examination.  The 
Committee finds that a detail ed project report on strengthe ning the zonal offices to 
enhance their functioning through adequate staffing and infrastructure, was submitted by 
CPCB in August, 2012.  As per the report, th e minimum requirement of one zonal office 
of CPCB was assessed to be of 49 scientif ic/ technical and 25 administrative manpower, 
where as the ideal requirement was assessed to  be 62 and 39 respectively.  As against the 
above minimum requirement, the maximum aver age scientific/technical staff available 
each with Kolkata and Bengaluru was 23 and onl y 8 with Shillong zonal office.  In terms 
of coverage of State/Union Territories by each zonal office, the number is obviously very 
high.  While the Lucknow zonal office cove rs 6 States and 1 Union Territory; the 
Shillong zonal office covers 8 States; Bengalu ru 5 States and 2 Union Territories; 
Kolkata 4 States and 1 Uni on Territory; Bhopal 3 States  and Vadodara zonal office 2 
States and 1 Union Territory.  In terms of  coverage of number of industries, Common 
Effluent Treatment Plants, Hazardous Waste Units, Hospitals, sewage treatment plants 
compliance, industries, critically polluted areas, etc. it goes as high as 87767 in case of 
Vadodra zonal office, 82359 in case of Lu cknow, whereas Bengaluru accounts for 19969 
and Bhopal 17467.  In contrast, the staff positio n of Bengaluru zonal office is 31 regular 
staff including 23 scientific/technical staff, while Lucknow has 25 regular staff out of 
which, 19 are technical and scien tific.  Vadodara zonal office ha s the staff strength of 37 
regular employees, out of which 21 are tec hnical/scientific.  The Committee wonders as 
to how zonal offices of CPCB with such a heavy workload and lo w manpower would be 
able to do justice with important activities like inspecting polluting industries for detailed 
investigation, to verify compliance of standards, undertake inspections of industries under 
public complaints, carry out performance studi es of Common Effluent Treatment Plants 
(CETP)/ Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs)  and Common Bio-Medical Waste Treatment 
Facilities, inspect water and air quality, etc.  The existing staff stre ngth of zonal office 
stands in stark contrast to the minimum staff required for environment surveillance of one 
major unit, which is assessed to be 9 and typi cally one industrial in spection takes 3 to 5 
days depending upon the distance to be covered.  In the give n scenario expecting a zonal 
office to carry out its designated activities in a satisfactory manner is like expecting 
Moon from them.   
16.4  The performance of Central Pollution Control Board is further marred by lack of 
necessary support/ cooperation from the St ate Pollution Control Boards/ Pollution 
Control Committees.  The Committee, accordi ngly, enquired from the Ministry as to 
what extent CPCB got such support an d whether there was any suggestion for 
improvement in the functioning of SPCB/PCCs.  The Ministry was not very forthright in 
its reply but indirectly admitted that CPCB had to evolve a system of close coordination 
with SPCBs and for this purpose CPCB needed to have one to one review with each 
SPCB on annual basis to assess the performance of the Board and identify the areas to be 
focused by SPCBs.   
 

16.5  The Committee takes note of some of the disturbing news appearing in the media 
in the recent past and disturbing data availa ble with the Committee.  One, such report 
stated that air pollution was the 5 th biggest killer in India,  other reports related to 
hazardous smog like situation in the making in  the Indian cites due to excessive air 
pollution.  As per the report appearing in the me dia, close to half of cities are reeling 
under severe particulate pollution while newer pollutants like Nitrogen Oxide, Ozone and 
air toxins are worsening public health challenge.  As per the Annual Report 2012-2013 of 
the Ministry, 131 cities exceed the permissible limit of PM 10 which is as high as 62 per 
cent and 19 cities exceed the level of NO 2.  Continuous growth of municipal solid waste 
generation in urban areas of the country has al so emerged as one of the biggest polluters 
of environment.  According to the latest survey of CPCB in 60 major cities of the 
country, the total municipal solid waste generated is 50,5 92 tons per day, while the 
country wide generation is estimated to be  of the volume of 1,50,000 tons per day.  Out 
of the above, only a small port ion is being processed and th e remaining waste is dumped 
in an open air leading to envi ronmental and health hazards in  cities and towns.  As per 
CPCB assessment, India generates 56 lakhs t onnes of plastic wast e annually with Delhi 
alone amounting for a staggeri ng 690 tonnes a day.  Out of the total plastic waste 
generated in the country only approximately 60 per cent is collected and recycled, while 
the rest remain uncollected an d littered.  43 out of the 88 prominent industrial clusters 
have been found to be critically pollu ted, based on Comprehensive Environmental 
Pollution Index (CEPI), which takes into acc ount pollution in water, land (ground water) 
and air with Ankaleshwar and Vapi in Gu jarat scoring 88.50 and 88.09 respectively on 
the CEPI scale.  The CEPI score of the neighbouring towns of Delhi is as high as 87.37 of 
Ghaziabad; 78.90 of NOIDA and 77.07 of Farida bad.  The Committee, in order to have 
an authentic information on the above matte r asked the Ministry as to whether air 
pollution, in fact, as per the assessment c onducted by Centre for Science and Education 
had actually emerged as the fifth leading cause  of death in the country and whether close 
to half of cities of our country were under severe particulate po llution.  The Ministry 
admitted that the Centre for Science & Education (CSE) had published a Report titled 
“Mobility Crises Agenda for Action – 201 0” which included the results of study 
conducted by World Health Organisation (WHO), Health Effect Institutes, Public Health 
and Air Pollution in Asia (PAPA) Projec t, World Bank, etc. on air pollution, health, 
cancer on mortality studies in India.  Howe ver, it was stated that the results were 
indicative and appeared to be not conclusive  because the effects of air pollution were 
additive and synergistic and included range of  variation and cumulative factors like food 
habits, socioeconomic status, medical history, genetic problems, stress, etc.  The Ministry 
further went on to add that it seemed that the estimate was based on correlation/ 
estimation in absence of any documentary evid ence since details of death/ illness were 
not documented in majority of hospitals.  Fi nally, it stated that CPCB had not conducted 
any study on mortality due to air pollution in the country.   
16.6  The Committee feels that the Minist ry should not outrightly reject the 
findings of the study conducted jointly by na tional and international institutes of 
repute and credible background unless it has credible evidence to prove otherwise.  
The Committee recommends that the Ministry  should conduct a study of its own on 
mortality due to air pollution in major Indi an cities and in case the study confirms 
the findings of the Report published by th e Centre for Science & Education, take 
urgent remedial measures to prevent the ad verse impacts of air pollution on health 
of citizens.   

 
16.7  The Ministry also failed  to give satisfactory repl y to a pointed and specific 
question as to whether the Ministry had tried to ascertain the extent to which 
environmental degradation was responsible fo r the burden of disease in India and how 
did it compare with the figure prevailing 5 ye ars back.  So was the case with yet another 
specific query about the number of critically polluted pockets in the country where cases 
of debility and deformity of the local residents on a large-scale had come to the notice of 
the Govt.  The curt reply of the Ministry wa s that the CPCB had not carried out any such 
studies, while, accepting that  43 industrial clusters, had b een identified as  critically 
polluted.  The Committee finds that although as per new ambient air quality standards 12 
parameters were required to be monitored, but presently CPCB is monitoring ambient air 
quality in 542 locations with respect to 3 parameters, namely, SO
2, NO2 and PM10.   
16.8  When the Committee enquired from the Ministry about the details of polluting 
industries in the country together with the details of surprise checks carried out and action 
taken against the erring industrie s during the last 3 years, th e Ministry did not give the 
exact figures of polluting industries in the country, but informed that during the last 3 
years, i.e., 2009-10 to 2011-12 and till November, 2012, CPCB had inspected 935 
industries and issued 308 directions under Section 5 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 
1986.  The Committee finds that as per the in formation furnished by the Ministry, there 
are around 4438 polluting industries in the coun try against which the Central Pollution 
Control Board could in 3 years inspect 935 industries only. 
16.9  The Committee expresses its serious con cerns over the rapid ri se in all types of 
pollution and feels that unless some serious and effective steps are taken by the CPCB, 
the situation would continue to go from ba d to worse; assume alarming proportions in 
days to come and prove to be detrimental for the entire countr y.  The Committee feels 
that in the given alarming scenario, adequate  expansion and strengt hening of monitoring 
and enforcing agencies is the need of the hour  so that the situation, at least, does not 
deteriorate further.  The Committee, therefore, recommends  that the zonal offices of 
CPCB proposed to be opened in Chenna i and Chandigarh must be expedited and 
made functional at the earliest possible.  Efforts should also be made to further 
increase the number of zonal offices so that  effective and successful monitoring of 
projects/ polluting units co uld be undertaken.  Besides, the report of CPCB for 
strengthening the existing zonal office s of CPCB must also be given due 
consideration and follow up action on it be taken in a time bound manner.  The 
Committee also expresses its concern over th e fact the CPCB has not been making 
optimum utilisation of the budgetary resources made available to it during the last 2 
years.  In 2011-12 as against the Plan allo cation of Rs. 40.00 Crores, it could utilise 
Rs. 38.81 Crores while in 2012-13, out of Rs. 42.00 Crores, RE allocation came down 
to Rs. 34.00 Crores, the expenditure was only to the tune of Rs. 25.50 Crores as on 
13
th March, 2013.  The Committee is happy to note that this year budgetary 
allocation under Plan Head has been subs tantially enhanced to Rs. 57.72 Crores as 
compared to the last year which in percentage terms works out to 2.4 per cent.   The 
Committee recommends that the Central Po llution Control Board should fully 
utilize this allocated outlay and the Ministry of Environment & Forests should take 
prompt steps to address the problems affl icting the CPCB, i.e ., appointment of its 
regular Chairman, expansion and strengthening of zonal offices, etc.  

17.  Environment and Forestry Clearances  
17.1  When the Committee enquired from the Ministry as to what needed to be done to 
fast track clearances while safeguarding the en vironment to ensure sustainable growth of 
the economy, the Ministry informed that it ha d taken various steps to fast track the 
environmental clearances process while not  compromising with the quality of the 
appraisal or the integrity of the environmen t, which included continuous monitoring of 
status of pending Projects, re gular and long duration of m eetings of Experts Appraisal 
Committee for consideration of projects in fore sts sector, etc.  Further, in order to 
delegate functions to the State level aut horities in respect of  Category-B Projects, 
State/Union Territory level Environment Im pact Assessment Authorities (SEIAAs) had 
been constituted to fast track environmenta l clearances.  The Forest Advisory Committee 
meetings were also being held regularly and for long durations.  The Ministry also 
submitted a list of 11 reform measures taken in  the past few months to further improve 
the holistic appraisal and streamline the environment/forestry clearance process.  Some of 
the important measures are as follows:-  
(i) Exempting public hearing for capacity  expansion proposals of existing 
coal mining projects which have obtained environment clearances and 
which are for one time capacity expansion of upto 25 per cent in the 
existing mining operation, within the existing mine lease areas; 
(ii) Prior environment clearance at the st age of renewal of mine lease would 
not be required for the mining project  or activities which have obtained a 
valid environment clear ance under the Environment Impact Assessment 
Notification, 2006.   
(iii) Modification of the guidelines issued  under the Forest (Conservation) Act 
1980 to streamline the procedure for obt aining approval fo r diversion of 
forest land required for execution of linear projects such as Roads, 
Railways, Transmission Lines, etc. f acilitating executing of linear projects 
on non-forest land (subj ect to certain conditions ) pending approval under 
the Forest (Conservation) Act for diversion of forest land involved; 
(iv) In case of linear projects now, the li nkage of environment clearances with 
Stage-I forest clearances has been re moved subject to ce rtain stipulated 
conditions.    
17.2  While, the Committee appreciates the measures taken by the Ministry to 
streamline the environment and forestry cl earances which would facilitate speedy 
execution of large developmental projects in the plains, it finds that even smaller projects 
in the hilly Himalayan Region are held up in the absence of required clearances.  Smaller 
projects involving requirement of forestry clearance for some 5 Kms. or 10 Kms. road, 
building hospital has been hanging fire since long.  The Committee feels that there is a 
need to adopt a positive approach to give clearance to these Projects which are badly 
required for development of the Himalaya n States, particular ly, Uttarakhand.  The 
Committee also came to know that permission fo r small irrigation projects, cutting of dry 
bamboo, etc. in tribal areas is not given in the garb of various laws.  The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should look into all such issues and take necessary 
measures to facilitate speed y clearance of projects required for development of the 
Himalayan and tribal region.  

18. National River Conservation Programme 
18.1  The objective of National River Conserva tion Programme is to improve the water 
quality of rivers, the major water sources  in the country thr ough implementation of 
pollution abatement work programmes.  Th e major emphasis on the pollution abatement 
works is on interception and diversion works to capture raw sewage and divert it for 
treatment; set up sewage treatment plan for treating the sewage so diverted; construction 
of low sanitation toilets to prevent the ope n defecation on river ba nk; construction of 
electric crematoria; river front developmen t works; afforestation on the river banks, 
public participation and awareness, etc.  Yet another in itiative for river conservation was 
taken with the constitution of National Ga nga River Basin Aut hority (NGRBA) in 2009 
as an empowered body to plan, finance, monitor and coordinate activities for the Ganga 
River.  The NGRBA at its first meeting held  in October, 2009 has decided that under the 
Mission Clean Ganga, it will be ensured that  by 2020 no untreated municipal sewage or 
industrial effluents flow into the Ganga.  But going by the pace with which the NGRBA 
has been moving, this target appears to be unattainable.  The comprehensive River Basin 
Management Plan for Ganga being prepar ed by a consortium of 7 IITs was to be 
completed by December, 2011 but it is now proposed to be completed by December, 
2013.  When the Committee wanted to know the main achievements so far of the 
Authority which has already completed over 4 years, the Ministry submitted that a total 
of 53 projects in 43 towns in Ganga states  costing Rs. 2600.00 Crores have so far been 
sanctioned which included projects worth Rs. 1341.60 Crores in Uttar Pradesh; Rs. 
441.86 Crores in Bihar; Rs. 659.41 Crores in  West Bengal and Rs. 155.60 Crores in 
Uttaranchal for undertaking sewage network, tr eatment plant, pumping stations, electric 
crematoria, development of river front, etc. related activities.   
18.2  The Committee with reference to an obs ervation made by Harvard Institute (U.K.) 
while carrying out cost benefit analysis of Ganga Action Plan during the 1995-97 that 
river clean up programme involves a longer period and large resources for effective 
action asked the Ministry to clarify if it ha d made any study to assess as to how further 
longer period and additional resources were st ill needed to restore the health of Ganga 
River to the pristine level in view of the fact that Ganga Action Plan was started way 
back in 1985 and hence in terms of tim e taken Ganga River Cleanup Programme was 
already over 27 years old.  The Ministry as us ual gave a general and elusive reply, which 
was not even distantly related with the purport of the question.   
18.3  The Committee finds that notwithstandi ng all the efforts made so far and a huge 
sum of money spent on river cleaning, the condition of major rivers of the country 
including Ganga and the Yamuna still continues to be pitiable and pathetic. The 
Committee during its recent visit to Allahabad, Banaras and Patna had a first hand 
experience of bitter story of utter neglect an d apathy that the Ganga water at these places 
had to tell.  The colour of the Ganga wate r was thick, dark with hardly much flow.  
Without going into the technicalities of harmfu l chemicals, bacterial coliforms and other 
pollutants present in the Ganga water, prima-facie, the water at these places did not 
appear to be fit for even bathing what to talk of drinking or for using for religious 
purposes.   All that the Committee can do, at this stage, is to express its serious 
displeasure and anguish over th e despicable state in which the Ganga and the Yamuna 
have reached now.  Once the Pathit Pawani Ganga, a drop of water of which if taken at 
the time of death, was believed to give eman cipation and ensure h eavenly abode, has, 
itself virtually reached its sick bed.  Once worshipped as the saviours Ganga, harbinger of 
hope and purifier of souls, the mighty river is now strugg ling for its own survival and 

easy breathing from the garbage and filth, et c. being dumped into it.  As per a news 
report, a study conducted by The National Canc er Registry Programme under the Indian 
Council of Medical Research, th e Ganga River is thick with heavy metals and lethal 
chemicals that cause Cancer of Gallbladder, kidneys, prostate, liver , etc. and the worst 
affected stretches are East Uttar Pradesh, the flood plains of Bihar and Bengal.  Arbitrary, 
unscientific, reckless discharge of industrial e ffluents such as arseni c, fluoride and other 
heavy metals has rendered the Ganga water a deadly source of Cancer now.  
18.4  The moot point is that when the reasons for continuous and consistent increase in 
pollution are well known why is it that we have turned into helpless spectators?  The real 
problem perhaps lies in lack of firm c onviction and resolve to  address them.  The 
Ministry itself has admitted that industrial pollution due to its toxi c, non-biodegradable 
nature contributed mainly by tanneries, disti lleries, paper mills and sugar mills are the 
major contributors.  The stretch from Kanna uj to Varanasi has been acknowledged as 
critically polluted.  In the entire Ganga  Basin, approximately 12410 MLD sewage is 
generated, for which the treatment capacity available is only of the volume of 5070 MLD.  
In the main stream of Ganga River about 290 0 million liters of sewage is discharged 
everyday from Class-I cities and Class-II towns located along the banks out of which 
only 1100 MLD is getting treated.   
18.5  When the Committee enquired from the Ministry about the number of leather 
processing units/ tanneries operational in Kanpur  and since when these were operational; 
what was the total volume of effluent gene rated by these units; and how many of them 
had effluent treatment plant facility togeth er with the details of  volume of untreated 
effluent discharged into the River Ganga by them, the Ministry of Environment & Forests 
informed that there were about 350 leathe r processing units/ tanneries in Kanpur and 
about 13 MLD effluents was collected from th e tanneries clusters an d sent for treatment 
at the combined effluent treatment plant,  which has a capacity of 36 MLD.  (9 MLD 
Tannery effluent plus 27 MLD Sewage).   After treatment done through Anaerobic 
Biological Treatment Process (UASB Technol ogy), the combined treated waste water 
was discharged into a dedica ted waste water irrigation ch annel running parallel to the 
Ganga River.  The Ministry further stated th at in normal situation effluent of tanneries 
should not join Ganga River, but at times due to bypass from some defaulting units or 
due to over flow from the co llection system, some effluent  joined Ganga River through 
the open drains in the area. 
18.6  An analysis of the above reply of th e Ministry, prima-facie suggests that the 
Ministry has tried to camouflage this serious issue in such a way as not to reveal the 
actual picture of the reality, but despite best of its efforts the Ministry left some loopholes 
in its reply whereby it becomes clear that the effluents arising out of tanneries in Kanpur 
is getting directly or indirectly discharg ed into the river Ganga.  The Ministry has 
admitted that about 13 MLD effluent is collected  from the tanneries clusters and sent to 
36 MLD capacity treatment pl ant with 9 MLD tannery effl uent plus 27 MLD sewage.  
Obviously, 4 MLD effluent does not get treate d and find its way into the River Ganga.  
The other loophole is that for whatever reasons, be it bypass from some defaulting units 
or due to over flow from the collection sy stem, some effluents do join River Ganga 
through the open drains in the area.  This rais es the question as to why all this is being 
allowed to continue?  The Committee is constr ained to observe that this may not be the 
real picture and the truth may be somewhat, if not altogether different. 
18.7  The Committee also enquired from the Mi nistry about the natu re and effect of 
effluents/pollutants generated in the tanneries and efforts made by it to stop the units 

from discharging deadly pollu tants into River Ganga.  The Ministry was candid to admit 
that the tannery effluent wa s characteristically known to have a high concentration of 
organic matter mostly in suspended form an d also high concentration of trivalent 
Chromium.  The effluent also contained high con centration of TDS.  On the issue of 
efforts made by the Ministry to  stop these units from discha rging deadly pollutants into 
Ganga, the Ministry stated that CPCB has i ssued directions to UP Pollution Control 
Board to check discharge of polluted effluents into Ganga from tanneries.  Besides CPCB 
had also undertaken an appr oach for pollution surveillance in Ganga basin under which 
inspections of polluting industries in Ganga basin were to be carried out every year.  The 
Committee feels that such a lukewarm nonchalant and pass ive action/ response on an 
issue which has acquired serious  dimensions with grave th reat to the life and the 
livelihood of sizeable number of populace living along the coast of Ganga, which has 
potential to hurt the cultural, traditional, relig ious and spiritual sentiments of crores of 
people and which has attracted people organi se mass movement and protests is not only 
unfortunate but also a cause of serious worry  for all of us because if the Ministry 
continues to go ahead with this approach, the condition of River Ganga will deteriorate 
even for worse.   
18.8  Apart from the River Ganga and Yamuna, the conditions of other major rivers of 
the country are no better.  As per the inform ation furnished by the Ministry, there are 35 
rivers spread over 12 States which has Biological Oxygen Demand (BOD) level above 35 
ml, 15 rivers which has BOD in the range of 20 to 30 mg per liter spread over 7 States 
and so on.  There are around 150 rivers spread across the country which are polluted 
though varying only in quantity.   
18.9  In order to know the exact volume of se wage generated in the country in general 
and in Class-I cities and Class-II towns in particular, the Committee asked for details in 
this regard.  In reply the Mi nistry stated that according to CPCB, against the estimated 
sewage generation of about 38254.82 million litres  per day from Class-I cities and Class-
II towns of the country, the treatment cap acity was available only for 1180.48 MLD.  
What is noteworthy in this regard, is that  out of the total treatment capacity of 1180.48 
MLD per day, capacity of only 4704 MLD has so far been created under the National 
River Conservation Plan, while, the rest has been done by other agencies under different 
programmes/ plans.   
18.10  The Committee feels that there are so me simple and effective solutions which 
could go a long way in tackling the problem of  rampant pollution in the River Ganga, but 
some how or the other, they have not found fa vour with the Ministry.  One such solution 
is to ensure minimum ecological flow in both the Rivers the Ganga and the Yamuna.  
Government had in fact got an assessment of cumulative impact of Hydropower Projects 
done by Alternative Hydro Energy  Centre (AHEC) IIT Roorki  and Wildlife Institute of 
India, Dehradun which inter-alia recommen ded that prescribed environmental flow 
should be released from every project ke eping in view hydrological requirements 
organism.  The Ministry informed the Comm ittee that an Inter-Ministerial Group (IMG) 
headed by Member, Planning Commission was constituted by Minist ry of Environment 
& Forests on 15
th June, 2012 to go into the issues re lated to River Ganga and to suggest 
environmental flow requirement for variou s stretches of Bhagirathi, Alakhnanda and 
other tributaries of the Rive r Ganga.  As per a News re port, the IMG has recommended 
that the plethora of dams built and planned in the Ganga Basin be reengineered to 
maintain 30-50 per cent of water flow in th e lean period of December – March.  The 

Group has also recommended that water flow at  25 per cent between April to October, 
the period when the river has a high water levels be ensured.   
18.11  When the Ministry was asked that one of the key features of the holistic river 
basin approach adopted to ensure effective abatement of pollution and conservation of the 
River Ganga, under the NGRBA was to dete rmine minimum ecological flow and to 
regulate water extraction and whether all the ri parian states had agreed to regulate water 
extraction, the Ministry gave a casual reply by saying that not much work had been done 
on environmental flows in Indian  rivers, particularly, the rive rs in the Ganga basin.  It 
also added that environmental flow assessmen t was both a social and a scientific process 
requiring expert knowledge of various fiel ds including, but not limited to hydrology, 
hydraulics, geomorphology, ecology and biodiver sity, socio-culture livelihood and water 
quality and pollution.   
 
18.12  Yet another solution which was suggested by the Committee in its 224 th Report 
was to treat river conservation as a soci al engineering problem and not entirely 
engineering centric, as the latter alone coul d not be successful.  The Ministry was, 
however, not found to very enthusiastic in a dopting this approach.  In its Action Taken 
Report, the Ministry replied th at measures were being init iated for public awareness and 
involvement in the conservation.  However, as per the information furnished by the 
Ministry, the Committee finds that the Ministry is still not very serious in pursuing this 
social-centric approach which gets reflected in the chart where major costs of works and 
their respective percentage cost incurred ha ve been given.  As per the chart while the 
engineering-centric  approach, i.e., the in terception and diversion of sewage and the 
sewage treatment plant account for 88.98 per cen t of the cost, the percentage cost of 
public participation and awareness is a meager  0.3 per cent.  The status of interception 
and diversion of sewage and the success of sewa ge treatment plants is before all of us to 
see.  It is an open secret that operati on and maintenance of STPs is primarily the 
responsibility of respective State Govts., ope ration of which is often marred by frequent 
power failure and inadequate power backup arrangements added by sub optimal 
utilisation of STPs due to l ack of connecting sewer networ king, etc.  As per the Annual 
Report of the Ministry 61 out  of 134 Common Effluent Tr eatment Plants were not 
meeting BOD, COD & TSS Parameters while 74 CETPs were not meeting TDS 
standards.     
18.13  In view of the above, the Committ ee recommends that the engineering 
centric approach adopted by the Ministry  should be supplemented with social 
centric approach.  In addition, the Mi nistry should seri ously consider the 
observations/ suggestions contained in th e preceding paragraphs, particularly, for 
increasing ecological flow of rivers so that  a holistic approach is adopted to restore 
Ganga, Yamuna and other rivers to thei r pristine glory.  The Committee also 
recommends a potent monitoring and accountability mechanism be also put in place 
to ensure proper utilisation of funds for National River Conservation Programme. 
19.  Public Hearing
 
19.1  While public hearing has been made mandatory in the scheme of things of 
according EC/FC Clearance for some of the proj ects particularly those which affect the 
local inhabitants, the Committee has been give n to understand that public hearing is not 
conducted in an objective and impartial manne r.  Often public hearing becomes a state 
managed and an eye-wash show conducted in  the presence of the project proponents 
where their representatives use it as a plat form to persuade, convince and coax the 
affected public to give their nod for the proj ect to the detriment of  their interest and 

welfare.  The Committee is of the view that such instances give ri se to discontentment 
among the public and sometimes also result in protest putting th e entire project in 
jeopardy.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Govt. must take necessary 
measures to curb such malpractices in pub lic hearing so that p ublic hearing serves 
the purpose for which these are intended.  The Committee further recommends that 
genuine concerns of the people must fi nd place in the envi ronment management 
plan and the project proponents take necessary preventive and curative measures to 
address the genuine concerns of the public.   
20.  National Green Tribunal 
20.1  The National Green Tribunal was set up fo r effective and expeditious disposal of 
civil cases relating to environmental protec tion and conservation of forests and other 
natural resources including enforcement a nd compensation for damages to persons and 
property.  It was to be set up at five places with its Principal Bench in Delhi.  But even 
after lapse of more than two years, the Mini stry has only been able to make operational 
only the benches in Delhi & Chen nai, the latter one w.e.f. 30
th October, 2012.  The 
reasons are obvious.  For meeting expenditure on setting up of Offices and for meeting 
other functional requirements, a provision of Rs. 6.50 Crores (RE) was made for 2012-
13, against which expenditure as on 31.01.2013 was only Rs. 2.81 Crores.  For 2013-14, 
the Annual Plan outlay is Rs. 14.00 Crores. When the Committee enquired about the 
additional activities proposed to be undertaken with the enhanced allocation, the Ministry 
informed that besides some c onstruction and interior work the regional benches at Pune, 
Bhopal & Kolkata, were proposed to be ope rationalized and all the sanctioned posts 
which could not be filled in 2012-13 would be filled up.   
20.2  The Committee expresses its serious concern over the slow and tardy 
progress in setting up of Benches of Nati onal Green Tribunal and underutilization 
of allocated outlay of the order of Rs. 7.07 Cr ores as against the B.E. allocation of 
Rs. 10.50 Crores.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry must take all 
necessary steps to make remaining regional benches of the Tribunal functional at 
the earliest and in any case during the cu rrent financial year itself and make full 
utilisation of the allocated B.E. resources of Rs. 14.00 Crores.   
21.  Man – Animal Conflict/ Poaching of Wild Animals 
 
21.1 The Committee takes note of the fact that Project Tiger has shown an encouraging 
trend of recovery in terms of tiger population which was once feared to be on the verge of 
extinction.  However, it feels that the gr owing incidence of ma n-animal conflict, 
poaching, killing of elephants in rail accidents, etc. sti ll remain a matter of serious 
concern.  As per the information furnished by the Ministry while th e number of tigers, 
rhinos and elephants who fell prey to poach ing was 28, 8 and 16 resp ectively in the year 
2010, in the year, 2012, the number of tigers and rhinos who became victims, went up to 
32 and 13 respectively.  In th e year, 2011, 26 elephants became the victim of poaching.  
As on 26
th March, 2013, while 3 tigers became th e victim of poaching, the number of 
rhinos was staggering 12.  Killing of elephant s in rail accidents despite the Project 
Elephant, launched in 1991-92 as a Centrally Spons ored Scheme with a view inter-alia to 
protect elephants, their habita ts and corridors and to addre ss the man-animal conflict.  
Yet another area of concern lies  in the fact that as per a report, Indian Crocodiles, King 
Cobra, South Andaman Krait and many types of  Turtles viz. Bengal roof Turtles, Red 
Crowned Roof Turtle, etc. are facing extinction and hence they  need to be protected.  
When asked about any scheme proposed to be  launched for their protection, on the lines 
of the Project Tiger/ Project Elephant, the Ministry stated that there was no centrally 

sponsored scheme or national programme a ddressing such species as they were not 
considered as umbrella or flagship species such as Tiger, Elephant and Snow Leopard.  
The Ministry, however, acknowledged that a recent collaborative study by the Zoological 
Society of London and the International Unio n for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) had 
revealed that 12.2 per cent of India’s reptiles were threatened with extinction.   
21.2  In view of the above, the Committee feels th at there is an urgent need to save 
the species facing extinction and reduce si gnificantly, if not eliminate altogether, 
incidents that kill animals like  man-animal conflict, rail or road accidents etc. and 
recommends that Ministry must  takes all necessary measu res in this regard.  The 
Committee also recommends that local inhabi tants should be involved in a big way 
for providing protection to the wild animal s, as well as, to forest cover.  The 
Committee understands that deployment of  local workforce is being undertaken 
under Project Tiger in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, 
Karnataka, Uttarakhand, etc.  The Commi ttee appreciates this measure and feels 
that such efforts need to be replicated in other States as well for protection of 
wildlife and forest cover.   
22.  All India Coordinated Project on Taxonomic Capacity Building 
(AICOPTAX) 
22.1  Taxonomy occupies a pivotal position in  biology as it deals with scientific 
classification of all living and extinct organism s .   I t  i s  a l s o  a n  i n t e g r a l  p a r t  o f  t h e  
conservation and sustainable utilisation of bi ological diversity.  It  is a well-known fact 
that India has been very rich in flora and fauna.  As such, it becomes imperative that 
India’s large variety of ecologi cal habitats with large variations in species of plants, 
animals and microorganisms are identified, classi fied and nurtured for present as well as 
future generations.  So far about 90,000 an imal species and 47,000 plant species have 
been identified and described.  A large number of animals and plants still remain to be 
explored and identified.  Howe ver, the Ministry of Envir onment & Forests in its Annual 
Report, 2012-13 mentioned that there is overa ll decline in expertise in the taxonomy of 
several groups of living orga nisms.  The existing taxonomy base is also eroding rapidly 
due to non-availability of professionals and lack of trained manpower to take the place of 
the retiring specia lists.  The Ministry has gone to the extent of saying that a wide gap 
exists between the magnitude of taxonomic e xpertise needed and th e available limited 
taxonomic knowledge base.  It has further emphasised that the issue of taxonomic 
impediments needs to be addressed urgently in order to manage the biological resources 
and to meet the challenges of the 21st Century. 
22.2 While, the Committee expresses its deep concern over the grim scenario presented 
by the Ministry, it feels that it is the Ministry itself which is to be blamed for this.  The 
Ministry had, in order to strengthen taxonomic base, set up an All India Coordinated 
Project on Taxonomic Capacity Building (AICOP TAX) in 1999.  30 thematic areas were 
chosen for investigation under AICOPTAX, out of which only 15 thema tic areas have so 
far been implemented.  Out of any outlay of Rs. 13.50 for XI Five Year Plan under 
taxonomic capacity building, Rs. 11.99 Crores could be utilised.  In the year 2012-13, out 
of the BE allocation of Rs. 2.90 Crores, a meager Rs. 0.30 Crores could be utilised by the 
Ministry as on 13 th March, 2013.  It would not be out of place to mention here that the 
expenditure by 31st January, 2013 was only Rs. 0.18 Crores which went up to Rs. 0.30 by 
13th March, 2013.  Perhaps, this  is the reason why this year allocation under this 
Programme has been kept at only Rs. 1.90 Lakhs.   
 

22.3  The Committee feels that a sound taxonomic base is a prerequisite for 
environmental assessment, ecological resear ch, effective conservation management and 
sustainable use for biological resources and despite a coordinated project on taxonomy, 
setup some 12 years back, the Ministry la ments that the existing taxonomic base is 
rapidly declining due to non-availability of pr ofessionals and lack of trained manpower.  
In the name of taxonomic capacity building pr oject, the Ministry is  extending financial 
support to Universities, research Institutes, et c.  It is not able to utilise the budgetary 
allocation fully because the release of grants  is linked to proper utilisation of earlier 
released grants and progress on activities.  The Committee feels that besides 
supporting research projects and organizin g training workshops, the Ministry 
should explore the feasibilities of setting  up a Centre in a reputed University for 
studies in Taxonomy or establish its own Institute for higher education and research 
in Taxonomy in order to produce expert and trained professionals in Taxonomy.   
For attracting bright and promising students in this area, the Ministry should also 
think in terms of awarding scholarshi ps for higher studies and research in 
Taxonomy.  In addition, the Ministry shou ld take on a priority basis all other 
measures necessary to build a pool of professionals in taxonomy for meeting the 
requirements of trained professionals in this field.

REPORT 
 
INTRODUCTION 
 Indian Space Programme had its modest be ginning with the setting up of Indian 
National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) in 1962 and launching of a 
sounding rocket from Thumba on November 21, 1963 was the first milestone in Indian 
space programme.  With the establishment of  the Indian Space Re search Organisation 
(ISRO) under the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) in November 1969, Indian Space 
Programme became institutionalised.    The Space programme got a fillip in June, 1972 
when the Government of India constituted the Space Commission and established the 
Department of Space (DoS) and ISRO becoming a part of the DoS.   
2. Over the last five decades, Indi an Space Programme has achieved many 
landmarks and   won laurels. In 2012, India added another glorious feat to its ongoing 
Space programme by launching its 100
th mission in space with the successful launch of 
the Radar Imaging Satellite -1, French Remote Sensing Satellite SPOT-6, and the 
Japanese satellite PROITERES through Pola r Satellite launch Vehicles -C21 from 
Sriharikota. A number of satellites launche d in 2012-13 have significantly enhanced our 
capabilities for space applications.    
3. OBJECTIVES OF INDIAN SPACE PROGRAMME 
The primary objective of the Indian Space Programme is to promote the 
development and application of space technology and space science for the socio-
economic benefits of the nation through estab lishment of operational space services in a 
self-reliant manner. The main thrust areas of the programme are: 
 Satellite-based communication and navigation for various applications. 
 Satellite-based resources survey and management and environmental 
monitoring. 
 Meteorological applications. 
 Space Science Research and Planetary Exploration, and 
 Development and operationalisation of indigenously built satellites, launch 
vehicles  
and associated ground segment for providing these space-based services. 
4. ORGANISATIONAL SETUP 
4.1 The DoS is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space 
Commission.  The space programme is execu ted through ISRO and Grant-in-aid 
institutions.  ISRO is the research wing of  the DoS and is responsible for executing the 
Research & Development (R&D) programme s and schemes of the Department in 

accordance with the directives  and policies that are laid  down by the Space Commission 
and the DoS. 
4.2 The DoS Secretariat and the Headquarter s of ISRO are located in Bengaluru, 
Karnataka. The Programme offices at IS RO Headquarters co-ordinate the overall 
programmes including satellite communication,  satellite navigation, earth observation, 
launch vehicle, space science, atmospheric science, space industry development, disaster 
management support, international co-operation, publications and public relations, budget 
and economic analyses and human resource development.  
4.3 The major centres, units and establishments of DoS/ISRO, responsible for 
carrying out R&D activities as well as for unde rtaking various projects and programmes, 
are as under:- 
i) Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre (VSSC ), Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala 
provides the technology base for the country’s indigenous launch vehicle 
(rocket) development; 
ii) Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre (LPSC), with its facilities at 
Bengaluru, Thiruvananthapuram and Ma hendragiri in Tamil Nadu is 
responsible for development of liqui d propulsion and cryogenic propulsion 
systems for satellite launch vehicles; 
iii) Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC-SHAR) at Sriharikota, Andhra 
Pradesh, is the launch base and also provi des the facilities for processing of 
solid rocket motors; 
iv) ISRO Satellite Centre (ISAC), Bengalu ru, Karnataka is entrusted with the 
prime responsibility of the satellite development;      
v) Laboratory for Electro-Optics System s (LEOS), Bengaluru, Karnataka is 
responsible for  development and produc tion of electro optical sensors for 
satellites; 
vi) Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad, Gujarat carries out R&D 
in space applications as well as development of application payloads; 
vii) Development and Educationa l Communication Unit (DECU), 
Ahmedabad, Gujarat is involved in th e conception, definition, planning and 
socio/techno-economic evaluation of developmental space applications; 
viii) National Remote Sensing Centre (N RSC), Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh 
is responsible for satellite data acquisition and processing, data dissemination, 
aerial remote sensing and decision support for disaster management;  
ix) Indian Institute of Remote Sens ing (IIRS), Dehradun, Uttrakhand is a 
premier training and educational institute set up for honing skills of trained 
professional in the field of Remote  Sensing, Geoinformatics and Global 
Positioning System (GPS) Technology for Natural Resources, Environmental 
and Disaster Management; 
x) ISRO Telemetry, Tracking & Command Network (ISTRAC), with its 
ground stations at Bengaluru, Srihari kota, Lucknow, Bearslake(USA), Biak 
(Indonesia), Brunei and Mauritius provide s the telemetry, track and command 
support and spacecraft mission management for Indian remote sensing 
satellite missions, space science mi ssions and satellite launch vehicle 
programmes; 
xi) Master Control Facility (MCF) with its main facility at Hassan, Karnataka 
and backup facility at Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh have the responsibility for 
control and operation of INSAT/GSAT/METSAT satellites; and 

xii) ISRO Inertial Systems Unit (IISU), Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala carries 
out research and development in the area of inertial systems for satellites and 
launch vehicles. 
4.4 A National Natural Resour ces Management System (NNRMS), with DoS as the 
nodal agency, has been establis hed to ensure optimal manage ment/utilisation of natural 
resources using remote sensing data in c onjunction with conventional techniques. Under 
NNRMS, five Regional Remote Sensing Se rvice Centres (RRSSCs) at Bengaluru, 
Dehradun, Jodhpur, Kharagpur and Nagpur have also been set up for the execution of 
remote sensing application programmes in the respective regions. With effect from 
December 2009, four out of five RRSSCs have  been re-designated as Regional Remote 
Sensing Centres (RRSCs), while RRSSC, De hradun has been merged with Indian 
Institute of Remote Sensing (IIRS).     
4.5 Apart from above-mentioned units/in stitutes the DoS has the following 
organisations as well which receive Grants-in-aid from the Department: 
i) Physical Research Laboratory (P RL), Ahmedabad, an autonomous 
institution supported mainly by the Depart ment of Space, carries out research 
in space sciences; 
ii) The National Atmospheric Research  Laboratory (NARL), set up at 
Gadanki near Tirupati, conducts atmospheric research; 
iii) The North-Eastern Space Applications Centre (NE-SAC), established as an 
autonomous body under the Department of Space, provides space technology 
inputs for developmental activities in the North-Eastern Region; 
iv) The Semi-conductor Laboratory, Chandi garh, an  R&D society, is 
entrusted with the design and developm ent of Very Large Scale Integrated 
Circuit (VLSI) devices and development of micro-electronic systems to meet 
the strategic needs of the country; and 
v) The Indian Institute of Space Sc ience and Technology (IIST), an 
autonomous body under the Department, aims at creating quality human 
resources tuned to suit the requiremen ts of state-of-a rt space research 
programme.  The Institute offers graduate, post-graduate and doctoral 
programmes in the area of space sc ience, technology and applications. 
Initially, IIST started the courses from the academic year 2007-08 with the 
existing infrastructure at Thiruvananthapuram.   
 
4.6 The ANTRIX Corporation Limited, Bengalu ru, established in September, 1992, a 
private Limited Company under the administrativ e control of DoS, is a marketing arm of 
ISRO for promotion and commercial ex ploitation of Space products, technical 
consultancy services and transfer of technol ogies developed by ISRO. It also facilitates 
development of Space related capabilities in India. 
4.7 Over and above the aforementioned, th e RESPOND programme of ISRO supports 
sponsored research activities in space science, space applications and space technology in 
several national academic/research instituti ons and Space Technology Cells in premier 
technological institutes of the country through grants-in-aid.  
4.8 The detailed budget allocation of the DoS for the year 2013-2014 was considered 
by the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science & Technology, 
Environment & Forests in its meeting held on the April 16, 2013. 

5. THRUST AREAS IN THE TW ELFTH FIVE YEAR PLAN  
5.1 The major thrust of Indian Space progr amme during the XII Five Year Plan 2012-
17 will be on augmentation INSAT/GSAT cap acity to meet demand for transponders, 
establishment of the Indian Regional Naviga tional Satellite System over Indian region, 
continuation of established services with impr oved capabilities with thematic series of 
Indian Earth Orbiting satellites, expansion of satellite based applications including 
societal applications, strengt hening of Polar satellite La unch Vehicle (PSLV) and Geo-
synchronous Launch Vehicle (GSLV) as th e workhorse vehicle, Realisation of 
developmental flights of next generati on launch vehicle (GSLV MK III) capable of 
launching 4 Tonne class INSAT satellites; pur suance of semi-cryo engine development, 
undertaking space science and planetary explorat ion; strengthening space-based Disaster 
Management Support and developing critical  technologies for the human spaceflight 
programme.   
5.2 In the area of Satellite Communicati ons, it has been planned to augment the 
INSAT capacity  to br idge the gap between the demand and supply of the transponders 
for meeting all the requirements of the count ry and also to maintain sufficient spare 
capacity to meet contingencies. Development of  state-of-the-art tec hnologies and latest 
applications areas is also to be pursued.   
5.3 The continuing programmes during the XII Five Year Plan include PSLV 
Continuation, GSLV Operati onal, GSLV Mk III Developm ent, Cryogenic Upper Stage 
Project, Semi-Cryogenic Engine Developmen t, Space Capsule Recovery Experiment-II, 
Satellite with Argos and Altika (SARAL), Indian Regional Navigational Satellite System, 
INSAT/GSAT satellites, Adva nced Communication Satellite  (GSAT-11), Geo-Imaging 
Satellite (GISAT), Chandrayaan-2, Astr osat, Aditya, Development of Critical 
Technologies for Human Spaceflight and vari ous Space Applications such as National 
Natural Resources Management System, Di saster Management Support, Atmospheric 
Research and Initiatives on Climate Change & Environment Studies.  The Committee has 
also been informed that during the XI Plan  period 29 missions (16 Satellite missions and 
13 Launch Vehicle Missions) were accomplis hed and during the XII Plan period, 58 
space missions are planned to be realised including 33 satellite missions and 25 Launch 
Vehicle missions.  
5.4 The Committee is happy to note that during the XII Five Year Plan period 
2012-17, the main driving force of the I ndian Space programme will be to carry 
forward and further strengthen space base d services aimed at socio-economic 
development of the country.  The Committee  hopes that as a part of the ongoing 
space programmes and efforts to develop advanced launch vehicles, the Department 
would also strive for mastering critical t echnologies so as to reduce the chances of 
failures of important missions.  
5.5 The Committee notes with happiness that  satellite launching target set for 
the XII Five Year Plan is 58, just double the XI Five Year Plan of  29.  Increased 
number of satellites would further stren gthen our capabilities in using space 
technology for benefit of our people and country.     
6. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION FO R THE XII FIVE YEAR PLAN  
6.1 As regards budgetary allocations in the XII Plan, the Committee was informed 
that the Department had proposed a Plan outlay of 47,500 Crores against which an 
indicative outlay of 39,750 Crores has been approved.  The proposed Plan demand has 
thus been reduced by 8, 750 Crores.  The Non-Plan budgetary support during the XII 
Five Year Plan is expected to be 7500.00 Crores approximately.

6.2 The Committee is happy to note that Planning Commission has accepted in

hopes that the Department would make opti mum utilisation of approved outlays for
